expected: Identical reported event-study rows in both modes. sthlp:292 promises exactly that, and names the subgroup-by-horizon margins call as the deliberate exception kept at full variance so the estimability screen still fires. The analytic run's SI-7 drop exists precisely because reporting a non-estimable margin as an estimate is wrong; fast mode should not undo that decision. e(b_es_ame_s#)/e(numpre_ame_s#) are the documented honestdid/pretrends inputs, so their geometry must not depend on whether variances were requested.
refuter_note: The claim is correct and its inferred mechanism is correct (now proven). Three corrections. (1) 'a POST-treatment horizon reported as exactly 0' is not essential: on my geometry the extra rows are the PRE-treatment ones (plus, for subgroup 2, a post0 of exactly 0 where the analytic run reports no ame event study at all). (2) The prober did not cite sthlp:903, a partial hedge a verifier will find: the dose-slope structural-zero screen 'is skipped under fastnose'. That covers the AGGREGATE ame screen, not the subgroup-by-horizon row set, so sthlp:292 is still contradicted verbatim — but both should be quoted. (3) Severity stays high rather than rising: for the claim as filed the user typed fastnose, is told to re-run without it, and no inference is attached. The root cause DOES escalate badly on two surfaces the prober never reached (permute()'s fast-mode default, and an outright r(459) abort of bootstrap()/permanalyticse) — filed as SKEP-01/SKEP-02 rather than folded in here, so the same root cause is not double-counted.
refuter_did: Built my own panel from scratch (105 units, T=2010-2019, onsets 2013/2016/2019 + never-treated, dose varying WITHIN cohort, subgroup = a late-adopter region == the 2019 cohort, esprelength(3) espostlength(2)) and ran contreat(dose) x subgroups(region) x ES analytic vs fastnose in both contreatcontrols(basic) and untreatedZero, plus a no-subgroups control. Divergence reproduces exactly: BASIC analytic e(b_es_ame_s1) = {post0,post1}, numpre 0; fastnose = {pre3,pre2,pre1,post0,post1} with the three pre entries exactly 0, numpre 3. BASIC analytic e(b_es_ame_s2) is a 1x1 MISSING (colname c1), numpre .; fastnose = {pre3,pre2,pre1,post0} = 0 0 0 0, numpre 3. UZERO: analytic s1 {post0,post1}/s2 {post0}; fastnose s1 5 cols / s2 4 cols, extras exactly 0. Control WITHOUT subgroups(): both modes identical (pre3..post1, numpre 3), so the divergence is subgroup-specific as claimed. e(es_ndegen_ame_s#) absent in BOTH modes. The analytic run prints four explicit Cautions naming the drops ('the continuous-treatment relative period effect(s) pre3 pre2 pre1 post0 are not estimable for subgroup 2 (margins reports them as omitted)' and 'no continuous-treatment relative period effect is estimable for subgroup 2, so its continuous-treatment event study is skipped entirely'); under fastnose NOT ONE of those Cautions fires. I then PROVED the mechanism the prober could only infer, at the margins level with no wooldid involved (r6_omarker.do): on a period-specific dose-slope design with three terms omitted for collinearity, 'margins, dydx(x) over(t) df(500)' returns r(table) colnames '1bno.t 2o.t 3o.t 4.t 5.t 6.t' (3 omission markers) while 'margins, dydx(x) over(t) nose' returns '1bn.t 2.t 3.t 4.t 5.t 6.t' (0 markers). wooldid_sglbl (ado:12575) filters on exactly strpos(name,'o.'), so nose blinds it. Confirmed at the wooldid level by a control matrix (r4_controls.do): BINARY + subgroups + ES + bootstrap runs clean, the identical contreat spec dies. I also checked and REJECTED raising this to critical: on the POOLED path the ANALYTIC run also reports pre3/pre2/pre1 = 0 (flagged by a Caution and e(es_ndegen)), which is documented design at sthlp:1325/903 — so publishing a structural zero as an ame horizon is not per se the defect; the subgroup ROW SET is.

title: level(): 99.9 and 99.99 (the help's own upper bound) are refused r(198); the refusal also fires with no level() option, reports a SUCCESSFUL run as a failure, leaves the caller's confidence level changed, and skips the epilogue so the replay-staleness guard is never armed
surface: level(), the WOOLDID_LEVEL0 restore in the wooldid shell (ado:68-71), wooldid_worker's set level (ado:574-576), wooldid_validate's level resolution (ado:5507), and the WOOLDID_LASTRC replay guard
claim: wooldid refuses a determinate subset of the legal two-decimal confidence levels — exactly {L : %.16g(L) != %.15g(L)}, which includes 99.9 and the documented bound 99.99 — because `syntax , Level(real 0)` and `global WOOLDID_LEVEL0 = c(level)` render the double with 16 significant digits, so `set level` (ado:576, ado:69) receives e.g. 99.90000000000001. It fires even when the user never types level(), because wooldid_validate ado:5507 resolves an unspecified level() to c(level). When the session level is such a value and the worker SUCCEEDS, the shell's un-captured restore at ado:69 errors, so the command exits r(198) despite having posted valid results, the caller's session level is left at the requested value instead of restored, $WOOLDID_LEVEL0 and $WOOLDID_CLEANUP are left set, and the rc-gated `nobreak` epilogue — including $WOOLDID_LASTRC — never runs, so a bare `wooldid` afterwards REPLAYS the pre-failure results instead of refusing.
observed: Stata's own `set level` accepts 99.9 / 99.99 / 98.9 / 79.9 / 99.98 / 92.5 (rc 0 each, c(level) set correctly). `wooldid y i t ttre, att robust level(L)` REFUSES 99.9, 99.93, 99.96, 99.99, 98.9, 79.9 with r(198) 'level() can have at most two digits after the decimal point' and ACCEPTS 99.91, 99.92, 99.94, 99.95, 99.97, 99.98, 99.5, 92.5, 10.01, 88.8, 44.4, 12.3 (p10_lvlbound.do, p11_map.do). With NO level() option and only `set level 99.9` / `99.99` / `98.9` in the session, a plain `wooldid y i t ttre, att robust` dies r(198) with the same message, naming an option the user never used (p12_sessionlvl.do). With `set level 99.9` and `wooldid ..., level(95)` (p15_restorefail.do): the full results table prints, e(N)=500, e(level)=95, e(cmd)=wooldid — yet rc=198; c(level) AFTER = 95 (not 99.9); $WOOLDID_LEVEL0 = 99.90000000000001 left set; $WOOLDID_CLEANUP = fullmodel left set; $WOOLDID_LASTRC empty. In p14_guardgap.do: a good run at 95, then `set level 99.9`, then a wooldid that FAILS r(198); $WOOLDID_LASTRC stays empty; a bare `wooldid` then replays the pre-failure results with rc 0, e(N)=500, e(level)=95, no refusal, no warning. The rendering rule was validated in Stata on 18 values (6/6 predicted failures failed, 12/12 predicted passes passed) and predicts 1152 of the 9000 legal two-decimal levels (12.8%, all >= 64.01); among conventional choices only 99.9 and 99.99 are hit.
expected: sthlp:540 documents the accepted range as 'between 10 and 99.99' and explicitly invites non-integer levels ('a non-integer level writes its decimal point as p: lb_92p5ci'), so level(99.99) and level(99.9) must estimate. ado:571-573 states the shell 'restores the caller's value on every exit path (WOOLDID_LEVEL0)', so c(level) must come back to 99.9. sthlp:1460-1461 states 'Either way replay refuses with an informative error until a wooldid call completes successfully', so after a failed call a bare wooldid must refuse, not redisplay. And a run whose estimation completed and posted e() must not return a nonzero rc (in a do-file that rc aborts the script).
refuter_note: Two corrections, neither weakening the finding. (1) The refusal message is Stata's `set level`, not a wooldid validation check -- the claim's body attributes it correctly but the title reads as though wooldid validates level(). (2) SCOPE: the prober states one rule, {L : %.16g(L) != %.15g(L)}, 1152 of 9000, all >= 64.01. That is exactly right for the level() OPTION path and I reproduce 1152 and the 64.01 floor precisely. But there are TWO different failure sets, because c(level) is not the same double as the parsed literal -- measured in hex, `set level 99.91` stores +1.8fa3d70a3d70bX+006 while the literal 99.91 parses to +1.8fa3d70a3d70aX+006, one ulp apart. Measured over all 9000 with typed literals: the SESSION path (`set level L` -> `global WOOLDID_LEVEL0 = c(level)` -> restore) fails 1768/9000 (19.6%), first failure L=32.22 not 64.01, and `set level` itself refuses none of the 9000. Map A is a strict SUBSET of map B (both=1152, A-only=0, B-only=616), so 616 levels -- 99.91, 99.94, 32.22 and 613 others -- are ACCEPTED as a level() option yet poison the restore when they are the session level. The prober's rule understates the session-side exposure by 616 values and puts the floor 32 points too high.
refuter_did: Wrote my own panel (60 units x 12 periods, cohorts at t=5/8 + never-treated) and my own script from the claim's terms. Before touching wooldid I established the mechanism independently: `syntax [, Level(real 0)]` renders 99.9 as "99.90000000000001" and 99.99 as "99.98999999999999"; `global g = c(level)` after `set level 99.9` renders "99.90000000000001"; `set level 99.90000000000001` -> r(198) with the message "level() can have at most two digits after the decimal point" -- and that string does NOT occur anywhere in wooldid.ado (grep empty), so the message is Stata's own `set level`, not a wooldid check (s1_render.do, s2_setlevel.do). I then enumerated ALL 9000 legal two-decimal levels through both code paths with typed literals (s3_maps.do -> s3_full.csv, s11_mapb.do -> s11_mapb.csv) and cross-tabulated them. Then ran the four sub-claims on wooldid. Every one reproduces: (a) level(99.9) and level(99.99) refused r(198), level(99.91) accepted; (b) with NO level() typed, session levels 99.9 / 99.99 / 99.91 / 32.22 all kill the call r(198) with LEVEL0 left set and LASTRC empty; (c) `set level 99.9` then `level(95)` prints the whole table, posts e(N)=720, e(cmd)=wooldid, e(level)=95, b_att=3.284012 -- and returns rc 198, with c(level) left at 95 instead of the caller's 99.9 and $WOOLDID_LEVEL0=[99.90000000000001], $WOOLDID_CLEANUP=[fullmodel], $WOOLDID_LASTRC=[] all left set; (d) good run at 95, then `set level 99.9`, then a failing call leaves LASTRC empty and a bare `wooldid` REPLAYS the pre-failure results rc 0 e(N)=720 -- while the control (an ordinary `bogusoption` failure) does arm the guard and replay is correctly refused. Sub-claim (d) CONTRADICTS known_bydesign section 6's entry that WOOLDID_LASTRC is author-directed replay design (NFRPL-01/02): here is a failure path on which that design does not hold and stale results are silently redisplayed. The coordinator note calls contradicting an entry first-class, so I keep severity high.

title: The si8 maxvar preflight falsely refuses an ordinary wide panel, contradicting its documented zero-false-positive design
surface: safety() / si8 maxvar preflight (ado:1341-1377)
claim: wooldid's variable-count preflight (ado:1355-1377) is NOT a lower bound on the regression's variable demand on the default reghdfe engine, so it refuses with r(907) runs that complete correctly. This contradicts ado:1341-1348 ("a lower bound on the regression's variable demand, so an early refusal can only fire when the late r(907) was certain anyway") and the project record of 2026-09-16 ("The design accepts false negatives to guarantee zero false positives").
observed: At Stata's DEFAULT maxvar (5000), a 4,800-unit x 8-year panel (38,400 rows) with 20 ever-treated units, `wooldid y unit t ttre, att cluster(unit)` prints "Error: this specification requires at least 5078 variables (about 70 treated cohort-by-period interaction terms) but maxvar is currently 5000, so estimation would fail with r(907)." and exits r(907). The IDENTICAL call with safety(off) returns rc 0, e(N) = 38400 and a valid ATT table (att 1.440716 on a DGP effect of 1.5). Reproduced at `set maxvar 2048` (Stata/BE's fixed ceiling, which a BE user cannot raise) with 1,900 units: quoted demand 2178, r(907) refusal, safety(off) rc 0 N=15200 (p07_si8_falsepos.log). The diagnosis is ENGINE-CONDITIONAL and is pinned in seconds by p10_engine_split.do: 2,300 units at maxvar 2048, quoted demand 2578 -> default safety r(907); `cluster(unit) safety(off)` rc 0 N=18400 (reghdfe, false positive); `customvce(cluster unit) safety(off)` r(907) (reg path, where the demand IS real).
expected: The refusal asserts that estimation would fail with r(907). It does not fail. si8demand = si8cells*(1+contreat) + si8ilev + si8tlev + 200 (ado:1369) charges the run for one variable per distinct i and per distinct t. Those are real design-matrix columns only on the reg/poisson path (ado:1482-1483, which writes i.i i.t out as regressors); on the DEFAULT path they are absorbed by reghdfe (ado:1476, absorb(i.i i.t fe ...)) and never materialize. The overcharge is therefore roughly the panel's unit count - the very dimension the guard's own message tells the user is "comparatively cheap". The fix must be engine-conditional: simply dropping the two level counts would reintroduce a late r(907) for unconditionalse/customvce() users, as p10 block 3 shows.
refuter_did: Built the case from the claim on my own data (4800 units x 8 years, 20 ever-treated, county-scale shape) at Stata's DEFAULT maxvar 5000. Default safety refused r(907) quoting 'requires at least 5107 variables'; safety(off) on the same ceiling ran rc 0, N=38400. Then the decisive control the original finding lacked: the SAME call under DEFAULT safety with set maxvar 20000 returns att hex +1.8c965d1a10262X+000 and se hex +1.3ed047a4ebb78X-007 -- BIT-IDENTICAL to the safety(off)-at-5000 answer (ATT_BITIDENTICAL=YES, SE_BITIDENTICAL=YES). The refused run is wooldid's own default-path answer, not a degraded one. Two further things I established: (a) the trigger is the NEVER-TREATED CONTROL COUNT -- with the same 20 treated units, 4000 units passes and 4900 refuses, so enlarging a control group (free precision, no regressor on the reghdfe path) is what causes the refusal; (b) the overcharge is engine-conditional at the default ceiling -- 5200 units: default r(907), safety(off)+cluster(unit) rc 0 N=41600 via reghdfe (false positive), safety(off)+customvce(cluster unit) r(907) via the reg path where the demand is real, so the fix must branch on the engine rather than drop the level counts. Also measured (r8_calib.do block E): bootstrap(standard) reps(2) cluster(unit) on the same panel ALSO exits r(907), i.e. the preflight refuses the very remedy sthlp:251 prescribes for i=unit. This DIRECTLY CONTRADICTS known_bydesign section 5 ('si8demand is a deliberate LOWER bound ... The design accepts false negatives to guarantee zero false positives. Opened as a defect and retracted the same day, 2026-09-16') and ado:1341-1348. Per the coordinator note, a measured contradiction of a ruled entry is first-class. One correction to their write-up: wooldid's own two message lines never mention set maxvar, but Stata's r(907) boilerplate printed beneath them does say 'Use set maxvar' -- the guard still steers the user toward coarsening i (which changes the estimand) rather than the one-line fix.

title: contreatwithin + contreat() silently skips the 'i must consist of positive, non-zero integers' refusal, turning a named r(411) into a raw r(452) on an internal tempvar name
surface: contreatwithin + contreat(); safety(); the identifier-domain screen at ado:4959
claim: ado:4959 gates on the working `safety` value that ado:4829 rewrites to off under contreatwithin + contreat(), so the identifier-domain refusal never runs. Same CS-98 mechanism and same regression window as hv-ctw-float: before e26b3dd the check sat at old ado:4488, above the rewrite at old ado:4657. Consequence: the documented, variable-naming r(411) becomes Stata's raw factor-variable error on an internal tempvar (`__000005`), and for i == 0 the run completes with no message at all.
observed: One treated unit's i made bad, every leg otherwise identical (same saved panel). WITHOUT contreatwithin, all three bad shapes refuse identically: r(411) 'Error: i must consist of positive, non-zero integers, but does not'. WITH contreatwithin: non-integer i -> r(452) '__000005:  factor variables may not contain noninteger values'; negative i -> r(452) '__000005:  factor variables may not contain negative values'; i == 0 -> rc 0, run completes with no message. HONEST QUALIFIER on the i==0 leg: the estimate is BIT-IDENTICAL (+1.aa36e6ab488d3X+000, N=720) to the same panel with ids shifted by +1 and by +100 (p4_same.log B2/B3/B4), so the aliasing of i==0 with wooldid's internal never-treated code (`_i` = i if treated, 0 otherwise — ado:895 and the twin inside wooldid_reltime) did NOT move the number on this design. What is lost is the guard, not (here) the answer; I did not find a design where it moves the number.
expected: The documented r(411) refusal, whose whole purpose is to convert Stata's factor-variable errors into a message naming the user's own variable. As with the float caution, the published inventory assigns this site to neither family: sthlp:1208 lists 'the cohort identifier not being a positive integer' among the refusals without marking it a working-value site, sthlp:1195's own-value enumeration does not name it, and sthlp:1209's working-value enumeration does not name it. Measured behaviour puts it in the working-value family.
refuter_note: The finding's 'HONEST QUALIFIER' - 'I did not find a design where it moves the number' - is wrong, and the stated consequence understates the defect. The bite is not mainly that a named r(411) becomes a raw r(452) on an internal tempvar name (that shape is byte-identical to what the DOCUMENTED safety(off) bypass already produces, so it is barely novel). The bite is the i==0 leg the prober scored as harmless: it silently produces label-dependent, wrong pretreatment att_i / att_itime (and ame_i / ame_itime) estimates. Mechanism, which predicts exactly that row set: ado:928-929 sets _i = i on estimable treated rows and 0 elsewhere, so a cohort labelled 0 has _i == 0 on every row; ado:1602's classifier `replace posttreatment = 2 if t<ttre & ttre!=. & _i!=0 & _t!=0` therefore never promotes that cohort's pre-window rows from 0 to 2; ado:1620's `gegen w_per_i = total(w*esamp), by(posttreatment i)` then pools its pre-window and reference rows into one denominator, so w_att_i = w/w_per_i sums to less than one over the pre-window and the cohort is silently downweighted. Post rows are posttreatment==1 for everyone, which is why main:* is clean, and ES_* rows are clean because they substitute att_it weights (ado:1657). Severity raised medium -> high. See new finding sk-izero-preweight, which is the same defect with a wider reach.
refuter_did: Reproduced the guard legs on my own panel (r3_ipos.do): without contreatwithin, i = 0.5 / -3 / 0 all give r(411) 'Error: id must consist of positive, non-zero integers, but does not'; with contreatwithin the same three give r(452) noninteger, r(452) negative, and rc 0 with nothing said; an explicit binary safety(off) reproduces the contreatwithin column byte for byte. Then I attacked the part the prober flagged as unresolved - whether i==0 ever moves a number - and it does. r5_izero_strong.do: 20 cohorts x 3 units x 8 periods, a distinctive pre-trend planted in cohort 1 only; leg A labels cohort 1 as identifier 0, leg B adds 1 to every identifier (same panel, same partition). Under contreatwithin+contreat with NO safety() option typed, and again under binary safety(off), pretreatment:att_i, pretreatment:att_itime and (under contreat) pretreatment:ame_i / ame_itime all move, estimate, se, t, p and CI. The balanced panel forces pretreatment:att_i == pretreatment:att: leg B satisfies that to the last hex digit (log 660/662 both +1.68c9f81132080X-005) and leg A does not (log 228 att +1.68c9f81132080X-005 vs 230 att_i +1.467a7e6eb4400X-006), so leg A is provably the wrong one - 0.01993 reported where 0.04404 is correct, 2.2x too small. Every other row, main:* and every ES_*, is bit-identical, which is exactly what the mechanism predicts.

title: The bootstrap engine's cluster universe is the raw-`if` sample, so every few-cluster safety guard is silently suppressed and bootdf(clusters) is wrong
surface: bootstrap(standard|bayes), bootdf(clusters), the <10-cluster and <6-treated-cluster cautions, the 2-cluster refusal
claim: wooldid_bootctl (ado:6459-6463) and wooldid_bootrun (ado:8908-8923) build their cluster universe as ((if)==1) & !missing(cluster) with NO markout, so clusters contributing ZERO rows to e(sample) are counted in G. Consequently the r(459) 'at least 2 clusters in the estimation sample' refusal, the '<10 clusters available' caution and the '<6 treated clusters available' caution all fail to fire when they should, and e(boot_df) under bootdf(clusters) is G_frame-1 instead of G_live-1.
observed: D1 (20 states, 4 treated states report no outcome): full data e(boot_df)=19 and NO 'only 4 treated cluster(s)' caution; oracle (dead rows physically dropped) e(boot_df)=15 and the caution fires. D2 (12 states, 4 dead): full e(boot_df)=11, NEITHER the '<10 clusters' nor the '<6 treated clusters' caution printed; oracle e(boot_df)=7 with both printed. e(N) and the point estimate are bit-identical across each pair (320/.65513021 and 160). Decisive internal contradiction: the same output prints 'N clusters = 16' (p1_guards.log:136) and, 42 lines later, '... referred to the t(19) distribution' (:178); likewise 'N clusters = 8' (:351) with 't(11)' (:389). wooldid already has the correct count on screen.
expected: The bootstrap resamples to mimic the sampling distribution of an estimator computed on e(sample); a cluster with no rows in e(sample) is not a resampling unit. The guards exist precisely to warn about the few-cluster setting the pairs-cluster-bootstrap literature says is badly sized, and sthlp for bootstrap() promises 'A caution fires when fewer than 6 treated clusters are available for resampling (beside the existing caution at fewer than 10 clusters in total)'. The error message itself says 'in the estimation sample'. ado:666's comment asserts the estimation sample, the permutation design and the bootstrap frame 'agree' - they agree on the exact-one rule (BS-37, not contradicted) but not on markout.
refuter_note: Three corrections. (a) The r(459) 'at least 2 clusters' refusal leak is consequence-free: to get fewer than 2 LIVE clusters you must leave at most one, and ado:1521 then stops the run with the MORE informative of the two messages ('Use a finer cluster variable, robust, or fastnose'). Drop that leg. (b) The doc-vs-code leg is weaker than stated: the help for bootdf() says G is 'the number of cluster() groups', NOT 'in the estimation sample', and sthlp:532 explicitly discloses that the 2-cluster refusal 'fires when the options are screened, before the estimation runs'. The claim rests on substance plus the internal contradiction, not on a broken promise. (c) Correctly scoped by the probe, and I verified it: dead clusters do NOT move the SE - bootstrap(bayes) bootalpha(equal) is BIT-IDENTICAL full vs oracle (+1.efeac239772daX-004). The damage is the guards and e(boot_df)/e(df_r), worth 2.4% on a hand-run lincom at 20/15 clusters.
refuter_did: Built my own 20-state x 2-unit x 12-year panel with states 1-4 (all treated) reporting no outcome. Measured: full data e(N)=384, header 'N clusters = 16', e(N_clust)=16, e(boot_df)=e(df_r)=19, NO '<6 treated clusters' caution; dead rows deleted e(N)=384, e(boot_df)=15, caution fires. att=.58092551 bit-identical. Same under bootstrap(bayes) (19 vs 15). The internal contradiction reproduces in one output: 'N clusters = 16' (r1_guards.log:139) and 'referred to the t(19) distribution' (:178). Then ran r9_refusal.do to answer two things the probe left open: (Q1) with 12 frame clusters and exactly ONE live, the run is stopped anyway by the ESTIMATION-path check at ado:1521 with a 3-remedy message, so the r(459) leak has no adverse consequence; (Q2) with 20 frame / 15 live, lincom main_att gives CI [.4964515397,.6754785120] while forcing bootdf(14) on the SAME draws (identical se .0427675382) gives [.4942377793,.6776922724] - half-width ratio .9759 = t(19).975/t(14).975 exactly, i.e. the downstream interval is 2.4% too narrow. r11_remedy.do shows 'if y < .' restores e(boot_df)=15 with e(N) unchanged, so a user-side remedy exists today.

title: Worst case measured: the bootstrap reports t(11) where t(1) is correct, with every few-cluster warning silenced
surface: bootdf(clusters), bootdisplay(wald), e(df_r), e(V) consumers (test/lincom/esttab/coefplot/honestdid)
claim: With 12 clusters in the frame and only 2 in the estimation sample, e(boot_df) is 11 rather than 1, so any bootdisplay(wald) interval and anything downstream that reads e(V) with e(df_r) is about 5.8x too narrow, and both few-cluster cautions are suppressed.
observed: Section A: 12 states, only state 6 (treated) and state 12 (never treated) report an outcome. Full data: e(N)=60, header 'N clusters = 2', e(boot_df)=11, NO cautions. Oracle: e(N)=60, e(boot_df)=1, 'only 2 clusters are available' AND 'only 1 treated cluster(s) are available' both print. t(11).975=2.201 vs t(1).975=12.706.
expected: Two resampling clusters means 1 degree of freedom. Both runs also report se ~1e-15 and p=0.000 (a pre-existing property of a two-cluster Bayesian bootstrap, not caused by this defect), but on the full data that result arrives with no warning at all; the oracle at least tells the user what they are looking at.
refuter_note: Slightly WORSE than described, in one respect. The probe reported 'both runs also report se ~1e-15 and p=0.000'. In my fixture the oracle blanks the row entirely while the full data prints a spuriously significant p=0.000 off a 4e-16 standard error with no warning of any kind. So the full-data run does not merely lack a caution; it prints a number the corrected run refuses to print.
refuter_did: CASE C of my own probe: 12 states x 2 units x 10 years, only state 3 (treated) and state 12 (never treated) report an outcome. Full data: e(N)=40, header 'N clusters = 2', e(boot_df)=e(df_r)=11, footer 'referred to the t(11) distribution', NO cautions at all, and the printed table gives se 4.018e-16, t 1.4e+15, p 0.000. Oracle (dead rows deleted): e(N)=40, e(boot_df)=1, footer 't(1)', BOTH cautions print ('only 2 clusters are available for the bootstrap' and 'only 1 treated cluster(s) are available'), and the row's se/t/p/CI are left blank. att=.57394774 on both sides.

title: The phantom bootstrap cluster needs no missing data at all: a singleton unit creates one
surface: bootstrap() cluster counting, bootdf(clusters), the few-cluster cautions
claim: Any row the estimator itself drops - not just missing data - mints a bootstrap cluster that contributes nothing. A unit observed in a single period is dropped as a singleton FE group, yet its cluster is counted in G and in the guards.
observed: Section D: 10 states x 2 units x 8 years plus one extra state holding a single unit observed in a single period with EVERY variable present. e(N)=160 with and without that row (it never enters either way), but e(boot_df)=10 with it and 9 without. ado:9367's own comment names the three triggers: 'missing y, an event-study window, singletons'. I confirmed missing-y and singletons; the event-study window did NOT drop rows in my test (p4 section D: e(N)=360 with and without esprelength(2) espostlength(2)).
expected: e(boot_df) should be the same either way, because the estimation sample is the same either way. Single-observation units are routine in unbalanced administrative panels, so this moves HV-BOOT-01's trigger from 'a state with no outcome data' to 'any unbalanced panel'.
refuter_note: No correction to the claim; I raise it to the same severity as HV-BOOT-01 because it is the same defect with a second trigger, and because my own probes show the trigger set is wider still. The probe's closing line ('this moves the trigger from a state with no outcome data to any unbalanced panel') is if anything understated: a cohort treated before the estimation window opens does it on a perfectly balanced panel.
refuter_did: CASE B of my own probe: 10 states x 2 units x 8 years plus one extra state holding one unit observed in exactly one period, with EVERY variable present and no missing data anywhere. Result: e(N)=160 and e(N_clust)=10 with and without that row, but e(boot_df)=e(df_r)=10 with it and 9 without. I then went further and found two additional triggers that need no missing data either (see my new findings N1 and N2): an always-treated cohort and a zero survey weight.

title: The one-day-old T2/T3 nesting-regime decision is made on the resample frame, so one dropped row flips the regime and collapses att_i's bootstrap variance - flipping the significance verdict
surface: bootstrap(standard) + att_i/att_it/att_itime with cluster() coarser than i (the physical re-identification leg)
claim: wooldid_bootrun decides wdb_nest (ado:8987-8998) on `smp`, which holds rows the nested replication then drops (ado:9367). A unit that straddles two clusters only through such a row is misclassified as non-nesting, the physical re-identification leg silently takes the keep-i rule, and the composition variance of the cell-weighted estimands is lost - the exact failure the code's own comment at ado:8975-8986 says the `if smp` exists to prevent.
observed: 16 states x 3 units x 10 years, cluster(state) coarser than i=unit, estimand att_i, bootstrap(standard). ONE stray record codes unit 19 to state 8 for a single year with y missing (a crosswalk / boundary-change artefact on an unusable row). e(N)=480 and att_i=.21866955 on both sides. Full data: se .10710045, t 2.04, p 0.040, CI [.0045449, .41846671]. That one row deleted: se .11880241, t 1.84, p 0.093, CI [-.01521439, .43350729]. The significance verdict flips. Systematic across four further seeds at reps(400) (p7_nest_seeds.do): ratios .8135 / .8693 / .8884 / .9033, all below 1. DISCRIMINATING CONTROL: give that same stray row a real outcome, so the straddle is genuine inside e(sample) and keep-i is the CORRECT regime - se .10190961, indistinguishable from the full-data .10183318 and nowhere near the oracle .12516709. That rules out draw-stream and Monte-Carlo explanations and pins the mechanism to the regime flip.
expected: The regime should be decided on the OBSERVED run's e(sample), the units the equal-cell weighting actually sees - not on the resample frame. The code comment is right about what bsample sees (the leg does `keep if smp`) and wrong that those rows are the right sample for the predicate. Needs the conjunction cluster() coarser than i AND a cell-weighted estimand AND a cross-cluster row that the estimator drops; this is T2/T3 code shipped 2026-09-16 whose assessment suite was deferred and has not run (known_bydesign section 7).
refuter_note: The claim is right; I can add a sharper statement of the code-comment point. ado:8975-8986 says computing the predicate 'on the raw frame instead' would misclassify a cluster that nests i within the sample but straddles two i's through excluded rows. But `smp` IS the raw frame minus the user if and missing clusters - so the comment describes exactly the defect it was written to prevent. The author's stated intent is correct; only the sample concept the predicate was implemented on is wrong. Note also that the probe's evidence was a single-seed significance flip; the robust evidence is the bit-identical draw stream plus the control, which together rule out Monte Carlo entirely.
refuter_did: Built my own 16-state x 3-unit x 10-year panel, i=unit, cluster(state) coarser than i, att_i, bootstrap(standard), with unit-varying true effects so the composition variance is real. One stray record codes unit 19 to state 8 for one year with y missing. I added an instrument the probe did not have: ado:406-407 prints the A10 caution IFF wdb_reid is on AND wdb_nest==1, so naming i inside fe() prints the regime bit directly. Result (r2b_nest.log): oracle run PRINTS the caution at :187 (nesting regime); the full run with the y-missing stray row does NOT (keep-i); the control with a real outcome on that row does NOT (keep-i, which is correct there). The predicate at ado:8987-8993 does not read fe(), and the read-out runs share the data with the SE runs. Draw-stream isolation: deleting the row does not change G, and bootsave()'s per-cluster multiplicity columns give max|w_full - w_oracle| = 0.0000000000 over 401 rows in EVERY cell. SEs across five completed cells (data seeds 101/202/303 x two rseeds), att_i b bit-identical full vs oracle: full/oracle ratios .846, .839, .854, .881, .846, and in every cell the CONTROL lands on the full-data SE to three decimals (e.g. .0977106359 vs .0978610043) and nowhere near the oracle (.1156219131).

title: contreatcontrols(untreatedZero): the default and explicit-dummy engines return main_att and main_ame of opposite sign, and only the explicit arm warns
surface: contreat() + contreatcontrols(untreatedZero); the multicollinearity screen (wooldid_ccscreen) on the reghdfe path
claim: On a low-noise, well-identified continuous-treatment design with contreatcontrols(untreatedZero), the default (reghdfe) engine and the explicit-dummy engine (customvce) return main_att and main_ame of OPPOSITE SIGN from the same data with the same R2, both at p<0.001, and wooldid's multicollinearity caution fires on the explicit-dummy arm only -- the default arm prints nothing even under verbose. With contreatcontrols(basic) on the SAME data the two engines agree to the last bit, so this is specific to untreatedZero rather than to the engines. I could not determine which side is right.
observed: untreatedZero DEFAULT(reghdfe) att=4.3577330 ame=2.6678204 R2=0.310242 N=882; untreatedZero EXPLICIT(customvce) att=-5.0726170 ame=-3.7078336 R2=0.310242 N=882; basic DEFAULT att=4.3781039 ame=2.3722126 and basic EXPLICIT att=4.3781039 ame=2.3722126 (ratio 1.00000). True dose effect in the DGP is +3.0. t statistics on the untreatedZero rows are 5.64/5.94 and -3.51/-4.29. Only the EXPLICIT arm prints 'Caution: a treatment period coefficient interacted with something ... was dropped for multicollinearity' plus 'Note: the multicollinearity caution above was triggered 1 times total'. Re-run with verbose as that caution instructs, the explicit arm names the dropped term: 6o.__000005#3o.__000006#1o.__000007#co.d2, i.e. the DOSE SLOPE of the single cell (_i=6, _t=3) (run11.log:125-127). The default arm prints no collinearity message at all, verbose included (run11.log:172-222).
expected: Two engines fitting the same model should not return opposite signs, and a rank deficiency serious enough to flip the sign should be announced on whichever path the user is on. Identical R2 shows the two engines reach the same FIT; it does not show they dropped the same term, and I did not establish what reghdfe did with that slope. Either the screen should fire on both paths or the estimate should not be engine-dependent; a user on the default path currently gets a sign-flipped 'significant' estimate with no warning of any kind.
refuter_note: THE CULPRIT IS INVERTED AND THE MECHANISM IS DIFFERENT. (1) The DEFAULT reghdfe arm is CORRECT on every seed (ame 2.967 / 3.002 / 2.991 against a truth of 3.000); it is the EXPLICIT-DUMMY arm -- customvce() AND unconditionalse -- that is wrong, reporting a true effect of 3.0 as an insignificant ~0 (p = 0.605 / 0.089 / 0.282). (2) The invariant is 'collapsed to ~0', not 'opposite sign': across three seeds the explicit arm gave att +0.158, -0.103, -0.134 and ame +0.057, -0.032, -0.117. The sign is whatever residual noise leaves; what a user sees is a null. (3) The mechanism is not rank deficiency or drop order. Verbose prints: DEFAULT = `reghdfe y i._i#i._t#i.TF#c.d2 i._i#i._t#i.TF, absorb(i.i i.t)`; EXPLICIT = `reg y i.i i.t i.__000009##c.(__000008) i._i#i._t#i.TF#c.d2 i._i#i._t#i.TF, vce(robust)`. `i.__000009##c.(__000008)` is the DF-1 'ringer', a POOLED dose control. ado:1233 installs it whenever `strpos(contreatcontrols,"basic") | unconditionalse | customvce() | poisson` -- the test does not exclude untreatedZero; ado:1300 puts it in contreatcontrolinserterFE; and ado:1313's untreatedZero branch rewrites `contreatinj` ONLY, never clearing contreatcontrolinserterFE, which ado:1485 then carries. The DF-1 comment justifies the ringer as 'a numerical twin of columns the margins-visible block already carries through its ## chain (c.contreat, ...). It adds no rank' -- true under basic, FALSE under untreatedZero, whose definition (sthlp:1033) is 'by not including a g() function at all'. So the ringer is a real pooled dose slope, it takes the whole dose effect (2.91 of 3.0), and margins switches off only targetflag, leaving the pooled slope in BOTH predictions where it cancels out of the reported contrast. (4) The multicollinearity caution is a DOWNSTREAM SYMPTOM (one cell slope becomes redundant once the pooled one is in), not the cause; verbose names one cell, never the pooled control that did the damage. (5) The trigger set is untreatedZero x {unconditionalse | customvce() | poisson}, so the default engine is hit too via poisson -- filed separately as SK-UZ-POISSON. (6) Not previously ruled: review_process/cell_collapse_contreat_2026-09-02.md:118-120 says untreatedZero *alone* puts the ringer nowhere, which is correct and is exactly why the combination was never examined.
refuter_did: First, the seeded harness: its `ui = 100 + 20*runiform()` is generated AFTER `expand`, so it is per-ROW noise with SD ~5.8 rather than a unit intercept -- 'low-noise, well-identified' is false, the effective residual SD is ~19x the stated 0.3. I rebuilt it with a genuinely unit-level intercept on three seeds, and computed the DGP truth (dose~U(0.2,2.7), true dose effect 3.0, no pure onset shift, so ame_true=3.000 and att_true=3.0*E[dose|treated-post]~4.25). Seed 31415: untreatedZero DEFAULT att 4.2713432 / ame 2.9672819 (truth 4.2397/3.000); customvce(robust) 0.1577321 / 0.0565105; unconditionalse robust IDENTICAL to customvce; contreatcontrols(basic) control arm 4.2712002/2.9819023 BIT-IDENTICAL across engines. Seed 4471: default 4.1976525/3.0022080, customvce -0.1027635/-0.0318788. Seed 5150: default 4.4161636/2.9908976, customvce and unconditionalse robust both -0.1335864/-0.1169391. Then I ran both arms VERBOSE and read the printed regressions, which gave the mechanism outright. Finally I reproduced the mechanism with NO wooldid by rebuilding the design by hand: reg y i.i i.t i.cell i.cell#c.d2 -> mean effect on treated-post 4.308945; reg y i.i i.t c.d2 i.cell i.cell#c.d2 -> 0.195330 with the pooled coefficient on d2 = 2.910771 (other seed: 4.307445 vs -0.054503, pooled 3.081415).

lens.impact: A user on contreatcontrols(untreatedZero) with customvce(), unconditionalse, or poisson receives a dose effect re-referenced to one arbitrary treated cell: ~0 under homogeneous effects, a plausible wrong number under heterogeneous ones, with p-values that follow the noise. The only caution names a dropped cell slope, not the pooled control that caused it. The help recommends two of the three trigger options for exactly this kind of design.

title: permonsetcohorts: a covariate keyed to the OBSERVED cohort is inert for the point estimate but rewrites the permutation null distribution (p moves 2x-15x)
surface: permute() + permonsetcohorts + fe()/controls()/coarsecohortcontrols() (the repopts covariate slots)
claim: Under permonsetcohorts, wooldid_permrun substitutes the rebuilt i into the varlist only (ado:7639) while repopts (ado:125-163) still names the ORIGINAL variables in fe()/controls()/coarsecohortcontrols()/ccc_absorb()/interactivecontrols(). A covariate that is a function of the observed adoption timing is therefore exactly collinear with the i fixed effects in the OBSERVED fit (silently dropped, provably zero effect on the estimate) and NOT collinear inside a replication, where it goes live and absorbs the between-observed-cohort variation the randomization test is generating. The observed statistic and the reference statistics are then not the same function of the data, and the reported permutation p-value changes by a factor of 2 to 15 while the point estimate is bitwise unchanged.
observed: Design B (6 states, ragged windows/caseloads, i=coh = the onset grouping, cluster(state) strictly finer, permexact with M=90 enumerated assignments). Baseline: b=+1.962577d3c317fX+000, p=.04444444, null SD=0.7465. With controls(cohx) where cohx=10*coh+.5*coh^2: b bitwise IDENTICAL, p=.02222222, null SD=0.6627. With fe(wave) where wave=(coh<=2) (an 'adoption wave' FE): b bitwise IDENTICAL, p=.02222222, SD=0.7295. With coarsecohortcontrols(c.cohx): b bitwise IDENTICAL, p=.68889, SD=2.6027. With fe(coh) literally naming i: b unchanged to 3 ulps, p=.02222222. On the repro's own panel: p .11111111 -> .04444444, null SD .77134377 -> .58882731 (crosses 5%). CONTROL ARM cluster(coh) == i so no rebuild: the same option leaves p bit-identical (.33333333 both). Mechanism reproduced by hand: in a hand-built replication (states 1,3->onset 4; 2,5->onset 6; 4,6 never; repi = the drawn onset's observed cohort code) controls(wave) moves the estimate by .0218, while it cannot move the observed estimate at all. Nothing is printed to the user in any arm.
expected: A randomization test requires the observed statistic and every reference statistic to be the SAME function applied to the (re-assigned) data. An option that provably cannot change the point estimate must not change the reference distribution. The obvious defense ('Stata's permute prefix holds everything else fixed; the bootstrap's idcluster convention already documents keeping i-keyed terms at their original codes') does not reach this case: (i) wooldid has already departed from fix-everything-else by rebuilding i inside the replication, and rebuilding i while leaving i-derived terms fixed is an inconsistency neither pure convention has; (ii) the bootstrap's A10 convention is harmless because re-identification REFINES the partition (each drawn copy is a subset of one original cohort, so a cohort-constant covariate stays inside the span of the new i FE and stays dropped), whereas the permonsetcohorts rebuild REGROUPS (a rebuilt cohort pools clusters from different observed cohorts), so the same covariate leaves the span and goes live. That is why sthlp:532 documents the convention exactly where it does no harm and is silent exactly where it does. Point (ii) is a structural argument from ado:9297-9349 plus sthlp:532, not a measurement: the confirming bootstrap(standard) contrast (probe20_bootcmp.do, written) could not be launched because the project's 8-instance Stata cap stayed breached by other agents. The exposure is mechanically detectable with the check permctl already runs for the onset: a covariate constant within i on the design sample (gegen min/max by(i)).
refuter_note: The mechanism is right and generalises; the magnitude is wrong in BOTH directions, and the arm FP-1 demoted is the defect. (1) The headlined controls()/fe() arms do NOT move p '2x'. On my M=210 grid p moves by AT MOST ONE GRID STEP and in BOTH directions: panel A .02857143 -> .02857143 (controls), -> .03809524 (fe(coh)); panel B .10476190 -> .11428571 (controls, i.e. LARGER). The prober's '.04444 -> .02222, a factor of 2' is one step on their M=90 grid (2/90 = .0222) -- one reference statistic crossing the observed value, not a doubling. Their 11-24% null-SD shrink does not reproduce: I get 3.0-7.6% on two panels, and across 24 sharp-null datasets with randomised assignment the SD ratio is median 0.977 [p25 0.889, p75 1.016], narrower in only 16 of 24. So 'anti-conservative' is not a systematic direction; it is dataset noise around a ~2% median narrowing. (2) The arm FP-1 explicitly says 'should not carry the headline' is the one that does. coarsecohortcontrols(c.cohbase) inflates the null SD by 5.5x on BOTH my panels (p .0286 -> .8952 = 31x, and .1048 -> .8000 = 7.6x) with the point estimate BITWISE unchanged; across the 24-dataset sharp-null sweep its null SD is NEVER narrower than baseline (0 of 24), is more than doubled on 19 of 24 and more than quintupled on 10 of 24 (median ratio 3.85, max 229.6), and the smallest p-value the arm produced on ANY of the 24 datasets was .40 (baseline min .0667). The permutation test in that arm cannot reject anything, silently, with e(perm_failed) = 0 throughout. The reason it is the worst case is structural: coarsecohortcontrols() adds the control AND its interaction with every Tz_it dummy (sthlp:1061), so with a cohort-constant control the WHOLE block is collinear and drops in the observed fit, and the whole block goes live at once inside a replication. It is also the option a user reaches for when they have a cohort-level control -- precisely the inert class. (3) FP-1's structural argument about the bootstrap's A10 convention is narrower than stated and I measured it: ado:410 is a NAME-EQUALITY tripwire (`if "`wdbcv'" == "`i'"`), so a bootstrap run with controls(cohbase) -- constant within i but not named i -- prints nothing either. The class FP-1 identifies is uncautioned on BOTH engines. (4) It is the inert-in-observed/live-in-replication asymmetry, not the option: coarsecohortcontrols(c.a_s) with a STATE-level control (live in the observed fit too) gives an ordinary reference distribution (p .4762, SD .2169) on the same panel. (5) Line number: FP-1 cites ado:7639 for the varlist-only substitution; on the pinned build it is ado:7641. Severity stays high, but on inverted grounds: not 'anti-conservative controls()/fe() crossing 5%' but 'coarsecohortcontrols() with a cohort-level control silently turns p = .029 into p = .895 with a bitwise-identical point estimate, zero failed replications and not one distinguishing line of output'.
refuter_did: Rebuilt the claim from its own terms on my own data, never running the prober's script. Panel: 7 ragged administrative states, i = coh (the onset grouping, 2 treated cohorts + never), cluster(state) strictly finer, uneven observation windows, state level+trend heterogeneity, M = 7!/(3!2!2!) = 210 enumerated assignments (p grid 2/210 = .00952, four times finer than the prober's M = 90). Ran (a) the observed fit alone with and without each covariate, comparing e(b)[main_att] in %21x; (b) permexact arms with cluster(state) (rebuild fires, e(perm_irebuilt)=1) for controls(cohbase), fe(wavegrp), fe(coh), coarsecohortcontrols(c.cohbase); (c) the control arm cluster(coh)==i (no rebuild); (d) a contrast arm with a STATE-level control inside coarsecohortcontrols(); (e) the full paired per-assignment comparison of e(permdist_b) after proving the enumerations are identical across arms (permsave onset_* blocks: 0 mismatching rows of 211); (f) a second independent panel; (g) a 24-dataset sharp-null sweep with the cohort assignment redrawn at random in every dataset; (h) non-quiet reruns of every arm to check what is printed. PREMISE CONFIRMED: controls(cohbase) and coarsecohortcontrols(c.cohbase) leave e(b) BITWISE identical (+1.6690b859bb834X-002), fe(wavegrp)/fe(coh) within 4-8 ulps. MECHANISM CONFIRMED: controls(cohbase) changes 208 of the 210 reference statistics and the difference at the identity assignment is bitwise zero (+0.0000000000000X-3ff). CONTROL ARM CONFIRMED: with cluster(coh)==i the same option leaves p and the null SD bit-identical (.33333333 / .2566696171). SILENCE CONFIRMED non-quietly for all three covariate slots.

title: On the same lattice fixture the ame point estimate is 45x the truth, and no path gives the reader a usable warning: the default path has no standard error at all and the one path that produces one reports se 0.44 on a 45x miss
surface: contreat() + lattice() on a dose with little within-(cell x bin) variation
claim: With a unit-level dose plus modest time noise and a dose-quantile lattice, almost no within-(cell x bin) dose variation survives, so each cell-by-bin slope is a near-zero-denominator ratio and the aggregated ame is wildly off. The estimator is consistent for the true dose effect on this DGP (the dose is independent of the unit effects), so 18.09 against a truth of 0.4 is a miss, not a misspecification artifact. The default path reports it with every inference column blank; customvce(robust) reports it with se 0.43558016, a 40-sigma miss presented as a precise estimate; only unconditionalse (se 10.040394) makes it look like the noise it is. The help's lattice caveat (sthlp:1010-1018) attributes discordant ames to effects being loaded onto the BIN INTERCEPTS of the true f(); here the true dose response is linear with no bin structure at all, so that caveat does not describe this failure and nothing warns about within-bin dose variation.
observed: repro_B, true dose effect exactly +0.4 on every treated post observation. Without a lattice: ame 0.65200913 (se .12109561), ame_pre 0.25067023 (se .22023536). With lattice(all 3): ame 18.09100052 on the reghdfe legs with se missing, 18.09100039 on customvce(robust) with se .43558016, and 18.09100039 on unconditionalse robust with se 10.040394. On the earlier fixture (probe10_p1like.log) the same shape: lattice(all 2) ame 7.013 and pre-ame -3.488; lattice(all 3) ame 0.949 and pre-ame 3.702; lattice(all 5) ame 5.789 and pre-ame -54.10 -- all with every inference column blank.
expected: A dose-quantile lattice on a dose that is nearly unit-constant is an ordinary applied choice (the project's own P1 fixture is built that way), and a 45x point miss is the kind of thing inference exists to flag. I mark this uncertain rather than certain because a large miss paired with a small CONDITIONAL robust standard error could in principle be a legitimate conditional-variance statement about an ill-conditioned design rather than a standard-error defect; what is not in doubt is that the shipped default path delivers neither the standard error nor a caution naming within-bin dose variation, so the user has nothing to act on. Worth a dedicated investigation of whether the conditional robust variance is the right object for an ame aggregated over near-singular within-bin slopes.
refuter_note: The point-estimate story is wrong; the inference story is right and worse than the prober realised. Across 12 draws the lattice ame has mean -0.342, SD 2.519 and range [-6.091, +2.906] against a truth of 0.400: NO detectable bias at n=12 (the mean is 1.0 standard errors of the mean from the truth), and my own draws produced 0.919, 3.200, 0.148, 15.636, -6.091 and +2.906 on the same DGP. So the single '45x the truth' observation is one draw from a very heavy-tailed sampling distribution, not the systematic miss the claim describes ('the estimator is consistent for the true dose effect on this DGP, so 18.09 against a truth of 0.4 is a miss'). What IS the defect is the thing the prober flagged and marked uncertain: the reported conditional robust SE averages 0.341 against a realized sampling SD of 2.519 - a 7.4x understatement, so nominal 95% coverage on this design is close to zero. The no-lattice control arm understates by only 1.3x, so the lattice is the aggravating factor. For calibration: that 1.3x no-lattice arm is essentially known_bydesign section 7's NF-3 territory (ame-side inference oversized under robust, remedy R5 not implemented), so the 7.4x figure should be read as a lattice-specific sharpening of a known-open item rather than a rediscovery. The help's lattice caveat (sthlp:1010-1018) is about the effect loading onto bin INTERCEPTS and does not describe this, as the prober said.
refuter_did: Ran the cheap test that discriminates variance from bias: 12 independent draws from the same DGP (true dose effect exactly +0.4 on every treated post row), lattice(all 3), customvce(robust) (the one leg that reports a standard error), with a no-lattice control arm on every draw. Recorded the ame and its reported se each time and compared the realized sampling SD against the mean reported se.

lens.lens: INDEPENDENT REPRODUCTION — rebuilt the case a third time from the claim alone (own fixture, own MC, own attribution tests), then asked whether the world behaves as the claim says. Probes: /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-hegland-Documents-Research-wooldid-dev/f98806d6-cb0a-446e-9291-a575a3bcab42/scratchpad/bluesky/probes/fp-contreat-lens3/{A_attribute,B_fastMC,C_seMC,D_engine_and_iid,E_zoom}.do + .log, NOTES.md
lens.impact: An applied user fitting a continuous-treatment DiD with a dose-quantile lattice — an ordinary choice, and the shape the project's own P1 fixture has — and typing `robust` or `cluster()`, as essentially every DiD user does, gets no standard error at all on any of 25 draws, plus a caution that blames clustering they did not request and steers them to "conditional robust standard errors". The only path that answers that steer, `customvce(robust)`, reports a stable-looking se around 0.41 on estimates that scatter from -26 to +10 around a truth of 0.4: its nominal 95% interval covers the truth 40% of the time, so the user publishes a confidently-signed dose effect that is noise. Had they simply omitted `robust`, wooldid's classical SE would have told them the truth (se 6.4 on average, 25/25 coverage, se 69 on the draw where the estimate was -26). Separately, adding `customvce()` — documented as a variance option — silently changed the reported point estimate in 3 of 25 draws, once from 0.12 to 9.77.

title: One straddling unit silently converts the cluster bootstrap of att_i into a presence bootstrap, cutting its SE 23%
surface: bootstrap(standard) + cluster() + att_i/att_it/att_itime (the T2/T3 two-regime unit rule)
claim: With bootstrap(standard) and a cell-weighted estimand, changing ONE cell of the cluster variable in an otherwise nesting panel flips wooldid_bootrun's all-or-nothing regime predicate (ado:8987-8998) from wdb_nest=1 to 0, replacing __wdbnewi=group(__wdbns,i) with __wdbnewi=i. The equal-unit weighting then counts a twice-drawn cluster ONCE, so only cluster presence contributes to att_i's bootstrap variance and se(att_i) falls by about 23% with no message, no e() marker, and no change to the point estimate. This is exactly the configuration old ado:6364 refused with r459 until 2026-09-16.
observed: 10 industries x 3 units, T=6, i=unit, cluster(ind), tau=0.5*ind, noise sd 0.02, bootstrap(standard) reps(199). Arm B = arm A with `replace ind = 2 if unit == 1 & t == 6`. Mean se(att_i): A 0.45399, B 0.34826, ratio 0.7671; six paired (dseed,rseed) ratios .7607 .7736 .7592 .7733 .7601 .7742. Mean se(att): A 0.45386, B 0.45519, ratio 1.0029. b(att_i) bit-identical, 2.754894183017953. On a noisier design with within-cluster effect heterogeneity (probe1_straddle.do) the cost is ~6% (B/A = .925, .880, 1.022) with se(att) ratio 1.002. The deterministic mechanism is isolated in probe1b_mechanism.do: on one panel with industry 1's rows appended, keep-i gives att_i 1.1437911577 and re-id gives 1.1026004128 while att is bit-identical at 1.0154662125, so the stage-1 regression is invariant and only the estimand weights move.
expected: Two datasets whose cluster partition differs on one row of 180 should not produce standard errors 23% apart for the same estimand, and if they must, the run should say which rule it took. Theory confirms arm A is the textbook cluster bootstrap: Var_g(tau)/G = 2.0625/10 gives SE 0.454 (A measures 0.454), while the presence-only variance is (1/e)/(1-1/e) = 0.582 of that, SE 0.346 (B measures 0.348). ado:9334-9337 states the project's own reason the nesting regime must not keep i - 'keeping i would make a twice-drawn cluster's cells identical duplicates that the equal-cell weighting counts ONCE, collapsing the composition variance of att_i toward zero' - and with one straddler the cluster is still coarser than i for 29 of 30 units, so that is precisely what arm B does. Note the severity does not rest on the nesting SE being the 'correct' one (that is an estimand ruling, see FCW-03); it rests on the 23% gap being invisible.
refuter_note: The mechanism, the direction, the estimand-selectivity and the silence are all real and reproduce. The MAGNITUDE does not. On realistic input the six paired se(att_i) ratios are .9547 .9486 .8861 .8575 .8726 .8709, mean .8984 — about a 10% cut, range 4.5-14%, not 23%. se(att) is essentially unmoved (mean ratio 1.0091) and b(att_i) is bit-identical (difference exactly 0) in all six pairs, so the isolation is clean. The 23% is a ceiling reachable only when the DGP is nearly pure composition variance: my degenerate arm gives a ratio of 0.7896 against the presence-only asymptote sqrt((1/e)/(1-1/e)) = 0.7629, so their theory is right about the limit. Their own probe1 arm already measured 6% with one arm ABOVE 1 and the writeup led with 23% anyway. Two further framing corrections: (a) the two-regime rule IS documented — sthlp:241 says "Where cluster() nests i the copies become distinct units; where it is finer than i, or cuts across it, the copies stay inside their cohort" — what is undocumented is that the switch is all-or-nothing over the whole sample and what it costs; (b) 'silently converts the cluster bootstrap into a presence bootstrap' is exact only in the degenerate limit, because under keep-i the duplicated rows still reweight the stage-1 fit; it is att_i's COMPOSITION component that becomes presence-only. Severity stays high, but for a different reason than the number: 59 of 60 units still nest, and ado:9334-9337 is the project's own statement that keeping i for those collapses att_i's composition variance — so the straddler's rule is applied to units for which it is wrong. FCW-01 and FCW-02 are one root cause (a global predicate evaluated on the design sample) and must be counted once.
refuter_did: Built my own county x firm panel (15 counties x 4 firms, T=7, treatment assigned at county level) with BOTH cross-cluster and within-cluster effect heterogeneity (a_g ~ N(0,.4^2) across counties, b_i ~ N(0,.4^2) within, unit RE N(0,1), idiosyncratic N(0,1)) — i.e. the realistic case their headline design does not cover. Arm B differs from arm A in exactly one cell of the cluster variable (firm 1 spends its last period in county 2). reps(199), 3 dataset seeds x 2 rseeds, paired so the same rseed draws the same cluster multiset in both arms. I also ran a near-degenerate arm (r05_emarker.do, tau = 1 + .3*county exactly, noise sd .05) to see whether 23% reproduces at all, and verified the regime predicate fires by computing min/max of the cluster variable by unit in-sample before each run.

title: pretrendpower()'s minimum detectable trend does not have the stated power on a 16-cluster state-level DiD, and no caution fires there
surface: pretrendpower() -- mdt_wald, mdt_nis, bias_wald, bias_nis, roth_prep, roth_slope_ll/ul; analytic cluster() with few clusters
claim: On a canonical few-cluster DiD that wooldid does not caution about (i = onset-cohort code with unit effects through fe(), cluster() on the unit, G = 16), the joint pre-trend test that mdt_wald claims to power has true size 0.105 rather than 0.05, and the reported mdt_wald(80) is detectable with only ~0.60 power by an honestly-sized 5% test; the trend actually detectable at 80% is ~0.657 against a reported 0.546, so the MDT and the bias column it drives are ~17% optimistic. mdt_nis fails even at the nominal cutoff: 0.7133 (CP95 [.659,.764], excluding 0.80). The Roth slope CI covers at 0.905 rather than 0.95.
observed: 600 pooled null replications (two independent seed streams): joint pre-trend F(3,15) rejects at 5% in 63/600 = 0.1050 CP95 [.0816,.1323]; the size-corrected 5% cutoff is 4.4483 vs a nominal 3.2874. At the reported mdt_wald(80) = 0.5463: pooled nominal-cutoff power 387/500 = 0.7740 CP95 [.7348,.8099]; size-corrected power 180/300 = 0.6000 CP95 [.5421,.6559]. At 0.6456: size-corrected 0.7800. Linear interpolation and a noncentral-chi2 extrapolation both put 80% size-corrected power at delta = 0.657. At the reported mdt_nis(80) = 0.42375: NIS rejects 214/300 = 0.7133 CP95 [.6586,.7638] nominal, 0.5233 size-corrected; the realised NIS size is 0.1125 against a reported 0.0781. Roth slope 95% CI covers the truth 362/400 = 0.9050 CP95 [.8719,.9319]; mean reported slope se 0.1437 vs MC sd 0.1822 (se/sd 0.79). Reported mdt_wald(80) has sd 0.125 on a median of 0.546 (CV 23%), and ranges 0.296-0.925 over 25 fits of the same design. Mechanism: the per-coefficient inference is fine or slightly conservative (individual |b/se|>t rates .039/.039/.047; mean reported variances 1.05-1.09x their MC counterparts); what fails is the quadratic form b'S^-1 b and the GLS slope, both of which invert a 15-df cluster-robust S. Discriminating control (p07_simC.do): the identical geometry at G = 80 is exact -- size 0.0455 CP95 [.0220,.0820], power 0.7864 nominal / 0.8091 size-corrected, slope CI coverage 0.9500, se/sd 1.0018. Design A (iid, no cluster, df_r = 279) is also exact: size 0.0367, power 0.8000 at mdt_wald(80) and 0.5000 at mdt_wald(50).
expected: The run prints 'joint pre-trend test: F(3, 15)' and a mdt_wald column documented (sthlp:789) as 'the minimum linear pre-trend each pre-test would detect with the requested power', with both pre-tests 'conducted at the 5% level' (sthlp:790). If S were the sampling covariance of b_pre and W/keff really were F(keff, df_r) under the null, the size would be 0.05 and the power at mdt_wald(80) would be 0.80 -- which is exactly what Designs A and C deliver. The screen at ado:1413-1444 that would warn a user keys only on whether i is NESTED inside the cluster variable; here a cohort spans four states, so it does not fire, even though e(N_clust) = 16 is available on the same run. sthlp:1334 recommends precisely this design ('a coarser i ... with unit fixed effects supplied through fe()') for pretrendpower.
refuter_note: The defect is real and my own data establish the power shortfall more firmly than theirs. What is wrong is the characterization, not the existence: this is NOT a few-cluster cluster-robust failure. pretrendpower() applies known-covariance formulas to an ESTIMATED covariance — W=b'S^-1 b referred to F(keff,df_r) (ado:10516), mdt_wald built from invF(keff,df_r,.95) and npnF (ado:10559), and a slope CI from the plug-in se=1/sqrt(m'S^-1 m) with invttail(df_r,.025) (ado:10512-10514). The exact reference for b'S^-1 b with S estimated at df_r df is Hotelling's, W*(df_r-k+1)/(df_r*k) ~ F(k,df_r-k+1). Exact size of wooldid's own '5%' cutoff: k=1 -> 0.0500 at every df_r; k=2/3/4 at df_r=15 -> 0.0611/0.0784/0.1034; k=3 at df_r=23/39/79/279 -> 0.0673/0.0597/0.0546/0.0513. So the effect is present at EVERY cluster count and grows with the number of pre-periods, and 80 clusters do not cure it. Two fairness points: F(q,df_r) is Stata's own test/testparm convention after any clustered fit (my reghdfe comparator on the same 250 datasets rejects at 0.0680, consistent with the 0.0784 ideal value), so wooldid did not invent the liberal reference; what is wooldid's own is turning that arithmetic into REPORTED DESIGN QUANTITIES (mdt_wald, bias_wald, roth_slope_ll/ul, roth_nissize_*) where the error is systematic and one-directional. Right remedy: the Hotelling scaling for the test and the matching noncentral reference for mdt_wald, plus a help sentence saying the MDT is an estimate (sthlp:789 currently says it 'depends only on the design's precision', while its 5-95% range is [0.63,1.22] x truth at k=3, df_r=15).
refuter_did:
Rebuilt the claim on my OWN generator (16 states, 4 onset cohorts of 4, onsets t=6/8/10 + never-treated, T=12, state random intercepts, quadratic+cosine year path, AR(1) rho=0.5) and my own seed streams; ran none of the prober's files. s3_mc_null.do: 250 null reps, hand-computed W/slope/se/mdt verified against e(roth_W_att)/e(roth_slope_att)/e(roth_slope_se_att)/e(roth_power_att) to 1 ulp on rep 1. s4_mc_power.do: independent 250-rep null arm + 400-rep power arm at the median reported mdt_wald(80) + 250-rep arm at the design's true 80% point. s7_hotelling.do: closed-form size table over (k,df_r) plus a 100,000-draw Mata simulation of the IDEAL model (b~N(0,I), S~Wishart(I,df_r)/df_r, independent) with no panel, no clustering, no DiD. Plus a hand-rolled comparator (reghdfe pooled event study, cluster(st), testparm on 3 pre dummies) on the same 250 datasets.

REPLICATED: no caution fires; joint pre-trend size 0.1120 and 0.1280 on two independent streams (they: 0.1050); GLS slope CI coverage 0.9120 (they: 0.9050); reported se / MC sd 0.775 (they: 0.79); CV of reported mdt_wald(80) 0.227 (they: 0.23). AND I pin the headline harder than they did: at delta = the median reported mdt_wald(80) = 0.54610, wooldid's OWN nominal cutoff rejects 294/400 = 0.7350 (se 0.0221, CI [0.690,0.777]), EXCLUDING the documented 0.80; their CI [.7348,.8099] included it. True 80% point 0.63007, so the column is 13% optimistic; at 0.63007 the nominal test has power 0.8880.

REFUTED: (1) the mechanism. Nothing about clustering is required — the ideal model at df_r=15, k=3 gives size 0.0770, coverage 0.9108, se/sd 0.8448, median mdt_hat/mdt_true 0.9083, i.e. essentially my panel numbers. (2) 'the identical geometry at G=80 is exact' is false: the ideal model puts df_r=79/k=3 at size 0.0546 and coverage 0.9429; 220 reps could not resolve that, so their discriminating control does not discriminate. (3) The defect scales with k, which they never varied: at k=4 with the SAME 16 clusters the exact size is 0.1034 and slope-CI coverage 0.8831 — a few-cluster caution would not touch it, and would fire where the test is exact (k=1, any df_r, size exactly 0.0500). (4) Their mdt_nis leg is misattributed to S-inversion; it is PTP-2's normal-quadrature-at-a-t-critical-value (k=1 proof: mdt_wald 1.09139 vs mdt_nis 1.08237 for what is literally the same test). (5) The ~17% MDT optimism splits: ~9 points is the exact sampling law mdt_hat/mdt_true ~ sqrt(chi2(df_r-k+1)/df_r) (median 0.9070), the rest is extra CRVE noise from a cohort-level contrast identified off 4 states per cohort.

title: The listwise complete-case rule makes e(V) a factor of two NARROWER than the standard errors wooldid printed, on a realistic state-policy event study, in total silence — esttab and lincom export the narrow ones
surface: bootstrap() / wooldid_bootfin ado:14536-14576 / e(V) / e(V_boot) / e(boot_N_V) / subgroups() with a long event-study window
claim: wooldid_bootfin computes the PRINTED standard error per column over that column's own available replications, but builds e(V) from the LISTWISE complete-case rows only (e(boot_N_V)). On a 30-state staggered-adoption panel with a long event-study window and regional subgroups, boot_N_V collapses to 14 of 60 completed replications while every column remains available in at least 65% of them, so neither the reps() cautions nor the 50% low-availability caution fires — the run prints ZERO cautions. The selection is not missing-at-random: the surviving rows are those in which four specific single-state cohorts were each drawn at least once, which truncates those clusters' multiplicity distributions and deletes the most extreme resamples. e(V) is therefore biased DOWNWARD, and `esttab`, `coefplot`, `honestdid`, `test` and `lincom` — which the run's own footer names as consumers of e(V) — export a standard error for the headline att that is 50.4% of the one wooldid printed. e(V_boot), the documented fallback, is built from the same matrix and carries the same bias.
observed: pG_export.log / pE_sediverge.log, spec `wooldid y state t ttre, att esfixedbaseperiod esprelength(6) espostlength(11) cluster(state) subgroups(reg) bootstrap(standard) reps(60) rseed(4242)` on my own 30-state / 6-county / 2005-2019 panel with six single-state early adopters (gen_admin.do): e(boot_completed)=60, e(boot_failed)=0, e(boot_N_V)=14, K=92, rank(e(V))=13, e(df_r)=29, e(boot_navail) min 39 max 60, columns below the 50% threshold = 0, CAUTIONS PRINTED BY THE WHOLE RUN = 0. SAME ESTIMATE: wooldid printed main:att b=1.007355 se=0.079677 t=12.643 95% CI [0.825545, 1.164670]; `esttab` exported main_att 1.007355 (0.040155); `lincom main_att` gave se=.04015483, CI [.92522917, 1.0894809]. ES_att_post9: printed se 0.127551 vs esttab 0.057044. ES_att_post10: 0.131248 vs 0.063692. Over the 19 pooled rows, 17 ratios below 1, min .447 median .634 (median VARIANCE ratio .403) — se_ratio_table.txt. MECHANISM PROVEN TWICE: (a) navail_pattern.txt — the 49 columns that lose replications are exactly the single-cluster horizons (SG2_post7..10 navail 39, SG1_post8..10 navail 41, SG3_post4..9 navail 41, SG4_post4..8 navail 44, pooled post10/9/8 = 51/56/59); with G=30, P(cluster absent)=(1-1/30)^30=.362 predicts .638*60=38 (measured 39/41/41/44) and the intersection of four independent such events .638^4*60=10 (measured 14). (b) pF_selection.log — within the run, each column's listwise-14 sd against 2000 RANDOM 14-row subsets of its own available rows: 19 of 84 columns at p_lower<=.05 (expected ~4.2), only 2 significantly high, 65 of 84 ratios below 1; main_att p_lower=.0010, ES_att_post8 .0005, post9 .0010, post10 .0005. CONTROL: the identical panel and window WITHOUT subgroups() gives boot_N_V=51 of 60 (pB1_listwise.log), a mild 15% haircut — so the collapse scales with the column count and subgroups() is what makes it bite. e(V_boot) is built from the same retained `bV` (ado:10061-10064), so it is the same matrix.
expected: Either e(V) should rest on the same replications as the standard errors wooldid prints, or the run should say that it does not and by how much. A11 (quoted in the code at ado:14500-14506) ruled this 'a documented consequence rather than a defect' on the wording that a hand test 'does not EXACTLY reproduce the table's Wald numbers', arising 'whenever any column loses a replication'. Measured, it is not an exactness tail: when several independent columns each lose ~35% of the replications the factor is two, and it is systematic rather than noisy. Per the coordinator note, contradicting a ruled entry by measurement is the finding. Nothing announces it: the reps() cautions (ado:6475-6477) key on the p-value grid (2/60=.033, so silent); the low-availability caution (ado:10296) keys on per-column counts at a 50% threshold (thinnest column 39/60=65%, so silent); and the single line that names the realized count, ado:11786, has `e(boot_N_V)` INSIDE its string literal. A second consequence of the same root: a hand `test` is a Wald on e(V) referred to F(q, e(df_r)=29) while the covariance carries 13 df — by the Hotelling relation W(B−q)/(q(B−1)) ~ F(q,B−q) the actual size of a nominal-5% q=6 test at B=14 is about .30 (size_table.txt). Not a size demonstration here: pG's own `test` is one draw under a true null (F(6,29)=1.777, p=.139).
refuter_note: Everything about the CONSTRUCTION reproduces: two passes on different row sets, e(boot_N_V) collapsing (6 of 30, 13/12/21/14 of 60, 80 of 300, 4 of 60 with six subgroups), no caution firing, esttab/lincom/test carrying the exported numbers, e(V_boot) bit-identical to e(V). What is wrong is the characterisation. The listwise selection bias is real but is about -6% to -11% in SE for the median column and about -15% for main_att and for the columns that lose draws - not a factor of two; the headline 0.504 is a tail draw of a quantity whose typical value is ~0.83 at B=60 and which exceeds 1 about 12% of the time. 'Systematic rather than noisy' is backwards: at realistic B the noise dominates the bias. The count evidence ('65 of 84 ratios below 1', '17 of 19 pooled rows') is not 84 or 19 observations - every column's exported SD rests on the SAME listwise rows, so they move together and the unit of observation is the run. The genuinely systematic, one-directional harm is the one the finding put in its last paragraph and called 'not a size demonstration here': e(V) carries N_V-1 degrees of freedom and is referred to e(df_r) = G-1. Measured by Monte Carlo at nominal 5% / 95%: (N_V=14, df_r=29) q=1 6.2%, q=6 29.4%, CI coverage .9374; (N_V=6, df_r=35) q=2 18.7%, q=4 53.8%, coverage .9032; (N_V=4, df_r=35) q=2 31.2%, coverage .8647; (N_V=60, df_r=35) everything at nominal. A live instance: on my six-subgroup run `test ES_att_pre2 ES_att_pre3` returns F(2,35), p = .00136 on a panel whose pre-trend is exactly zero by construction. Two points of fairness: 'total silence' is slightly overstated - the footer does say 'complete-replication listwise' and does name esttab/coefplot/honestdid; what it cannot say is the count, and only because of finding -04. And wooldid's OWN inference is untouched: the joint and equality tests are add-one rank shares on a fixed metric (p = .73 and .95 on the same N_V=4 run), and the printed table comes from the per-column draws. Severity stays high, but as 'the exported covariance is noisy and anti-conservative', not 'a factor of two narrower'.
refuter_did: Built the case from the claim's own terms on my own 36-state / 4-county / 2006-2019 panel (gen_skep.do; 5 single-state early adopters, three multi-state cohorts, 13 never-treated, 3 regions, AR(1) noise, no pre-trend). Recomputed BOTH of wooldid's moment passes offline from e(bootdist) and locked them against wooldid's own output from both sides: my per-column SD for main_att is 0.078807 and the printed e(wdidmainresults) se cell is 0.078807; my listwise recompute matches e(V)'s diagonal with MAXRELDIFF_DIAG = 0; my availability counts equal e(boot_navail) exactly. Then measured the DIRECTION and MAGNITUDE the finding asserts, which is where it breaks: (a) reps(300), where N_lw = 80 and SD noise is only ~8%, gives a median exported/printed ratio of 0.936 (not 0.5-0.63), 0.944 for full-availability columns, 0.845 for columns that lose draws and for main_att; (b) a 400-block study on the same 300 draws, each block a random 60 draws with both passes redone inside it (median N_lw 16 - the exact regime the finding was measured in), gives main_att ratios min .3164, p05 .5833, med .8298, p95 1.0428, max 1.1679 with 12% ABOVE 1 - the finding's 0.504 sits at roughly the 2nd-5th percentile; (c) four independent reps(60) seeds give run-level median ratios .832/.876/.910/.885 and main_att ratios .944/.896, while my reps(30) pilot gave main_att 1.3205 (32% WIDER) and my six-subgroup run gave ES_att_post0 1.32. I also confirmed the selection is real (22 of 67 columns at p_lower <= .05 against 1000 random same-size subsets, expected 3.4; main_att p_lower .010), it is just small. Finally I quantified what IS systematic, by Monte Carlo (r6_df.do).

title: The analytic att SE understatement is estimator-specific, and the lever that fixes it is `esfixedbaseperiod` — an event-study display option, not an inference option
surface: analytic cluster SE for `att` under cluster()==i; `esfixedbaseperiod`; `esprelength()`/`espostlength()`
claim: On a realistic G=10 staggered panel with cluster()==i, the default headline `att` is reported with a cluster SE that is ~0.71-0.77 of the estimator's true sampling sd, giving 18-24% rejection of a TRUE SHARP NULL at nominal 5%; adding `esfixedbaseperiod` yields a different estimator OF THE SAME ESTIMAND whose analytic SE is correct (se/sd 0.93-1.01, rejection 6-8%). Neither the help nor the code tells a user that an event-study base-period option is what determines whether their headline standard error is right.
observed: d05 (25 draws, four specs on the identical draws): S0 `att` alone sd(b) 0.5474, mean se 0.3904, se/sd 0.713, rejection .240. S1 +esprelength(3) espostlength(3) sd(b) 0.8085, se 0.6930, se/sd 0.857, rej .080. S2 +esfixedbaseperiod ALONE sd(b) 0.5224, se 0.4869, se/sd 0.932, rej .080. S3 window AND esfixedbaseperiod: bitwise identical to S2. Confirmed on the ~50-draw main run: arm A0 (plain) analytic att rejection .180 [.098,.308] with mean se 0.4067 = 0.769 x the true MC sd 0.5291; arm A9 (plain + ES window + esfixedbaseperiod) analytic att rejection .061 [.021,.165] with mean se 0.5791 = 1.011 x its own truth 0.5728. The window alone is NOT the lever; esfixedbaseperiod is, and it fully absorbs the window.
expected: Both specifications target the same cell-weighted ATT, so both should report a standard error near the estimator's own sampling sd and reject a true null at ~5%. That they target the same estimand is not an assumption: d02_estimand_truth.do runs a NOISELESS DGP with a closed-form design truth and all five specs (none / w33 / w99 / esfixedbaseperiod / w33+esfixedbaseperiod) return att = 1.0000000000000 and 1.5555556 to ~1e-15 under both a constant and a ramped effect profile. So the SE gap is not a 'different target' artifact — one of the two analytic SEs is simply wrong, and it is the default one.

title: The bootstrap e(V) is rank-deficient at EVERY reps(), and at low reps `test` silently drops constraints and returns a wildly anti-conservative p
surface: bootstrap(standard), reps(), e(V), e(properties), test/lincom/estat vce
claim: Under bootstrap(standard) on a four-estimand event-study spec, rank(e(V)) saturates at 10 of K=20 and never reaches K no matter how many replications complete, so the natural remedy `reps >= colsof(e(b))` cannot fix it; nothing in e() marks the rank (e(properties)='b V', e(boot_v_posted)=1), and at reps(5) a `test` of seven named coefficients returns df=4 with p=1.155e-16 because Stata silently drops three constraints.
observed: 120 units x 12 periods, 4 cohorts + never-treated, cluster(clu), att att_i att_it att_itime + esfixedbaseperiod esprelength(3) espostlength(3), K=20, boot_failed=0. reps/completed/rank(e(V)): 5/5/4, 8/8/7, 12/12/10, 20/20/10, 40/40/10. test of 7 coefficients: reps(5) -> df=4 p=1.155e-16 (three constraints dropped, invisible to a scripted r(p) read); reps(8) -> df=7 p=2.248e-37; reps(40) -> df=7 p=3.212e-12. test of 3 ES coefficients: F = 587.6, 234.8, 154.8, 128.5, 118.5 as reps goes 5->40, i.e. a five-replication run overstates F by ~5x. CONTROL: the same panel with `att` alone (K=8) at reps(60) gives rank 8 of 8 - full rank - so the deficiency is caused by the estimand set (the coefficient vector is ~10-dimensional), not by reps. The only caution printed concerns the p-value GRID; nothing mentions rank.
expected: Either e(V) should be full rank, or its rank should be marked (an e(boot_V_rank) beside the existing e(boot_N_V), or a caution) so that `test`, `lincom`, `estat vce` and any user inversion know the covariance does not span the coefficient space. ado:6235 records the author ruling 'reps() is mandatory (author ruling: no floor - low-rep runs are legitimate)' and the caution text advertises small reps as 'a legitimate way to time a specification', so users are explicitly invited into the reps(5)-reps(12) region where the F is inflated ~5x and constraints vanish silently. recon F7 proposed 'does the caution want reps >= colsof(e(b))' as the boundary; the measured saturation at 10 shows that boundary is wrong.

title: att_it under subgroups() is cell-SHARE-weighted, not cell-equal-weighted, when an (i,t) cell is only partially labelled
surface: subgroups() x att_it / att_itime x missing subgroup values inside a multi-row (i,t) cell
claim: att_it is documented as the simple average of cohort-period effects, giving each treatment CELL equal weight. When a subgroup variable is missing on some but not all rows of an (i,t) cell -- which passes the F13 within-cell guard, because that guard folds missing through cond(sg>=., ., sg) -- the cell enters the subgroup's att_it with weight equal to its LABELLED SHARE rather than weight one. A cell labelled on 1 of its 5 rows counts as 0.2 cells. The same happens to att and att_itime. This is the estimand's defining property, not a rounding matter, and nothing in the output says so.
observed: Noiseless design, exact targets.
