By contrast a parse-stage failure (option typo `attt`, r198) leaves e(cmd)=wooldid intact. CONSEQUENCES MEASURED -- silent: a `capture`-guarded scripted harvest reads e(b)[1,1]=0 and e(N)=600 (or 456), both plausible-looking wooldid quantities; `lincom _b[1.__000005#1.__000006#1.__000007#c.dosep]` returns rc 0 with b=.74796608, se, t and CI from the internal model; `estimates table good failed, keep(main_att)` prints a blank column for the failed run with no warning. Loud: `predict` -> r(111) 'variable __000005 not found'; `estimates table, keep(main_att)` -> r(198). REFUTED SUB-CLAIM: recon asserted predict 'silently predicts from the internal regression' -- it does not, it errors r(111), because the internal regressors are tempvars that no longer exist. Recovery: `est store` BEFORE the failing call then `est restore` fully recovers (recovered att == 2.3371429 == truth); without a pre-emptive store the prior results are unrecoverable. No other residue: frame back to `default`, c(emptycells) back to `keep`, no stray variables, no stray ___wooldidfullmodel in `estimates dir`, no _ppmlhdfe_d, and the next good run is bit-identical (+1.2b277f6afeef2X+001) with or without an intervening failure -- e() is the single unhandled piece of state.

Decisively, wooldid itself already uses the store/restore idiom everywhere else: `qui est sto`/`qui est restore` bracket the permutation rep loop (ado:168/172) and the bootstrap rep loop (ado:367/396), and the worker stores the stage-1 model at ado:1494 and restores it at 1797/3092/3132/3220/3432/3478. title: e(roth_nissize_*), documented as 'the actual size' of the NIS pre-test, evaluates a normal probability at a t critical value
surface: pretrendpower() -- e(roth_nissize_*) and the mdt_nis/bias_nis columns
claim: ado:10366 sets ptpniscrit = invttail(df_r,.025) and feeds that bound to mvnormalcvqp(), a MULTIVARIATE NORMAL probability. The test being described rejects when |b/se| > invttail(df_r,.025), and b/se is referred to t(df_r) everywhere else in the run. With few clusters the reported size is far below the real one and points the wrong way: at k = 1 it reports 0.033 for a test whose size is exactly 0.05 by construction.

At k = 3 on the same design the reported size is 0.0781 while the realised rate is 45/400 = 0.1125 CP95 [.0833,.1476]. Also at k = 1 the two detectable-trend columns disagree although they power the SAME test: mdt_wald 0.77712 vs mdt_nis 0.77069. Scale by df_r: 0.0331 (-34%) at 15, 0.0386 (-23%) at 23, 0.0431 (-14%) at 39, 0.0490 (-2%) at 279.
expected: sthlp:1384 calls e(roth_nissize_*) 'the actual size of the any-individually-significant pre-test', and sthlp:790 says the size is reported 'since it exceeds its nominal level when there are several pre-periods'. The number is printed to warn the user that the pre-test OVER-rejects. With few clusters it understates that size, and at k <= 2 it reports a size below 5% for a test that is exactly 5%.
refuter_note: Confirmed, with three extensions the prober did not have. (1) The right reference is a multivariate t, not a different critical value: on my 250 null reps at k=3, df_r=15 the realised NIS rejection rate is 0.1000 CP95 [0.0658,0.1441], the same rectangle under mvt(15) averages 0.1094 (inside that interval), and what wooldid reports averages 0.0769 — a 30% understatement sitting at the interval's edge. (2) The mdt_nis COLUMN inherits the bug, not just the size scalar, and there is a simulation-free proof: at k=1 the NIS test and the joint Wald test are literally the same test, so the two detectable-trend columns must be identical, and wooldid prints mdt_wald 1.09139 vs mdt_nis 1.08237 (mdt_nis optimistic). (3) The bug is confined to the ptpdfok branch — on the no-df (poisson) branch ptpniscrit is invnormal and the quadrature is then self-consistent (my poisson run reports 0.1331 for a genuinely normal-referenced test), so the poisson user gets the correct NIS size and the gaussian user the wrong one.
refuter_did: Section B of s1_orient.do, on my own 16-state panel with esprelength(1): e(roth_nissize_att) = 0.033052124846 and 2*normal(-invttail(15,.025)) = 0.033052124846, difference printed as 0.000000000000; 2*ttail(15,invttail(15,.025)) = 0.050000000000 exactly. title: contreatwithin + contreat() silently suppresses the float-above-2^24 silent-merge caution — a regression introduced by CS-98 (e26b3dd, 2026-09-09)

title: The reps() p-value-resolution Caution is unreachable without cluster() — a 2026-09-13 regression, and a doc-vs-code divergence

title: lattice() + contreat(): the all-zero covariance is an artifact of the absorbing engine, not of the design -- plain regress on the identical fit returns an ordinary robust VCE
surface: contreat() + lattice() on the default reghdfe path, robust or cluster()
claim: On a realistic 12-state / 5-12-counties-per-state-year-cell panel with a unit-level dose, every lattice() run on wooldid's default (reghdfe) estimation path returns an all-zero covariance and loses every reported standard error, while the SAME model fitted by plain regress on the SAME data -- identical N, df_r, rss, r2 and point estimates to eight significant digits -- returns finite standard errors. The zero is therefore neither the documented cell-containment geometry (sthlp:1076, which requires cluster() at or above i; this fires under bare robust with no cluster at all) nor a lattice-construction defect (a user-supplied lattice variable does it too). This settles the 'undetermined' classification of review_process/held_for_ruling_2026-09-13 item 5, which asked for exactly this diagnosis run.
observed: repro_B (N=2200, esprelength(2) espostlength(2), contreatcontrols(basic)): every leg reports df_r=1663, rss=3249.87, r2=0.653964 and identical point estimates on every row. `lattice(all 3) robust', `... robust regtol(14)', `... ccnoabsorb robust', `lattice(latu) robust' (user lattice variable): ALL standard errors missing. `lattice(all 3) customvce(robust)': att se .13937285, att_pre se .15399566, ame se .43558016, ame_pre se .74495755. `lattice(all 3) unconditionalse robust': att se .14966591, ame se 10.040394. probe11_lat_diag.log reproduces the same split on an independently generated fixture (rss 3.317e+03, df_r 1672, att 0.78718487 / att_pre 0.15042830 on every leg; regtol 6, 9 and 14 all give the zero, so it is not a tolerance artifact; cluster(st) gives it too). probe10_p1like.log shows lattice(all 2) and lattice(all 5) do it as well (rss 3.637e+03 and 2.938e+03, df_r 1795 and 1511). Reproduced outside wooldid entirely (probe14_reghdfe_repl.log): `reghdfe y_dose ib0.cell##i.lat##c.dose_it, absorb(i.st i.year i.lat##c.(ringer)) vce(robust)' -> max|e(V)| = 0, df_r 2004, rss 4100.2092, rank 160; the same with the controls explicit -> max|e(V)| = 0, rank 165; `reg y_dose i.st i.year i.lat##c.(ringer) ib0.cell##i.lat##c.dose_it, vce(robust)' -> max|e(V)| = 2923.571, df_r 2004, rss 4100.2092, rank 154. reghdfe retains 6-11 more columns than regress drops as collinear (probable specific cause; the engine split itself is certain).
expected: An all-zero covariance is documented at sthlp:1076 only for the cell-containment geometry -- continuous treatment with cluster() at or above i -- and known_bydesign.md section 5 states explicitly that an all-zero e(V) under robust or cluster(unit) on realistic data is NOT documented and IS a finding. Under robust there is no containment argument, df_r is 1663-2004 and the residual sum of squares is 3.2e+03-4.1e+03, so the variance is not algebraically zero; the plain-regress leg proves it by computing it on the identical fit. This also contradicts the premise of the 2026-09-08 ruling recorded at ado:1546-1565 that removed the AMESE R4 att-rescue refit ('what it bought was the subset of standard errors that survive a specification whose cell-level containment has already made the ame inference invalid'): on this design there is no containment, the R1 predicate cannot fire because it only runs over clusvars, and the rescue would have recovered genuine standard errors. A wooldid-side remedy is cheap because the vzero screen already detects the condition and wooldid already knows how to drive regress (the customvce path).
refuter_note: The claim stands and is STRONGER than stated: 6/6 on my fixture, not 'on some designs'. Two framing corrections. (1) The ame's invariance across two different collinearity drops (identical to 6 decimals under reghdfe's rank-227 parameterization and regress's rank-177 one) is positive evidence the ame is ESTIMABLE, which the prober did not establish and which is what makes the regress covariance a legitimate object and the reghdfe zero a recoverable artifact. Worth adding to the case. (2) 'an artifact of the engine, NOT of the design' overstates it: the design IS rank-deficient - reghdfe retains 40-55 more columns than regress drops on an identical fit - so the engine split is the proximate cause and the near-singular design is the ultimate one. Minor: the claim's 'identical N, df_r, rss' is off by one on df_r in my runs (854 vs 855); N, rss and the point estimates are identical.
refuter_did: Built my own fixture (12 states x 5-12 counties per state x 10 years, county-level dose plus a within-county time-variation knob, i = state, staggered onsets, bare robust with NO cluster() token anywhere) and ran six replications in which each engine sees the VERY SAME saved dataset. Every rep: wooldid's default path reports the ame with se missing, wooldid customvce(robust) reports the identical point estimate with a finite se; and outside wooldid on the same data, reghdfe returns max|e(V)| = 0 while regress returns max|e(V)| = 108.98-645.59, with rss identical to 4 decimal places (e.g. 1345.1673 both) and margins-ame identical to 6 decimals (e.g. 0.223331 both). Ranks 221-230 (reghdfe) vs 174-190 (regress). Also captured the equivalent split in R6 at a second dose-variation setting.

lens.lens: realism and impact — how likely is a real applied economist to hit this, what exactly do they lose, and would they notice (silent wrong number weighted far above a loud failure)
lens.impact: On a state-`i` / county-dose administrative panel with `lattice()` and either `robust` or `cluster(county)`, the att and every event-study att horizon lose SE, t, p and CI — inference that my Monte Carlo shows is valid (12/12 coverage, SE/SD ~1.3) — on 7 of the 8 lattice spellings I tried, including two clustered FINER than `i` where the documented containment caveat cannot apply. The user is told the cause is "analytic clustered SEs, with clusters occuring at a high level of aggregation" when they specified no cluster at all, and that it is "a property of the specification, not a numerical accident" when the same command returns SEs on 4 of 12 samples of the same DGP. `customvce(robust)`, which restores the att SE in seconds, is never named. What they do NOT lose is anything valid on the ame row: under a lattice its analytic SE covers 42% at nominal 95% whichever engine computes it, so the blank is protective and the proposed wholesale remedy would print that wrong number instead. They are not stranded — the bootstrap the caution names works and returns honest, wide ame inference — but they pay runtime for a failure they were told the wrong reason for.

title: semielasticity on a non-positive outcome fails in margins and is never diagnosed; under fastnose — what permute() selects by default — the run returns rc 0 with a printed results table and no e(b) at all
surface: permute() (fast-mode default) x fastnose x semielasticity
claim: semielasticity (margins' eydx) divides by the prediction. When the outcome takes non-positive values margins fails, and wooldid never says so in its own words. The failure surfaces in four ways and on one of them the run reports SUCCESS: with fastnose it returns rc 0, prints a complete results table headed "Treatment Effects Presented as Semi-elasticities" with R2 lines and an att row whose every column is missing, and posts NO e(b) at all. Under permute() — which selects fastnose by default — the same run stops with r(459) "the observed comparison statistic for att could not be read from the rep-0 run", blaming the comparator when the observed run produced no coefficients either. Without fastnose it dies r(3598) with a raw Mata traceback, or r(459) with Stata's own margins message "inconsistent estimation sample levels 0 and 1 of factor __000007". Shifting the same outcome by a constant to be strictly positive fixes all of them.
observed: PX03_repro.log / p16_semi.log / p17_semi2.log / p19_bracket.log. Panel A (40 units, 8 years, onsets 2003/2005, heterogeneous effects, y in -3.70..6.86): plain run rc 0 with e(b)=main_att; `semielasticity fastnose` rc 0 with e(b) ABSENT and e(cmd)=wooldid; `semielasticity permute(shuffle) permreps(30)` r(459); `semielasticity` alone r(3598) with `variable __00001O not found / st_data(): 3598 Stata returned error / __marg_cr_eval() / deriv__call2user_v() / _deriv__compute_value() / _deriv() / st__marg_cr_compute()` and e(cmd) left as reghdfe with tempvar column names. Panel B (plainer inline panel, y in -2.63..5.33): `semielasticity fastnose` r(459) with `inconsistent estimation sample levels 0 and 1 of factor __000007`. The SAME outcome +10 (strictly positive) on both panels: rc 0, e(b)=main_att, for fastnose, permute and full. y+3.8 (positive but predictions near zero) is also clean, so the trigger is the sign, not the scale. fastnose alone on the same outcome posts e(b) normally, and a plain run on the same outcome is fine, so neither fastnose nor the data is the cause on its own. The rc-0 table printed is: `N clusters = 40; N = 320 (0 obs dropped) / R2 = 0.8989 ... / Main Results: Treatment Effects Presented as Semi-elasticities / att | . . . . .` then `matrix e(b) not found`.
expected: wooldid screens comparable conditions and names them in its own words — on the same data under poisson it prints "ppmlhdfe dropped every observation of the treated cohort-period cell unit == 17, relative-t == 4 (perfect separation: the outcome is zero on all of them, so the cell's coefficient does not exist). This is not multicollinearity...". semielasticity on a sign-crossing outcome deserves the same. At an absolute minimum a run that produced no coefficients must not return rc 0, and must not print a formatted table with an R2 line and a semi-elasticity header as if it had estimated. The help's only hedge is "this option tends to require large samples and a y-variable that is not sparsely distributed"; it does not say the outcome must be strictly positive and does not warn that the failure can be silent. Under permute() the error the user does get names the wrong object.
refuter_note: Three corrections. (1) THE STATED TRIGGER IS WRONG. 'the outcome takes non-positive values' is neither necessary nor sufficient: at shift 2 the outcome is non-positive on 30 of 720 rows and the fitted value on 14 of them, and the run completes and reports att .23864029 with se .0783198, t 3.05, p 0.003 and a 95% interval. What moves the run across the threshold is how much mass the model's FITTED VALUES put at or below zero (17 treated non-positives -> fail, 5 -> fail, 3 -> succeed), not the raw outcome's sign. (2) The more interesting behaviour is on the SUCCESS side of that threshold, which the finding does not mention at all -- filed separately as SK-01. (3) Two specific observations did not reproduce: I never saw the rc-0/no-e(b) branch in 21 attempts (though I can now name its mechanism, SK-02, and their own log corroborates it), and under permute() my runs died with the same bare margins message as the plain run, before the permutation engine was reached -- the claimed r(459) 'observed comparison statistic for att could not be read from the rep-0 run' did not appear. Severity down from high to medium: what survives is an undiagnosed bare margins error on erroneous-but-plausible input plus a help entry that never says the prediction must be positive -- brief categories 4 and 5, not category 1.
refuter_did: Ran semielasticity on my own sign-crossing outcome through all four paths, then attacked the stated MECHANISM with a level ladder and a fitted-value oracle. (i) The crash half reproduces: `semielasticity` alone -> r(459) 'could not calculate numerical derivatives -- discontinuous region with missing values encountered'; with fastnose -> r(459) 'inconsistent estimation sample levels 0 and 1 of factor __000007'; under permute() -> r(459), the same bare message; e(cmd) left as reghdfe with tempvar coefficient names on all three; shifting the outcome up fixes all of them. (ii) Level ladder (R5b): the same outcome shifted by c=0..10 gives r(459) at c=0,1 and rc 0 from c=2 on, where min(y) is still -2.418, -1.418 and -0.418. (iii) Fitted-value oracle (R10, and now section C of RF03): refitting wooldid's own att-only specification -- TWFE absorbing i and t with one dummy per treated (cohort, relative period) cell -- gives non-positive fitted values 160/58/14/3/0/0 at shifts 0..5, of which 17/5/3/0/0/0 lie inside the treated-and-post subpopulation the att averages over. (iv) rc-0 hunt (R7): eight independently drawn 40x8 two-onset panels, `semielasticity fastnose` -> r(459) every time; 21 attempts in total across three panel shapes and eleven level shifts, never rc 0. (v) I traced the rc-0 branch in code instead and measured its premise (see SK-02). (vi) I also checked, and cleared, two things their write-up implies: the denominator really is the FULL fitted value including the absorbed effects (R3: dydx level-invariant at 1.394985 for y+12 and y+120 while eydx is .10003225 and .01143591, both within 3.5% of dydx/mean(y|treated,post)), and the caller's frame and variables are intact after a failing run (default frame, all user variables, N unchanged).

title: simultaneousbands under boottstat yields a band NARROWER than the pointwise percentile-t interval, which sthlp:525 says is impossible
surface: simultaneousbands + boottstat + bootstrap(standard)
claim: Under `bootstrap(standard) boottstat simultaneousbands`, the level(95) simultaneous band for an event-study family can lie strictly INSIDE the level(95) pointwise percentile-t interval at one or more horizons of the same family, contradicting the help's explicit claim that the studentized band 'can never come out narrower than the interval it accompanies'.
observed:
Run 1 (repro_band_narrower.do, 20 states x 3 units x 8 years, log-normal outcome error, cluster(state), reps(399), 6 horizons; e(esband_engine)=bootstrap-studentized, e(esband_crit_att)=9.5180674):
  horizon pre3   pointwise [-9.64223368, 0.65471983]   band [-6.96720703, 4.39249989]
  -> band lower endpoint 2.68 units INSIDE the pointwise one. HORIZONS_WITH_BAND_INSIDE_POINTWISE=1, FAIL=1.
Run 2, independent design with GAUSSIAN errors (p09_bandskew.do run K2: 12 states, one treated cluster with a 14x larger effect, 2 horizons, reps(999)):
  horizon post0  pointwise [-4.76649500, 9.35624776]   band [-4.43840483, 9.39162977]  -> BANDVIOLATIONS=1.
So skewed errors are not required; a single influential cluster suffices.
expected: wooldid.sthlp:525, of this exact engine: 'Under boottstat that deviation is studentized by each replication's own standard error and the endpoints use the observed analytic ones - a genuine percentile-t, on the same scale as the pointwise intervals printed beside it, SO THE BAND CAN NEVER COME OUT NARROWER THAN THE INTERVAL IT ACCOMPANIES.' Mathematically a simultaneous band at level() must be at least as wide as the pointwise interval at level() at every horizon of the family; that is what makes it simultaneous. The mechanism the help correctly flags for the coefficient-draw displays applies here too: the pointwise percentile-t interval is EQUAL-TAILED from the SIGNED t-quantiles, [b - q_.975(t_r)*se, b - q_.025(t_r)*se] (wooldid_boottp, ado:14389; wired at ado:9874), while the band is SYMMETRIC, b +/- q_.95(max_h |t_rh|)*se (wooldid_bootband, ado:16866-16876). q_.95(|t|) = q_.975(t) only for a symmetric t_r distribution; skew breaks the equality and the two shapes cross. The percentile-t pointwise interval IS a rank interval and IS not symmetric, so the sentence exempting boottstat is unsound as written.
refuter_note: Three corrections. (1) The stated premise -- 'a simultaneous band at level() must be at least as wide as the pointwise interval at level() at every horizon' -- is FALSE. Width dominance holds only between intervals of the SAME SHAPE; boottp is equal-tailed, bootband is symmetric-in-|t|, and two valid level() objects of different shape can cross. That is exactly what the help's OWN preceding sentence says about percentile/bc/bca. The real defect is narrower: sthlp:528 EXEMPTS boottstat from that caveat when percentile-t is itself a rank interval and itself asymmetric, so the exemption is unsound. Category 5 (doc-vs-actual), not category 3. (2) Their Run 1 does not support the title: band [-6.967, 4.392] has width 11.36 against the pointwise 10.30, so the band is WIDER -- that run shows non-nesting, the documented behaviour, not narrowness. Only their Run 2 is narrowness, by 2 percent. (3) The one case where I could make it STRICTLY narrower had e(esband_crit_att)=30.9 and a pointwise interval of [-1.5106454, 66.1101377] -- i.e. it is the SAME event as SK-02's critical-value inflation, not an independent one. On well-behaved data I get non-nesting only. High -> medium.
refuter_did: Cell A of my own repro (20 states, 2-4 units each, 9 years, log-normal errors, 5 horizons, cluster(state), reps 299, boottstat simultaneousbands) plus a 6-cell sweep (r08_bandsweep.do cells 1-6) and 5 cells in r03_bands.do. I measured NESTING and WIDTH as two separate quantities, which the finding conflates. Result: non-nesting reproduces (2 of 6 sweep cells; r03 S1; cell A), strict narrowness reproduces only in cell A. The percentile-display control on the same data (r03 S2) shows no violation, confirming the studentized engine is the locus. I also read wooldid_boottp (ado:14332, equal-tailed signed quantiles) and wooldid_bootband (ado:16776, symmetric b +/- q_lev(max|t|)*se) to confirm the shape mismatch.

title: The finer-than-i remedy is incomplete: the analytic-SE understatement is a gradient in clusters-per-treated-cell, not a binary in the nesting relation
surface: cluster() strictly finer than i on the default analytic path (sthlp:251, "What level to cluster at")
claim: wooldid.sthlp:251 presents the analytic-SE understatement as a property of the nesting relation ("At or above the level of i ... the remedies are a finer cluster()"), but the shortfall is continuous in K, the number of clusters inside a treated cohort-by-period cell, and a finer cluster() only moves K off 1. With cluster() STRICTLY FINER than i throughout - the documented remedy, unchanged - wooldid's mean reported SE over the empirical sampling SD is about 0.95 at K=10, 0.88 at K=5 and 0.84 at K=3, and 95% coverage falls from ~0.94 to ~0.86. csdid, on IDENTICAL point estimates with IDENTICAL sampling SD, holds SE/SD at 0.92-1.12 across the whole ladder.
observed:
Verified run (repro_fewclus_gap.log, sentinel REPRO_RFG_DONE), 150 draws per rung, 40 states x 4 units x 12 periods, cluster(state) with 40 clusters in every rung, i = the onset cohort in every rung, only K changes:
   K  hor       SD   SE_csdid  SE_wooldid   wd/cs   SE/SD_cs  SE/SD_wd  cov_cs  cov_wd
   3  post0   0.2285    0.2543     0.2086   0.820      1.113    0.913   0.947   0.900
   3  post1   0.2821    0.2608     0.2122   0.814      0.924    0.752   0.880   0.847
   3  post2   0.2542    0.2636     0.2110   0.800      1.037    0.830   0.927   0.873
   3  post3   0.2656    0.2744     0.2251   0.820      1.033    0.848   0.920   0.847
  10  post0   0.1602    0.1722     0.1590   0.923      1.075    0.992   0.967   0.967
  10  post1   0.1609    0.1717     0.1587   0.924      1.067    0.986   0.947   0.927
  10  post2   0.1627    0.1697     0.1521   0.896      1.043    0.935   0.933   0.933
  10  post3   0.1759    0.1775     0.1639   0.923      1.009    0.931   0.953   0.947
Median wooldid coverage 0.860 at K=3 (csdid 0.923), 0.940 at K=10 (csdid 0.950). Independently, an 800-draw MC across four other designs (RESULTS_LADDER_K{3,5,10}.txt, RESULTS_DGP_F.txt, RESULTS_DGP_S.txt) gives median wooldid SE/SD 0.845 / 0.884 / 0.912 at K=3/5/10, and DGP-F (five adoption waves of 3 states each, 200 draws, a wholly ordinary staggered design) gives 0.865 SE/SD and 0.905 coverage against csdid's 0.979 and 0.915 on identical points - crossing both halves of the pre-registered gate. The measured ratios track sqrt((K-1)/K) across seven independently generated designs (pred 0.816/0.816/0.894/0.949/0.949/0.949/0.987 vs measured 0.845/0.865/0.884/0.912/0.933/0.970/0.999); cluster()==i is the K=1 limit of the same formula.
expected: The help names a finer cluster() as THE remedy for the at-or-above-i understatement, with the only qualitative condition being "so that a treated cohort-by-period cell contains several clusters". A user who satisfies that condition (3 adopting states per wave is 'several') should get an interval at its nominal level. csdid on the same draws does, at 0.92-0.95; wooldid gives 0.85-0.90. The mechanism is the same one the help already describes - a saturated cohort-by-relative-period dummy removes the within-cell residual variation - except that it is continuous: when the cell holds only K clusters, most of that variation was BETWEEN those few clusters, so the CR1 meat still loses ~1/K of it. reghdfe applies a global G/(G-1) correction with G=40 and nothing corrects the K that identifies the cell. So this is an inherited property of CR1 cluster-robust inference rather than a wooldid coding error - but the help presents the remedy as a fix for a binary condition, and the run gives the user no signal about what K they have. The concrete fix is a caution keyed on the smallest treated cohort-by-period cell's cluster count, plus a quantitative form of the help's qualitative clause.
refuter_note: The K=3 end of the claim reproduces cleanly and independently (0.869 SE/SD, 0.858 coverage on the att row, below both halves of their pre-registered gate), and the mechanism they name - clusters inside the saturated treated cell - is confirmed by a paired test with no SD noise. Three things in the transmitted claim are wrong. (1) The K=10 rung does NOT reproduce: I measure 1.013 SE/SD and 0.958 coverage where they report 0.912 and ~0.93, and my number agrees with the project's own 500-draw 2026-09-14 figure of 0.972/0.934 at the same geometry. The defect is concentrated at few clusters per cell, not spread along a ladder. I tested AR(1) errors, the only structural difference in their generator, and it costs 1.8% of the ratio and nothing in coverage, so their K=10 number is not explained by their own mechanism. (2) 'The measured ratios track sqrt((K-1)/K)' is wrong as a fit: under the stated mechanism SE/SD = sqrt(1 - phi/Kc) with phi<=1, so sqrt((Kc-1)/Kc) is a FLOOR, and their own K=10 measurement of 0.912 sits below the 0.949 floor their mechanism cannot generate, while mine sits above it. The gradient is real; the functional form is not established, and the seven-point table is within MC noise (+/-6% at 120-150 draws) of other shapes. (3) 'csdid holds SE/SD at 0.92-1.12' is paired in the transmitted claim with 'coverage falls from ~0.94 to ~0.86' as if csdid held coverage; their own FINDINGS.md concedes csdid's coverage drops to 0.880-0.947 at K=3 (median 0.923, under their own 0.93 gate) and did_imputation undercovers at 0.76-0.85, so the gate's 'both controls in band' clause does not fire at K=3. What is specific to wooldid is the SE LEVEL, not the coverage gap alone. Separately, remedy #2 in the same help sentence, bootstrap(standard), appears to close the K=3 gap: paired se_bootstrap/se_analytic = 1.17 over 26 completed draws against the 1.15 needed, so 'the remedy is incomplete' is true only of the first remedy taken alone. Severity stays medium: the K=3 failure is real and is exactly what known_bydesign s7 calls genuinely new, but it is inherited CR1 behaviour that any saturated-dummy TWFE shares, and at three adopting states per wave the design is hard for every estimator.
refuter_did: Wrote my own generator (40 states x 4 units x 12 periods; two adoption waves of K states at t=5 and t=7; state RE .8 + state-by-year shock .4 + unit RE .5 + iid .4), my own truth in closed form, and three arms on the same 120 draws per rung: A = i=coh cluster(state) esfixedbaseperiod (cluster STRICTLY FINER than i), B = same with the pooled reference, C = i=state cluster(state). K in {3,10}. I never ran their do-files. Results (att row / median ES row): K=3 arm A 0.869 SE/SD, 0.858 coverage, 0.828 / 0.871; K=10 arm A 1.013 / 0.958, 0.986 / 0.938. I then ran a PAIRED mechanism test (mc2_mech.do, 120 draws) on a DGP with no state-level dependence at all, where three arms share identical point estimates so no sampling SD enters: mean(se at 3 clusters/cell)/mean(se at 12 clusters/cell) = 0.871 against 0.853 predicted. Finally I chased the one structural difference between our generators, AR(1) errors, with probe_ar1.do (120 draws each way at K=10): iid 1.019/0.942 vs AR(1) 1.001/0.942 - it explains nothing. I also read review_process/se_coverage_2026-09-14/se_cov_mc.do and confirmed its 'i = cohort id' arm is in fact cluster-finer-than-i with 10 clusters per treated cell.

title: sthlp:251's "roughly 0.66 to 0.75" is not the size of the at-or-above-i SE understatement on realistic data; it runs to 0.18, and coverage to 0.29
surface: cluster() at or above i on the default analytic path (sthlp:251)
claim: The help quantifies the at-or-above-i understatement as "measured at roughly 0.66 to 0.75 of the reference on the diagnostic fixtures". On ordinary state-policy DGPs that include a state-by-year shock - the single most standard variance component in applied DiD, and precisely the component a saturated i-by-relative-period dummy absorbs - the measured ratio of mean reported SE to empirical sampling SD falls to 0.18 and 95% coverage to 0.29. The documented band is not a floor and the help does not say so.
observed:
Verified run (repro_remedy_works.log, sentinel REPRO_RRW_DONE), 150 draws, 40 states x 5 units x 12 periods, state-level onset, state RE + state-by-year shock + unit RE + AR(1) errors:
  i = state, cluster(state)  [cluster AT i]: empirical SD 0.1343, mean reported SE 0.0759, mean(SE)/SD = 0.565, coverage of the true att = 0.693
  i = coh,   cluster(state)  [FINER]:        empirical SD 0.1343, mean reported SE 0.1266, mean(SE)/SD = 0.942, coverage = 0.940
  csdid Tp0 (control): mean(SE)/SD = 1.082; largest |b(i=state) - b(i=coh)| over 150 draws = 6.37e-14
The larger MCs go further. DGP-S, 283 draws, i=state + cluster(state): att SE/SD 0.610 / coverage 0.763, worst ES row 0.430 / 0.580. DGP-F, 200 draws: att 0.384 / 0.595, worst ES row 0.175 / 0.294 - the reported SE is 5.7x too small and the nominal 95% interval covers 29% of the time. DGP-U (ragged) 0.589 / 0.772. DGP-P with i=icoh + cluster(icoh) 0.618 / 0.738. In DGP-S both external controls (csdid 0.982/0.936, did_imputation 0.987/0.943) sit inside the bands in the same draws, so the pre-registered gate fires rather than abstains.
expected: The quoted band is scoped to "the diagnostic fixtures", so nothing in the sentence is false - but it is the only magnitude a user is given, and a user calibrates to "my t-statistics are about 1.4x too large". On an ordinary staggered state-policy panel the factor is 2 to 6. The reason my designs are harsher is identifiable and one-dimensional: they contain a state-by-year shock. Remove it and the band reproduces - DGP-P, which has no cluster-level shock at all, gives 0.739 SE/SD and 0.852 coverage on the i=unit arm, squarely inside the documented band and matching the project's own 500-draw figures of 0.838 and 0.794 (and 0.644 against their 0.661 on the pooled arm). So the documented band describes a DGP without cluster-level shocks; adding the commonest one doubles to quadruples the damage. The help should say the band is a floor, or give the range measured with a cluster-level time shock present.
refuter_note: The substance is confirmed and is worse than they reported on the honest statistic: sthlp:255's 'roughly 0.66 to 0.75' is not a floor, and on the ATT ROW - not a minimum over rows - I measure 0.315 SE/SD and 0.467 coverage on an ordinary staggered state-policy panel. Four corrections. (1) The stated MECHANISM is wrong, and this is the sharpest refutation. Their EXPECTED says 'The reason my designs are harsher is identifiable and one-dimensional: they contain a state-by-year shock. Remove it and the band reproduces.' It does not: mc2_mech.do arm G runs on a DGP with no cluster-level time shock and no state-level component whatever (unit random effects plus iid errors) and gives 0.362 SE/SD and 0.567 coverage - further outside the band than any of their state-shock designs. What drives the magnitude is the share of Var(bhat) sitting inside cells the treated dummies saturate; one observation per treated (i,period) cell achieves that with no cluster-level shock anywhere. Their proposed fix, re-measuring the band 'with a cluster-level time shock present', would therefore not bound it. (2) The '0.18 / 0.29' headline is a selection statistic - the MINIMUM over eight event-study rows in a 200-draw MC. On my runs the min ES row runs 25-30% below the att row (0.223 vs 0.315; 0.483 vs 0.634). The claim should be stated on the att or median ES row, where it is still decisively outside the band. (3) The severity argument rests on a reading the help forecloses: their EXPECTED says 'a user calibrates to my t-statistics are about 1.4x too large', but the sentence immediately after the quoted band reads 'There is no plug-in correction - at that level the analytic covariance is the WRONG OBJECT rather than a mis-scaled one', which is an explicit instruction not to treat 0.66-0.75 as a calibration constant; the band is also scoped to 'the diagnostic fixtures' in the same sentence, which the claim concedes. (4) This is a rediscovery of known_bydesign s1, ruled three times, with a larger number; the value is documentation-only. Severity medium, not higher: the behaviour is documented and thrice-ruled, and only the magnitude is understated.
refuter_did: Arm C (i=state, cluster(state) = cluster AT i) of the same 120-draw runs, on the same draws as arms A and B so the point estimates and empirical SD are shared and only the reported SE differs. I reported the att row and the median ES row, not the minimum. K=3 (6 treated states): att 0.315 SE/SD, 0.467 coverage; median ES row 0.289 / 0.434; min ES row 0.223 / 0.358. K=10 (20 treated states): att 0.634 / 0.800; median ES 0.612 / 0.750; min ES 0.483 / 0.658. I then tested their stated mechanism directly with mc2_mech.do arm G (i=unit, cluster(unit), 120 draws) on a DGP containing NO cluster-level time shock and no state-level component of any kind.

title: With a continuous covariate in controls(), the default cell collapse and nofastcollapse return different VARIANCES (up to 5.5e-6 relative), reaching the printed se and CI digits — against sthlp's measured "about 1e-16" and "no digit wooldid displays is affected"
surface: nofastcollapse x controls() (and coarsecohortcontrols()); binary and continuous treatment; the margins/delta-method variance stage
claim: On an ordinary staggered panel, whenever a CONTINUOUS, coefficient-bearing control varies within the collapse's (cohort, relative-period, targetflag) cell, wooldid's default run and its `nofastcollapse` run report different variances: up to 5.49e-06 relative on e(V) and 3.46e-06 on e(wdidmainresults), which changes the 6th-7th printed decimal of standard errors and confidence-interval bounds. Coefficients are unaffected (1e-16 to 1e-15). The trigger is isolated by three arms that all return to ~1e-14: make the same control constant within the cell, absorb it with fe() or ccc_absorb() so it carries no coefficient, or make it a factor. coarsecohortcontrols(c.x) triggers it too (1.38e-06). It is deterministic (noise floor exactly 0, four ways, three sessions) and it is NOT solely attributable to the collapse: a plain row permutation of the same data with the collapse OFF moves e(V) by 2.92e-07, so the collapse is the larger of two perturbations of the same underlying instability in margins' delta-method variance.
observed: EXECUTED AND VALIDATED (p13.log). Seven arms, `att att_i att_it esprelength(3) espostlength(3) jointtests`, max relative difference over all of e(V):  N noise floor (collapse arm twice) 0.00e+00 EXACTLY | A no controls 5.78e-16 | C controls(xpct) 5.49e-06 FAIL | D same control made cell-constant 1.29e-15 | E fe(region) absorbed 5.47e-16 | F row shuffle, collapse OFF 2.92e-07 | G row shuffle, collapse ON 2.28e-07.  Arm C's 5.49e-06 was measured identically in three independent sessions (p07 w05_pct, pnf, p13).  Printed table, controls(xdollar xdollar2), p07.log DISPLAY_A vs DISPLAY_B: se `.16194921` vs `.1619492`; CI lower `-.30483918` vs `-.30483917`; CI lower `-.41771` vs `-.41770999`; ES estimate `.16215286` vs `.16215285`; ES estimate `.2176445` vs `.21764449`.  Cell-by-cell on w05_pct e(wdidmainresults): pretreatment att se 0.125623208243 vs 0.125622905190 (2.41e-06), lb_95ci 1.99e-06, ub_95ci 3.06e-06; pretreatment att_it ub_95ci 3.46e-06; ES_att post0 p 1.38632744935e-24 vs 1.38632351379e-24 (2.84e-06).  Other triggering cells: controls(xdollar) 2.01e-06; +robust 2.01e-06; +cluster(region) 2.56e-06 (joint_horiz p 2.47e-08); contreat+controls 8.75e-07; bootstrap+controls (analytic V only) 2.32e-07; subgroups+controls 4.81e-06 with the subgroup joint tests moving 1e-08; coarsecohortcontrols(c.xdollar) 1.38e-06; controls(x1 x2) 5.34e-09.  Clean: ccc_absorb(xdollar) 5.76e-15, controls(i.region) 5.04e-14, interactivecontrols(xdollar) EXACTLY 0 (ineligible in both arms).  In every failing cell the regression-stage scalars F, N, df_r, ll, ll_0, r2, r2_within, rmse, rss are BIT-IDENTICAL between the arms, so reghdfe ran identically and the divergence is confined to the margins stage.
expected: The project's indifference threshold is rtol 1e-10, so anything above it is a difference by the project's own standard; this is 4-5 orders past it. wooldid.sthlp makes three MEASURED claims that this contradicts, all in the nofastcollapse entry on the pinned build: (a) sthlp:338 "Standard errors and variances do not amplify at all: they were measured at about 1e-16 relative regardless of the scale of the predictions" — measured here at 5.49e-06, ~10 orders out; (b) sthlp:350 "For almost all work, not at all: no digit wooldid displays is affected" — the printed se and both CI bounds differ; (c) sthlp:332 "The difference is bounded, in absolute terms, by about one unit in the last place of the linear prediction ... every difference measured was a small integer multiple of that one quantum" — holds for coefficients, fails for variances. The option's stated purpose (sthlp:299-300) is byte-for-byte reproduction of an archived result, and the help tells the user the default and the option agree to every displayed digit; they do not. NOT contradicted, and I retract an earlier claim that it was: sthlp:357's row-permutation calibration ("a row permutation moves the same near-zero coefficient about 19 times more than the collapse does") is CORRECT as written — measured 15.5 on b_es_att[pre2] = -0.0417 (row permutation 2.06e-14 vs collapse 1.33e-15). The expectation that variances should agree is not merely documentary: the gate's own argument (wooldid.ado:5588-5610) reasons only about the derivative of the prediction cancelling between xb(targetflag=1) and xb(targetflag=0), which the coefficients confirm at 1e-15; it is never extended to margins' delta-method Jacobian, where the same cancellation is between two nearly equal quantities and survives as residue that depends on which row the collapse retained.
refuter_note: The headline is CONFIRMED and I reproduced it independently: on a realistic 3-cohort staggered panel with a percentage-scale control the two arms differ by 6.59e-06 on the DIAGONAL of e(V), and the printed pretreatment standard errors and confidence bounds differ (se .11036045 vs .11036009; lb -.24568926 vs -.24568854), so sthlp:338's measured 1e-16 and sthlp:350's 'no digit wooldid displays is affected' are both contradicted. Three corrections. (a) TRIGGER: 'whenever a continuous, coefficient-bearing control varies within the cell' is false as a sufficient condition. On the same panel and the same control, bare att is 1.92e-16 and esprelength(1) espostlength(1) is 6.47e-16; an event-study window of two or more horizons is also required, and the cells that move are the PRETREATMENT rows, the main estimand moving only 2.7e-08. On a 6,000-row micro panel (i=state or i=3-value cohort, controls at scale 1 to 5000, 2 or 3 onsets, ES 2/2 and 3/3) nothing moves above 7e-16 at all. Some third property of the failing shape is required and I did not identify it. (b) ATTRIBUTION: 'it is NOT solely attributable to the collapse ... the same underlying instability in margins' delta-method variance' is REFUTED here. With the collapse OFF, a row permutation moves e(V) by 1.32e-15 (their claimed 2.92e-07 does not reproduce, and their own repro header states 7e-16 for that same arm) and an algebraically irrelevant constant shift of the control moves nothing above 1e-9, while the same two perturbations under the default move 6.59e-06 and 3.46e-06. The default path is the inaccurate side; nofastcollapse is the exact one. (c) MECHANISM: 'ULP residue of the cancelling partial sums' does not account for a quantity this size - the identical geometry outside wooldid reproduces the exact oracle c'Vc to 0.00e+00. What is established is that the retained row's RAW controls() value is the cause: one line handing controls() to wooldid_fcol's existing dose-averaging branch (so the retained row carries the cell's weighted mean, as it already does for the contreat dose) closes the gap to 4.84e-16 and removes the sort-order dependence, without moving a point estimate (e(b) 1.31e-15). A real fix must be restricted to CONTINUOUS controls (the averaging branch takes a numeric varlist; factor controls are clean anyway), and coarsecohortcontrols(c.x), which the prober measured at 1.38e-06, presumably needs the same treatment - untested by me. Severity stays medium: nothing a user decides changes at 1e-6 on a standard error, but it is a measured help claim wrong by ten orders and the default path is the one that fails.
refuter_did: Built the case from the claim's own terms on my own data, never running the prober's script. (1) r1.do: an administrative micro panel I generated (30 states x 25 individuals x 8 years, i=state, 25 rows per collapse cell) with controls(z), controls(age, mean 35) and controls(inc, mean 40000) - default vs nofastcollapse agreed at 0.00e+00 to 6.84e-16 on e(V), SE[1] hex-identical, so the claim did NOT reproduce there. (2) r2.do: rebuilt the collapse geometry outside wooldid - plain reghdfe + margins [aw=], dydx(tf) subpop() on full data vs a hand-collapsed one-row-per-cell dataset carrying the summed weight and the FIRST row's covariate - and compared both to the EXACT delta-method oracle c'Vc: 0.00e+00 everywhere, at mean |xb| up to 3504. (3) r3.do: regenerated the prober's SHAPE with my own code (150 units, 3 treated cohorts + never-treated, 10 periods, i=cohort, control 50+8*x1) - it reproduces, 6.59e-06 on e(V) AND on its diagonal; jointtests irrelevant; a scale ladder (control = c + 8*x1, only |xb| moves) gives 3.27e-07 at c=0 rising to 4.73e-05 at c=5000. (4) r4b.do: named the moving cells (all pretreatment rows: pretreatment_att_it se .11036045 vs .11036009, rel 3.29e-06; main att_i only 2.7e-08) and swept the request: bare att 1.92e-16, ES 1/1 6.47e-16, att att_i att_it with no window 5.41e-16, ES 2/2 5.35e-07, ES 3/3 1.51e-06. Also ran the test the prober never ran: adding a pure CONSTANT to the control is algebraically a no-op, and nofastcollapse is invariant to it (nothing above 1e-9) while the default moves up to 3.46e-06. (5) r5.do/r6.do: micro panel clean at i=state AND at i=3-value cohort, at control levels 0/50/5000, with 2 and 3 onset cohorts and ES 3/3 (6.72e-16); on the failing panel a row permutation with the collapse OFF moves 1.32e-15 while the same permutation with it ON moves 6.59e-06; a cell-constant control is clean at 2.81e-15; the printed table differs (pretreatment se .11036045 vs .11036009, ci -.24568926 vs -.24568854). (6) r8.do: copied the ado and added one line in the collapse gate so controls() goes through wooldid_fcol's existing dose-averaging branch - patch inert 6.59e-06, patch armed 4.84e-16, shuffle under the armed patch 1.38e-15, e(b) unmoved at 1.31e-15.

title: pretrendpower()'s joint pre-trend test under bootstrap() is an uncorrected k-dimensional Wald referred to F(k, e(df_r)) instead of F(k, n-k)
surface: bootstrap() x pretrendpower(); wooldid_ptp ado:10342-10560, the Ftail at ado:10545
claim: After bootstrap(), wooldid_ptp (ado:10545) computes the printed "joint pre-trend test" as Ftail(keff, e(df_r), W/keff), where W = b'S^{-1}b is formed on e(V_es_att) — a SAMPLE covariance estimated from n = e(boot_completed) replications — while e(df_r) is the bootstrap reference df for a ONE-dimensional t (bootdf(clusters) => G-1 = 39 here; missing, hence chi2, under bootdf(normal)). The correct reference for a k-dimensional quadratic form in an n-draw sample covariance is Hotelling's: (n-k)/((n-1)k)*W ~ F(k, n-k). wooldid's version inflates the F statistic by (n-1)/(n-k), so the printed p falls without bound as n approaches k. sthlp:532 explicitly promises this statistic is NOT printed: "Neither is the Wald test on e(V) that a hand test reproduces; that one is a normal-theory test on the bootstrap covariance and is not printed."
observed: 40 states x 20 periods, cluster(state), esfixedbaseperiod, esprelength(6) espostlength(4), jointtests pretrendpower(80); 6 pre-period coefficients, same data and rseed(4242) throughout. CONTROL (analytic): e(roth_prep_att) = e(joint_horiz) = hand `test` p = .01003909, all three identical. BOOTSTRAP (wooldid's printed p | Hotelling-corrected | wooldid's own immune rank test e(joint_horiz) | inflation factor): reps(7) 2.362e-12 | .3482 | .1250 | 6.00 ;  reps(8) 2.703e-06 | .3006 | .1111 | 3.50 ;  reps(10) 1.788e-06 | .0912 | .0909 | 2.25 ;  reps(15) .3654 | .6418 | .3125 | 1.56 ;  reps(25) .2981 | .4553 | .2692 | 1.26 ;  reps(50) .3299 | .3937 | .3333 | 1.14 ;  reps(200) .4941 | .5013 | .4527 | 1.03. A hand `test` over the same six coefficients returns the SAME number as e(roth_prep_att) to every printed digit at every reps — they are one statistic. e(df_r) drives it and nothing else does: at reps(8) with identical data and seed, bootdf(clusters) gives 2.703e-06, bootdf(normal) (e(df_r)=., chi2(6)) gives 4.023e-10, bootdf(3) gives .04797, boottstat gives 2.703e-06, while the Roth slope (.10420368) and its se (.02469802) are bit-identical across all four (p14_ptpvariants.log). ORDINARY REPS: 11 pre coefficients with reps(60) prints .4984 where the Hotelling reference gives .6431, and ZERO caution lines are printed in the run block (p09_calib.log, C60).
expected: Either the Hotelling / F(k, n-k) reference, or a guard keyed on e(boot_completed) relative to the tested block's dimension, or a refusal — the treatment jointtests already gets. The analytic control proves F(k, e(df_r)) is correct only when e(V_es_*) is not a sample covariance; the bootstrap path reuses a scalar that was reposted (deliberately, ado:10225-10246) for one-dimensional t statistics. sthlp:532 states this exact Wald test is not printed, so the help and the code disagree.
refuter_note: The mechanism and the DIRECTION are right, but three legs need fixing. (1) Magnitude: the finite-draw excess over the reference's own Sigma-known limit is 7.4x at (k=6,n=20), 2.7x at (k=6,n=50), 1.7x at n=100, 1.3x at n=200, 1.05x at n=999. In ABSOLUTE terms the printed test over-rejects against nominal 5% only for n/k below roughly 8 - .175 at (6,20), .109 at (11,50), .101 at (11,60,G=40) - while (k=6,n=200) is .031, BELOW nominal. Every dramatic figure the prober quotes (2.4e-12, 2.7e-06) comes from reps<=10; at reps>=25 their own table shows the two references nearly agreeing, and on my data at realistic reps wooldid's ptp Wald and its own bootstrap RANK joint test agree (reps 50: .778 vs .784; reps 300: .621 vs .580). (2) More clusters at fixed reps is worse in absolute terms: size .063 at G=30 vs .096 at G=200, both at (k=6,n=50). (3) The doc leg as stated does not stand: sthlp:532's 'Neither is the Wald test on e(V) ... is not printed' sits inside the jointtests paragraph ('Neither [of those two bootstrap forms] is ...'), and the SAME paragraph says of pretrendpower 'The method is unchanged - only the covariance it consumes', which is exactly what the code does. The version of that leg that does stand is my BX-N1. Severity high -> medium: a real inference-path defect, but confined to a long pre window with a modest reps().
refuter_did: Built my own 60-county/30-state/16-period panel with NO pre-trend in the DGP and hand-formed W = b'S^-1 b on the pre block of e(b_es_att)/e(V_es_att). Ftail(keff, e(df_r), W/keff) equals the printed value and e(roth_prep_att) to every digit at reps 20/50/100/300 and under bootdf(clusters)/bootdf(normal)/bootdf(3); e(df_r) = 29 = G-1 at every reps(). r11_boottstat.do shows a hand `test` over the six pre coefficients returns the identical number (.4708198565 == e(roth_prep_att) at reps(60)). I then measured what the prober never did - the SIZE of the test - with a Wishart oracle using the exact divisor and centring wooldid_bootves uses (ado:14622-14625), plus the same reference's Sigma-known limit as the honest baseline (r03_oracle.py, r03_limits.out).

title: pretrendpower()'s rank guard stops firing at completed = k+1, where the reported pre-trend slope flips sign, its CI excludes zero on the wrong side, and mdt_wald understates the detectable trend 3.8x
surface: bootstrap() x pretrendpower(); wooldid_ptp rank screen ado:10495-10510
claim: Separate defect from BOOTX-1 and it needs a different fix: the GLS quantities Roth's method reports — slope = (m'S^{-1}b)/(m'S^{-1}m), its se = 1/sqrt(m'S^{-1}m), its level() CI, and the mdt_wald / bias_wald columns — are different NUMBERS when S is a bootstrap covariance from few draws, not mis-referred ones, so no degrees-of-freedom correction repairs them. wooldid's only screen is diag0cnt(invsym(S)) on the k x k pre block, which fires only while completed <= k. At completed = k+1 it goes silent and stays silent, and that is exactly where S^{-1} is worst. sthlp:532 claims protection: "the existing rank guard applies to the bootstrap block as it does to the analytic one, skipping with a caution if it is not invertible."
observed: Same 40-state design, k = 6 pre coefficients, pretrendpower(80), rseed(4242). ANALYTIC: keff 6/6, slope -.06623, se .02758, 95% CI (-.1220, -.0105), mdt_wald .1101, bias_wald .6203. reps(7): keff 6/6 (NO rank caution), slope +.08134, se .00722, CI (+.0667, +.0960) — wrong sign, excludes zero on the wrong side — mdt_wald .02885, bias_wald .1625. reps(8): slope +.10420, CI (+.0542, +.1542). reps(10): slope +.11512, CI (+.0649, +.1654). reps(15): -.04258. reps(25): -.05956. reps(50): -.04690. reps(200): -.03247. Where the guard DOES fire (completed <= k) it behaves correctly: reps(3) keff 2/6, reps(4) keff 3/6, reps(6) keff 5/6, each with the documented rank-deficiency caution (p08_lowest.log). The only caution printed at reps(7) is the generic 2/reps p-value-GRID caution (ado:6477), which is about Monte-Carlo resolution of the percentile p and explicitly blesses low reps. At 11 pre coefficients with reps(60) the bootstrap run reports keff 11/11 with no caution while the ANALYTIC run on the same data reports keff 9/11 and DOES print one.
expected: mdt_wald is the column the diagnostic exists to provide — 'a pre-trend this size would have been caught 80% of the time'. Understating it 3.8x is a false reassurance, and a sign-flipped slope with a tight CI is a false alarm in the opposite direction. A guard keyed on e(boot_completed)/k (wooldid already has e(boot_N_V)), or a refusal below some ratio, is the shape of the fix; the invertibility guard the help points to is not it.
refuter_note: The headline mechanism is REFUTED. The analytic zero direction is v proportional to 2*pre4 - pre7, with v'S_analytic v = -2.17e-17 (exactly zero) but v'S_bootstrap v = 1.10e-01, which is 71% of that block's mean bootstrap variance, and the SD of v'b_r over the 199 listwise-complete draws in e(bootdist) is 0.331. r06 locates it: the analytic pre block is rank 5 of 6 under cluster(state), cluster(county) AND `robust`, and full rank 6 of 6 under iid. So the analytic exact rank deficiency is an artifact of the sandwich covariance (I traced it to singleton treated cells - see BX-N3), NOT a property of the estimator; the bootstrap's full rank is CORRECT and the ANALYTIC caution is the false alarm. 'The guard goes silent exactly where S^-1 is worst' is not what happens on realistic data. The prober's reps(7) numbers (sign-flipped slope, CI on the wrong side, mdt_wald 3.8x understated) are reps(7) artifacts: the systematic understatement of mdt_wald is sqrt((n-k-2)/(n-1)) = 7.4% at (k=6,n=50), 13% at (k=11,n=50). The doc leg is wrong: sthlp:532 promises only that the guard skips 'if it is not invertible', which is precisely what runs. WHAT SURVIVES, and is the reason this is still medium rather than low: the printed slope/se/CI/mdt_wald carry an unrecorded Monte-Carlo component - four seeds on one dataset at reps(50) give slopes .0505/.0195/.0011/.0110 (SD ~.021) against a printed se of .029-.043, and printed joint p .271/.714/.399/.679. Oracle coverage of the nominal-95% slope CI is 92.8% at (6,50), 88.7% at (11,50). Filed separately as BX-N2.
refuter_did: Reproduced the boundary arithmetic and, more importantly, the 'realistic' leg on my own plain panel: the ANALYTIC run reports keff 5 of 6 WITH the rank-deficiency caution while every bootstrap arm (reps 50 and 200, four seeds each) reports keff 6 of 6 with no caution. Then I tested whether the bootstrap's full rank is spurious: I took v, the eigenvector of the analytic pre block whose eigenvalue is ~0, and measured that direction under the bootstrap. r06_whyrank.do checks whether the analytic deficiency is VCE-specific; r02_rank.do measures the seed-to-seed scatter of the printed slope at reps 50 and 200.

title: At cluster()==i, bootstrap(bayes)+safety(off) reports standard errors 4.4x apart for a bit-identical point estimate, and the cell-weighted SE is exactly invariant to the variance component it is documented to omit
surface: bootstrap(bayes) x {att_it, att_i, att_itime} x safety(off), at cluster() == i
claim: Under bootstrap(bayes) with safety(off) at cluster() == i, the reported bootstrap standard error for the cell-weighted estimands (att_it/att_i/att_itime) does not respond AT ALL to cross-cluster treatment-effect heterogeneity, and on data where att and att_it are bit-identical numbers with bit-identical analytic standard errors, bootstrap(bayes) reports standard errors differing by a factor of 4.4 while bootstrap(standard) reports them bit-identically. The refusal text's conditional ('can be too small when treatment effects vary across clusters') is therefore too narrow: the SE is 0.60 of the bootstrap(standard) value with NO cross-cluster heterogeneity at all.
observed: One run of p19_homogeneous.do, 24-cluster balanced staggered panel, reps(400) rseed(31337), cluster(st) with i = st. het=0 arm: analytic se(att)=0.099348 with att and att_it bit-identical in b AND se; bootstrap(standard) se(att)=se(att_it)=0.123593 (ratio exactly 1.0000); bootstrap(bayes)+safety(off) se(att)=0.113876, se(att_it)=0.074588 (ratio 0.6550); bayes/standard att=0.9214, att_it=0.6035. het=1.2 arm (a cluster-level shock on the treatment effect): standard se(att)=se(att_it)=0.343761; bayes se(att)=0.328771, se(att_it)=0.074588 (ratio 0.2269); bayes/standard att=0.9564, att_it=0.2170. standard's att_it SE rises 2.8x with the heterogeneity; the bayes one is IDENTICAL to the printed six decimals (0.074588 in both). Independently on a second, unbalanced design (p09_cellwtd.do, 30 clusters, 300 reps): se_bayes/se_standard = 0.895 for att, 0.187 for att_it, 0.179 for att_i and att_itime. p15_attvsattit.do gives the hex-identical b and analytic se (+1.047e22bacc981X+000 and +1.96ee6cfe4673bX-004 for both estimands).
expected: A bootstrap standard error must be the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the statistic printed beside it. When two estimands are the same functional of the data - here every treated (i,relyr) cell holds exactly one row, so the observation-weighted att and the equal-cell-weighted att_it are the same number with the same analytic se, and bootstrap(standard) confirms this by reporting them bit-identically - their bootstrap standard errors must also agree. They differ by 4.4x. The mechanism is exact: with cluster()==i the Dirichlet multiplier is constant within a cohort, so a cluster-constant shift of its treated cells adds a constant to every replicate of an equal-cell-weighted estimand and leaves the replicate SPREAD unchanged; all of the between-cluster variability enters through the cell weights, which att_it/att_i/att_itime discard by construction. The package documents the DIRECTION (sthlp:241, ado:6439 'can be too small when treatment effects vary across clusters') and gates the combination behind safety(off) - which the refusal message itself instructs the user to type - but neither the magnitude (4.4-5.6x, a nominal 95% interval with roughly the content of a 26% interval) nor the exact insensitivity nor the presence of the understatement under homogeneity follows from that text. SCOPE: every measurement is at cluster() == i; the magnitude at cluster() coarser/finer than i is untested.
refuter_note: Four corrections. (1) THE BIG ONE: the DEFAULT ANALYTIC clustered se is exactly as blind. In the same two arms it is bitwise identical (+1.2fdb96bdb85e9X-004), for att as well as att_it, while bootstrap(standard) moves +199%. The exact invariance is therefore a property of the geometry (a treated cell inside one cluster is fitted by its own dummy, its residual is exactly zero, so a post-only shock changes no score), not of the Dirichlet engine; singling out bootstrap(bayes) misplaces the blame. (2) The predicate is 'cluster() NESTS i', not 'cluster() == i' (they said coarser/finer was untested): coarser collapses identically, finer does not collapse at all, and singleton cells are not required. This is the same predicate as the documented analytic weakness at sthlp:255. (3) The documentation framing is half wrong: the PRIMARY clause of both the refusal (ado:6439) and sthlp:241 is unconditional and exactly right ('omit the cell-sampling variance component'); what is genuinely misleading is only the second clause, 'when treatment effects vary across clusters', which my het=0 arm contradicts at 0.50. It is a wording defect, not the documented-vs-actual divergence they describe. title: level(99.9) and level(99.99) refused with a message that contradicts both the input and wooldid's own range check
surface: level()
claim: wooldid refuses level(99.9) and level(99.99) with r(198) 'level() can have at most two digits after the decimal point', although those inputs have one and two decimals, plain Stata's set level accepts both, and wooldid's own validator advertises 99.99 as the upper bound. The levels it accepts are exactly the binary-representable ones, so the level is being re-rendered at full double precision before set level.
observed: Plain Stata: set level 99.9 -> rc 0, c(level)=99.9; set level 99.99 -> rc 0, c(level)=99.99; 97.5, 90.25, 99.5 all rc 0. Through wooldid: level(95) rc 0, level(99.5) rc 0, level(97.5) rc 0, level(90.25) rc 0, level(99.9) rc 198, level(99.99) rc 198, both with 'level() can have at most two digits after the decimal point'. Separately, level(150) and level(5) are correctly refused with wooldid's own 'level() must be between 10 and 99.99'.
expected: level(99.9) and level(99.99) accepted like 99.5 / 97.5 / 90.25. wooldid's own validator (ado ~line 5863/6263) tests `level < 10 | level > 99.99`, so it explicitly permits 99.99 and then a later `set level` rejects it — the command contradicts itself. 99.9% intervals are ordinary in multiplicity-adjusted reporting, and the message tells the user something false about what they typed, so it gives no route to a fix.
refuter_note: The refusals are real and the contradiction with wooldid's own 'between 10 and 99.99' validator (ado:5863/6263, sthlp:540) stands. But 'the levels it accepts are exactly the binary-representable ones' is FALSE - 99.95, 68.27, 84.13, 92.5 and 99.8 are all accepted and none is exactly representable. The rule is: a level breaks iff its 16-significant-digit rendering carries more than two decimals, which is 12.8% of the two-decimal grid and 40% of the one-decimal grid above 90. The affected set is therefore much wider than the two values reported (level(99.1) and level(90.1) are ordinary requests that fail). Severity stays medium for the claim as filed; the larger escalation - the same re-render applied to c(level), needing no level() option at all - is carried separately as new finding SKEP-LEVELSTATE so as not to double-count.
refuter_did: Confirmed the refusals independently (level(99.9) and level(99.99) -> r(198) 'level() can have at most two digits after the decimal point'; plain set level accepts both) and then attacked the stated mechanism. Wrote a one-line program with the same 'syntax , Level(real 0)' and echoed the local: 99.9 -> '99.90000000000001', 99.99 -> '99.98999999999999', 95.4 -> '95.40000000000001', but 99.95 -> '99.95', 68.27 -> '68.27', 84.13 -> '84.13'. So Stata renders macro '=' results at 16 significant digits and set level parses the LITERAL TEXT - confirmed by 'set level 99.9000' and 'set level 99.900' both failing r(198) in plain Stata. Mapped the whole legal range by emulating wooldid's own step (echo, then cap set level): 1152 of the 9000 two-decimal levels in [10,99.99] break, first at 64.01; 144 of 900 one-decimal levels break, of which 40 are in [90,100) - 90.1, 91.1, ..., 99.1, 99.4, 99.6, 99.9. An independent Python reproduction of %.16g agrees exactly (1152 and 144). Verified through wooldid that level(95.4), level(99.1) and level(90.1) are also refused, none of which the prober found.

title: estimates replay after wooldid fails r(198) and blames a command line the user never typed

claim: `estimates store m1` followed by `estimates replay m1` exits r(198) printing 'Error: command line input should feature all of y i t ttre; too few variables specified', although the user typed no wooldid command line. The replay gate is keyed on a strictly empty `0', so even a trailing blank defeats it.

LARGER: a failed 'estimates replay' poisons the bare-wooldid replay for the rest of the session (estimates restore does not clear it; only a refit does), so his reported RESTORE_RC=0/BARE2_RC=0 does not reproduce. This is NOT a rediscovery of the ruled WOOLDID_LASTRC design (known_bydesign.md section 6, NFRPL-01/02): the ruling's own stated premise at ado:34-35 is that 'the stored e() results predate the user's latest (failed) attempt', and after estimates replay nothing predates anything - the e() in memory is exactly the estimation the user asked to see, and the failed invocation was Stata's post-estimation machinery, not a user estimation attempt. refuter_did: Re-ran the sequence from a clean state with WOOLDID_LASTRC explicitly dropped first, and instrumented the global at each step. REFUTED the trailing-blank sub-claim: from a clean state 'wooldid' followed by two trailing blanks returns rc 0 and replays the full table - Stata has already stripped them before the ado:26 gate sees `0'. Found something bigger: the failed estimates replay sets global WOOLDID_LASTRC=198, and the working route is then refused - BARE BEFORE rc=0, BARE AFTER STORE rc=0, ESTIMATES REPLAY rc=198, BARE AFTER FAILED REPLAY rc=198, estimates restore m1, BARE AFTER RESTORE rc=198, and only BARE AFTER REFIT rc=0. The refusal text is 'the last wooldid call failed with r(198); the stored results predate that failed call', which is false here.

title: contreatelasticitytype() without contreat() is not inert — it relabels a plain level ATT as an elasticity
surface: contreatelasticitytype(); results-table header (ado:11313-11317), event-study tables and graph titles (ado:13306-13310), histogramcohorteffects labels (ado:1930-1933); e(wdid_cetype)

The heading moves from 'Main Results (Full Estimation Sample):' to 'Main Results (Full Estimation Sample): Marginal Treatment Effects Presented as Elasticities' (eyex), '... Semi-elasticities (eydx)' (eydx), '... Semi-elasticities (dyex)' (dyex), and e(wdid_cetype) goes dydx -> eyex. title: semielasticity / contreatelasticitytype(eyex|eydx) has no domain screen: a silent inference row, r(459), or an opaque Mata r(3598), depending on data and weights
surface: semielasticity, contreatelasticitytype(eyex|eydx); the margins reporting scale
claim: d ln E[y]/dx is undefined where the fitted outcome is not positive, and wooldid screens nothing there. On an outcome whose fitted values cross zero it returns a complete inference row (estimate, se, t, p, CI) with no caution of any kind on one panel, dies with Stata's generic margins r(459) on a second, and dies inside Mata with r(3598) 'variable __00001O not found' — an internal tempvar name — on a third when an aweight is present.
observed: Panel A, one model, two outcomes differing only by an additive constant of 7 (so the LEVEL ATT cannot change and does not: 0.790571 for both). ypos (fitted values strictly positive): semi-elasticity 0.102704 unweighted, 0.104949 with aw — sensible, 0.79/7.7. yneg (fitted values cross zero, min -2.13): rc 0, att = 1.327828, se .090441, t 14.68, p 0.000, 95% CI [1.149347, 1.506309], printed under 'Treatment Effects Presented as Semi-elasticities', WITH NO CAUTION; 1.351847 under aw and under pw. Panel B (min(y) = -3.58): the same option gives r(459), Stata's generic 'could not calculate numerical derivatives -- discontinuous region with missing values encountered', unweighted and weighted alike. Panel C, built with the shared blue-sky generator (min(ync) = -3.17): unweighted r(459); with [aw=w] r(3598), 'variable __00001O not found' / st_data(): 3598 / __marg_cr_eval() / deriv__call2user_v() — a raw Mata traceback naming an internal tempvar. Control on the same data without semielasticity: rc 0. sthlp:243 warns only that the option 'tends to require large samples and a y-variable that is not sparsely distributed' — nothing about the sign of y, and nothing about the result being meaningless rather than absent. The same family covers contreatelasticitytype(eyex|eydx), which wooldid's own F-collapse text (ado:5074, sthlp:370) groups with semielasticity as 'divide by the prediction'.
expected: wooldid screens almost everything else with a named message (five requires-parent screens, a lattice domain assert, a cfxlattice domain assert, an onset-commensurability tier, a subgroup containment tier). A reporting scale that is undefined on part of the treated sample should draw a named refusal or caution, and an option should not have three different failure modes on three panels of the same ordinary shape — least of all a Mata traceback that names an internal tempvar, which a user cannot act on. NOT established, and the single check that would move this to high: whether 1.33 is (a) margins averaging 1/yhat over every treated cell — a complete but meaningless number — or (b) margins silently dropping the non-positive-yhat rows, in which case it is the semi-elasticity of a shifted subpopulation and a silently wrong number for the requested estimand.
refuter_note: Two corrections to the finding, and one correction to a claim of my own. (1) The r(3598) is NOT 'the weighted leg'. Every r(3598) I obtained is UNWEIGHTED - r_f3c_pole.do has no weight statement anywhere and dies r(3598) at shifts -8.4 through -20. The prober's attribution to an aweight does not hold. (2) Nobody, including me, has characterized what selects among the three behaviours. My first rule ('depth of the straddle') is refuted by my own logs: panel Q reaches roughly -2.7 in fitted value and returns a number, while pole shift c=-8.4 (min y over treated-post only -0.745) dies r(3598). What the crashing configurations share is fitted values tightly CLUSTERED near zero rather than spread across it, which is where a numerical derivative of ln(yhat) is worst behaved - the traceback is Stata's own _deriv() machinery, and my plain-reg oracle never crashes because that path differentiates analytically. That is a hypothesis consistent with both datasets, not a measured rule. (3) THE FINDING'S OWN OPEN QUESTION IS ANSWERED, and the answer is (a), not (b), and it is worse than the finding says. On a genuinely straddling domain the standalone oracle gives: hand-computed mean(_b[x]/yhat) over the subpop = -.24488522; ratio-of-means alternative = 1.00068; `margins, eydx(x) subpop(if x==1)` = -.24488522, rc 0. Exact match, repeated on a tighter straddle (.67907475 both ways). So margins' eydx is the MEAN OF PER-OBSERVATION RATIOS and drops nothing - a treatment whose true effect is +1.0 on an outcome whose fitted values average +1.0 is reported as a semi-elasticity of -0.24. The sign is wrong, the magnitude is meaningless, and nothing is said. (4) Evidence-citation correction: the silent-number leg should be cited from panel Q, not from pole c=-8, where min y over treated-post is only -0.345 against a residual sd of 0.3 and I did not establish that the fitted values cross zero - the same inference I would not accept from the prober. The pole run remains the evidence for the knife-edge (0.4 in the units of y moves a confident complete inference row to a Mata traceback) and for the unweighted r(3598). Confidence raised probable -> certain; severity stays medium. NOT ESTABLISHED by either party: the contreatelasticitytype(eyex|eydx) half of the family - my contreat designs died on wooldid's multicollinearity screen r(322).
refuter_did: Four probes. (a) r_f3b_semantics.do: a panel whose treated-post fitted values unambiguously straddle zero (unit effects U(-4,4), resid sd 0.2, R2 0.997, min y over treated-post -2.87) - `semielasticity` returns rc 0, 1.0437756, se .0431678, t 24.18, p 0.000 under the header 'Treatment Effects Presented as Semi-elasticities' with NO domain caution; weighted legs ([aw=w] and [pw=w], weights BEFORE the comma) also rc 0. (b) r_f3c_pole.do: one panel, one model, one additive shift c on y, with the level ATT pinned at .7543601 at every c as the invariance control - a sweep of c across the fitted-value support. (c) r_f3d_scope.do: the same straddling data with an event-study window, and with att_it. All three of the finding's failure modes reproduce on my own freshly generated data: rc 0 with a complete row, r(459), and r(3598) 'variable __00001O not found' with a Mata traceback through st_data() / __marg_cr_eval() / deriv__call2user_v(). title: The permutation design assigns onsets to clusters that contribute nothing, and the design is misreported to the user by four orders of magnitude
surface: permute(shuffle|probabilities), permsave(), the treated-resampling-cluster caution, the possible-assignment count
claim: wooldid_permrun (ado:7479-7488) and wooldid_permctl (ado:5957-5959) build the same unscreened sample, so the randomization design ranges over clusters with zero rows in e(sample). The reported number of possible assignments and the treated-cluster caution therefore describe a design the analysis does not support.
observed: Section A (20 states, 8 treated, 4 treated states report no outcome). permsave() writes one onset_<id> column per cluster the design assigns to: 20 columns (onset_1...onset_20) on the full data versus 16 (onset_5...onset_20) on the oracle - direct evidence the dead clusters are in the design. Reported possible assignments: 634,888,800 vs 43,680. The caution 'only 4 of the resampling clusters are ever treated' fires on the oracle and NOT on the full data. e(N)=320 and the estimate .65513021 identical. NOTE: sections B and C of this do-file are invalid (my own targeting bug, documented in its header) and are superseded by p5_perm_refusals.do.
expected: The user should be told how many assignments their analysis actually admits and how few treated resampling clusters their inference rests on. HONEST CAVEAT: unlike the bootstrap, a defensible reading exists for permute - randomization inference conditions on the assignment mechanism, which physically operated on the clusters with no outcome data too. I did not measure size and do not claim the p-value is invalid. What is not defensible under either reading is the reporting: 634,888,800 named for an analysis supporting 43,680, and the guard silenced by clusters that carry no data.
refuter_note: Two things. (1) The probe explicitly disclaimed any statistical consequence ('I did not measure size and do not claim the p-value is invalid'). There IS one, and it is measurable: the permutation null distribution is 13-20% TIGHTER on the full data against about 3% Monte Carlo noise at 600 reps, in the same direction on all three seeds, so every p is smaller; at one seed the 5% verdict flips (.0499 vs .0799, though that single gap is only about 3 MC SEs and is an illustration, not the evidence). The mechanism is countable: the 20-cluster design gives a replication 8x(16/20)=6.4 live treated clusters against the observed run's 4, so its null is narrower than the observed statistic's. (2) 'the design is misreported to the user by four orders of magnitude' is not right. 317,444,400 is the arithmetically correct count FOR THE DESIGN WOOLDID RAN, and both designs are valid randomization models - the full design's exclusion of non-estimable assignments is conditioning on a deterministic function of the assignment with the observed assignment retained, which is a valid conditional test. The defensible criticisms are that the few-treated-cluster guard is silenced by clusters carrying no data, that nothing in the output says which design ran, and that the count calibrates the 'permreps() exceeds 10% of the possible assignments' advice.
refuter_did: Reproduced the reporting claims on my own 20-state panel with states 1-4 (treated) reporting no outcome: permsave() writes 20 onset columns (onset_1..onset_20) on the full data and 16 (onset_5..onset_20) on the oracle; reported possible assignments 317,444,400 vs 43,680; the caution 'only 4 of the resampling clusters are ever treated' fires on the ORACLE only; e(N)=320 both. My first run was uninformative about the p because both sat exactly on the add-one floor 2/301, so I re-ran (r3b_perm.do) at a weak effect with permreps 600 and the same rseed over three data seeds. Null permutation SD full vs oracle: .11977383/.15011282 (.798), .11848298/.13573510 (.873), .11484640/.13482312 (.852). p full vs oracle: .46589018/.50582363, .04991681/.07986689, .27287854/.37271215.

title: The advertised honestdid handoff on e(b_es_ame)/e(V_es_ame) returns a robust confidence set IDENTICAL at every M - it reports the continuous-treatment effect as fully robust to violations of parallel trends when it carries no pre-trend information at all

Delta^RM bounds the post-treatment violation by M * max|pre-period violation|; the pre-period coefficients are exactly 0 with exactly-0 variance, so that bound is 0 for every M. MITIGATION THAT EXISTS, stated honestly: the help names the precondition ('a covariance with no structurally degenerate rows (see e(es_ndegen_type))'), e(es_ndegen_ame)=3 is posted and survives estimates save/use, and two run-time cautions fire at estimation. Nothing blocks or warns at the point of use, and honestdid's own output is indistinguishable from a legitimate insensitive result.
expected: A Rambachan-Roth sensitivity analysis whose pre-period covariance is degenerate should either refuse or be refused. Returning an M-invariant confidence set is the single most dangerous possible output: it is maximally reassuring, it is the exact conclusion the method exists to prevent a researcher from drawing, and the user's only cue is a caution that has scrolled away by the time they run honestdid. The M-invariance is honestdid's own behaviour given ANY degenerate pre block -- demonstrated with a hand-built matrix and no wooldid in the session -- so wooldid computes none of it and no change short of withholding the matrix could prevent it. What wooldid does do, all measured: ado:4160 prints a caution at estimation that NAMES THE CONSUMER ('inspect the diagonal before joint inference - honestdid/lincom on those rows is not meaningful'); sthlp:1321 makes 'a covariance with no structurally degenerate rows (see e(es_ndegen_type))' a REQUIRED condition of the positional handoff; sthlp:1322 states that geometry violations hand honestdid the wrong geometry SILENTLY, i.e. silence at the point of use is the documented character of a positional handoff; and e(es_ndegen_ame)=3 survives estimates save/use. Documented precondition + named-consumer caution + machine-readable flag leaves a UX defect, not a high-severity inference failure. Sharpening the case in the prober's favour: the OTHER handoff the same help advertises (sthlp:802, Roth's pretrends) REFUSES loudly on identical inputs (r198, 'PreTrendsPower(): Power level .5% too high ... PreTrendsBisect(): Invalid starting points') while working on att (slope for 50% power = .10215).
refuter_did: Reproduced the M-invariance on my own data (iid: ame CI [-0.3430373248, 4.828910034] identical at M = 0, 0.5, 1.0; cluster(hid): [-0.2242453055, 4.659319125] at all three; att on the same run widens [-0.227,0.502]/[-0.338,0.554]/[-0.510,0.621]). Then ran the decisive control the prober did not: a hand-built b = (0,0,0,1.2,1.0,0.8) with an exactly-zero 3x3 pre block and an ordinary post block, fed straight to honestdid with NO wooldid anywhere in the session. CTRL_M_INVARIANT_no_wooldid=1 ([0.6186186186, 1.783783784] at M = 0, 0.5 and 1.0); the same b with a non-degenerate pre block widens (CTRL2=0). honestdid delta(sd) dies r(3498) on the hand-built matrix too. I also read ado:4130-4165 and sthlp:1321-1325. Separately I tested the bootstrap neighbour: under bootstrap(standard) reps(100) the rebuilt e(V_es_ame) still carries the exact zeros AND still fires the caution and posts e(es_ndegen_ame)=3, and honestdid is M-invariant there too.

title: bootstrap(bayes) at G=10 rejects a true sharp null 16-20% of the time and its SE is statistically indistinguishable from the analytic SE it is offered as the remedy for
surface: bootstrap(bayes), bootdisplay(percentile|bc|wald)
claim: `bootstrap(bayes)` does not deliver nominal level at few clusters and is not narrower-or-better than the analytic cluster SE: at G=10 with cluster()==i, percentile p rejects a TRUE SHARP NULL at .163 [.085,.290] and bias-corrected at .204 [.115,.336] against nominal .0506/.0500, and its mean SE is 0.781 x the true Monte-Carlo sd versus the analytic path's 0.769 x — i.e. it does not repair the understatement that sthlp:255 names bootstrap() as the remedy for.
