observed: 49 draws, G=10 (6 treated clusters in 3 cohorts of 2, 4 never-treated), T=8, reps 79, y generated with NO dependence on onset. Arm A7 bootstrap(bayes), att: percentile .163 [.085,.290]; bc .204 [.115,.336]; wald .122 [.057,.242]. p-value ECDF at alpha = .05/.10/.20/.30 = .20/.22/.35/.41 (bc) — the whole distribution is shifted, not a tail artifact. Mean se 0.4130 = 0.781 x the true MC sd 0.5291; mean 95% width 1.6856 against the 2.0740 a correct interval needs. Mechanism (d03, 3 draws at reps=399, same seeds): sd(bayes replicate draws)/sd(standard replicate draws) = 0.812, against the 0.953 that Dirichlet(1,...,1) vs the multinomial pairs bootstrap predicts at G=10 (variance ratio G/(G+1)=0.909). On the same 49 draws the analytic path it replaces rejects .180 [.098,.308] with Wilson intervals that overlap, so the honest statement is 'no better', not 'worse'.
expected: Nominal 5%. wooldid's own help offers bootstrap() as the remedy for the few-cluster SE understatement, and ado:6491-6499 shows the author already knows the pairs bootstrap is badly sized at few TREATED clusters; the novel content here is that the Bayesian/Dirichlet variant does not escape it either, that its dispersion shortfall is larger than the Dirichlet-vs-multinomial theory predicts (0.812 vs 0.953), and that the measured level is 3-4x nominal on input an applied economist would plausibly bring.

title: bootstrap(standard) at G=10 halves the level distortion but does not remove it (.122 at nominal 5%)
surface: bootstrap(standard), bootdisplay(percentile|bc|wald)
claim: At G=10 with cluster()==i, `bootstrap(standard)` rejects a TRUE SHARP NULL at .122 [.057,.242] for both `att` and `att_i`, identically across all three bootdisplay() families, against nominal .0500/.0506.
observed: 49 draws, arm A5: percentile/bc/wald all .122 [.057,.242] for att and for att_i — 6 of 49 draws, the same draws in every family. Mean se 0.4888 = 0.924 x the true MC sd 0.5291 (mean 95% width 2.0307 vs the required 2.0740). p ECDF at .05/.10/.20/.30 = .12/.18/.27/.37. Replication census: completed min 75 of 79, so up to 4 replications failed on a clean null draw (noted, not itself a finding). A5's `att` row is in the reid regime because att_i is requested; on a 2-draw smoke the A5 att statistic matched the A8 (no-att_i) att to the printed precision, consistent with the help's statement that frequency reweighting and physical resampling give the same att statistic.
expected: Nominal 5%. bootstrap(standard) is the option the help names as the few-cluster remedy; 0.924 x truth is a real improvement over the analytic 0.769 x but leaves 2.4x nominal level. This is the quantitative gap between what bootstrap() is offered for and what it delivers at G=10.

title: Contradicts a §7 known_bydesign entry: bootstrap(standard) at cluster()==i does NOT over-cover att_i on a neighbouring geometry
surface: bootstrap(standard) coverage of att_i under cluster()==i
claim: The §7 record that bootstrap(standard) with cluster()==i OVER-covers att_i (149/150 = .9933) does not generalize: on a design that differs only in having two states per onset cohort instead of one, measured coverage of att_i is .878 (rejection .122 [.057,.242]) — under-coverage, not over-coverage.
observed: 49 draws at G=10 = 3 cohorts x 2 treated states + 4 never-treated, cluster(st) with i==st, permreps/reps 79. att_i CI-exclusion of the true null value: .122 [.057,.242] in all three bootdisplay families, i.e. coverage .878 [.758,.943]. The §7 figure .9933 lies outside that interval. The likely mechanism is geometry: with one state per cohort the cohort-specific effect is a single cluster's mean and the pairs bootstrap degenerates toward over-dispersion; with two it does not.
expected: If the §7 entry is read as a general property of bootstrap(standard) at cluster()==i, a neighbouring realistic geometry should also over-cover. It does not, so the entry is geometry-specific and should be scoped. I mark this uncertain because I did not rebuild the §7 design itself (one state per cohort) and compare head-to-head on identical draws; that is the single experiment that would settle it.

title: boottstat is correctly sized but pays for it with intervals ~2.7x too wide at the median and 22x at the worst draw, on a path whose coverage the help says has not been measured
surface: boottstat, bootdisplay(tpercentile)
claim: At G=10, `boottstat` rejects a true sharp null at .025 [.004,.129] — correctly sized or conservative — but its 95% intervals have median width 5.69, mean 7.98, p90 14.4 and max 45.1, against the 2.0740 that a correctly calibrated 95% interval for this estimator needs. sthlp:550 states this path's coverage has not been measured; it now has been, and the answer is that the level is fine and the length is not.
observed: 40 draws, arm A6 bootstrap + boottstat: tpctl rejection att .025 [.004,.129], att_i .025 [.004,.129]; p ECDF at .05/.10/.20/.30 = .03/.03/.15/.25. 95% interval width median 5.69, mean 7.98, p90 14.4, max 45.1, against the true-sd-implied 2.0740. (The 'mean se 0.4155' that appears in my Table 2 for A6 is the ANALYTIC se that boottstat reports alongside, not the studentized interval's dispersion — the width quantiles are the right statistic.) Completion census clean at min 77 of 79.
expected: A studentized bootstrap should be roughly correctly sized AND of roughly correct length. Correct level with a median 2.7x over-length means the path is buying its size with power, which a user reading only the p-value will not see. This is a measurement of an explicitly unmeasured path, so it is documentation-completing rather than a wrong number.

title: The analytic joint horizon test rejects a true sharp null 75.5% of the time at nominal 5% — far outside the 11-36% oversizing the project documents
surface: jointtests / adversarial with the analytic VCE at few clusters
claim: On a G=10 event-study spec with `jointtests`, the ANALYTIC joint test over event-study horizons rejects a TRUE SHARP NULL at .755 [.619,.854] at nominal 5%. The project's own record characterises the analytic joint/adversarial tests as oversized at 11-36%; .755 is 2-7x that band and its Wilson lower bound .619 clears .36 decisively. The adversarial test at .286 [.178,.424] does sit inside the documented band.
observed: 49 draws, arm A9 = wooldid ... att att_i, esprelength/espostlength, esfixedbaseperiod, jointtests, adversarial, analytic VCE, cluster(st), G=10: joint-over-horizons rejection .755 [.619,.854]; p ECDF at .05/.10/.20/.30/.50 = .76/.78/.84/.86/.96 — the p-value distribution is crushed against zero, not merely tail-heavy. Adversarial .286 [.178,.424]. On the SAME DGP the rewired engines are fine: permutation joint .050 [.014,.165], permutation adversarial .000 [.000,.088], bootstrap joint .025 [.004,.129] (40 draws each).
expected: Nominal 5%, or at worst the documented 11-36%. A joint Wald over many horizons with a rank-deficient few-cluster VCV degrades much faster than the single-coefficient tests the 11-36% figure was derived from; a user with 10 clusters who reads a joint pre-trend/horizon p is reading a statistic that fires three times in four under a literally true null. The finding is the magnitude, not the sign: the direction was known, the size was understated.

title: level(99.9) - and a session `set level 99.9` with no level() option at all - make wooldid exit r(198) with a message that contradicts what the user typed
surface: level(), set level, e(level), the lb_<L>ci/ub_<L>ci column-naming contract
claim: wooldid refuses level(99.9), level(90.1) and level(99.99) with 'level() can have at most two digits after the decimal point' (99.9 has one), while `regress ..., level(99.9)` and `set level 99.9` are both accepted by Stata on the same data; and after `set level 99.9`, a wooldid call with NO level() option fails the same way, so the command is unusable in that session.
observed: Grid of 12 levels, each put to regress/set level/wooldid: regress rc 0 for all 12; set level rc 0 for all 12; wooldid rc 0 for 90, 95, 99, 97.5, 99.5, 68.5, 99.95, 68.3, 92.5 and rc 198 for 99.9, 90.1, 99.99. Second route: `set level 99.9` (rc 0), then `wooldid y id t ttre, att att_i att_it att_itime esfixedbaseperiod esprelength(3) espostlength(3)` with no level() -> the message twice, r(198), and e() still holds the previous run (e(level)=92.5, columns lb_92p5ci/ub_92p5ci), so a scripted read silently gets the wrong interval. Mechanism measured: a Stata `real' macro-expands with %18.0g; `local x = 99.9' gives 99.90000000000001, 90.1 gives 90.09999999999999, 99.99 gives 99.98999999999999, while 68.3/99.95/92.5/97.5/99.5 round-trip clean. The failing set is exactly the set whose expansion shows more than two decimals, which `set level' refuses.
expected: Every other Stata estimation command accepts level(99.9). The help at sthlp:1310 documents the interval-column naming rule for fractional levels ('a fractional level writes its point as a p, so level(97.5) gives lb_97p5ci'), which implies lb_99p9ci should be reachable. Sites: ado:551 `syntax ... Level(real 0)`, ado:574-576 `if `level' != 0 { ... set level `level' }`, and ado:5507 `if `level' == 0 local level = c(level)` (which is why the no-option route fails too). Passing the user's literal text through, or `set level `=round(`level',0.01)'`, closes both routes.

title: e(V_es_<fam>) is singular with a strictly positive diagonal, and e(es_ndegen_<fam>) is a diagonal-only scan, so the help's "its absence marks a clean covariance" is false
surface: e(V_es_<fam>), e(es_ndegen_<fam>), cluster(), the honestdid/pretrends handoff
claim: On a plain binary staggered design with cluster() and a unit-level i, e(V_es_att) comes back rank 6 of 8 with every diagonal entry strictly positive and e(es_ndegen_att) not posted; the help states that the absence of e(es_ndegen_<type>) marks a clean covariance, and ado:4130-4136 computes that count by scanning only the diagonal, so no rank or eigenvalue check stands between a singular block and pretrends/pretrendpower()/lincom/test/cholesky.
observed: 120 units x 12 periods, 3 treated cohorts at t=4/7/10 + never-treated, clu=ceil(id/6), att att_i att_it att_itime esfixedbaseperiod esprelength(3) espostlength(5) (H=8). cluster(clu): e(V_es_att) 8x8 rank 6, eigenvalues -8.35e-17 -8.37e-18 4.09e-04 2.60e-03 8.44e-03 3.09e-02 7.89e-02 1.77e-01, min diagonal 1.57e-02, e(es_ndegen_att) ABSENT, cholesky(makesymmetric(.)) returns 36 missing cells with rc 0, and rank(e(V)) = 20 of K=24. Same data iid: rank 8. Same data robust: rank 8. `att` alone + cluster: the identical rank-6 matrix (so it is not the estimand set). Narrow window esprelength(2) espostlength(2): rank 4 of 4. CONTROL on the design the help endorses (i = cohort + fe(id)): rank 8 of 8 and cholesky clean under cluster(), robust and iid alike. Wider variants in p11_singular.log: att block 12x12 rank 9; a subgroup geometry giving rank(e(V)) 68 of 76.
expected: The help's e(b_es_*)/e(V_es_*) entry promises '...flagged by a Caution and by e(es_ndegen_<type>) (the count of degenerate rows, posted only when such rows exist - its absence marks a clean covariance)'. Here the absence marks a rank-6-of-8 matrix. The statistical hazard of cluster() with a unit-level i IS documented in prose in the 'Design conditions for every consumer of e(V_es_*)' block, so I grade this MEDIUM rather than high: what fails is the machine-readable marker a script would rely on, and the diagnosis is one line - add rank() or a smallest-eigenvalue test beside the diagonal loop at ado:4130-4136. Note the unit-level i + cluster() geometry is the most common way this command is run.

title: A run that reports r(198) can leave a COMPLETE, CORRECT wooldid e(), and the replay refusal then tells the user something false about it
surface: wooldid_display (ado:11577), subgroups() + adversarial, the bare-wooldid replay refusal
claim: A failure after ereturn post (ado:4051) and after `ereturn local cmd "wooldid"` (ado:4198) leaves e(cmd)=wooldid with a byte-for-byte complete and correct result surface, yet the call reports an error and the bare-wooldid replay refuses with 'the stored results predate that failed call' - which is false, they ARE that call's results; the crash site is a READ of an over-long e() name in wooldid_display (ado:11577), not a post, so the sthlp:1293-1299 'silently skipped' contract cannot apply.
observed: `wooldid y id t ttre, att esfixedbaseperiod esprelength(3) espostlength(3) subgroups(sg8) jointtests adversarial cluster(clu)` with sg8 in {10000000,10000001}: the full main table, ES table and joint tests all PRINT, then 'adversarial_pval_att_it_s10000000 invalid name' and r(198). Afterwards e(cmd)=wooldid, colsof(e(b))=24, and the e() name set is the SAME 77 entries (34 scalars) as the identical run with 7-digit subgroup values that exits rc 0. lincom main_att -> rc 0, est 3.0946, se 0.30871. estimates store -> rc 0. Bare wooldid -> r(198) with the message above. `macro drop WOOLDID_LASTRC` then bare wooldid -> r(198) again, because the replay re-enters the same display. Site: ado:11577 `if e(adversarial_pval_`typetext'_s`sgcase') < .`; adversarial_pval_att_it_s10000000 is 33 characters, and referencing e(<33-char name>) is a hard r(198). The matching posting site ado:4349 is gated on `cap confirm matrix` and never ran for att_it, so nothing is missing from e().
expected: Stata convention is that an estimation command either succeeds and posts results or fails and does not claim them. Here the estimation is complete and every stored result is correct, yet it is reported as a failure and made unreachable through wooldid's own replay. The general half of this - that the replay refusal's wording 'the stored results predate that failed call' is wrong for EVERY failure after ado:4051 (any display- or plot-stage failure) - is not specific to long names. Scope note: the r(198) itself is inside the ruled 8-digit-subgroup caution family (wooldid_solved_issues.md:180; the help names `adversarial` as exposed), so do not re-file that; what is new is that the site is a READ that a strlen guard would turn into one skipped display line, and the false message.

title: Failure-site enumeration: only 3 of 20 sites destroy the prior e(), one of them is new, and the replay-staleness message never fires for exactly those 3
surface: the rc-gated shell epilogue (ado:60-100), e(cmd), the bare-wooldid replay guard, ccc_absorb(), contreat()
claim: Of twenty distinct wooldid failure sites, only three leave reghdfe's internal saturated model in e() - contreat() with a unit-level i (r322), an 8-digit subgroups() name overflow (r198), and ccc_absorb() with a unit-level i (r459, NOT on recon F1's list) - the other seventeen leave the user's previous good wooldid e() completely intact; user-owned estimates/matrices/scalars/Mata functions always survive; and in the reghdfe state the bare-wooldid replay guard cannot fire because it is keyed on e(cmd)=="wooldid", so the user gets a parse error about missing variables instead of the staleness message.
observed: Baseline before every site: e(cmd)=wooldid, K=16, N=1440, plus a user `estimates store USERM`, a user matrix and a user scalar. Destroying sites: F08 contreat(dose) with i=unit -> rc 322, e(cmd)=reghdfe, K=963, e(sample) N=1440; F10 8-digit subgroups + four estimands -> rc 198, e(cmd)=reghdfe, K=1058; F16 ccc_absorb(id) -> rc 459, e(cmd)=reghdfe, K=2 and e(sample) marks 768 observations, a DIFFERENT sample from the user's own run. Non-destroying (e(cmd)=wooldid, K=16, N=1440 preserved): bad option, too few variables, missing variable, bad if, no never-treated, negative weights, fweights, contreat without contreatcontrols, straddling subgroup, permreps(10), stray reps(), poisson on negative y, pretrendpower with no pre periods, empty if, one-cluster bootstrap. User objects survive on all twenty (estM1=1 mat=1 scal=1 matafn=1). Consumers after F08: ereturn display rc 0 (prints 963 internal cell dummies), predict r(111), predict xb r(111), estimates store rc 0, test rc 0, estat vce rc 0, bare wooldid r(198) 'command line input should feature all of y i t ttre; too few variables specified.'
expected: recon F1 claimed the reghdfe state is reached by failures 'at or after the internal regression' and that 'predict silently predicts from the internal saturated regression'. Measured: predict errors r(111) (the model's regressors are tempvars that no longer exist), which is the good news; the destruction is narrower than F1 implies (3 of 20 sites); ccc_absorb is a new site and the worst one because e(sample) then marks a different sample; and the shell's replay-staleness refusal at ado:26 is unreachable in exactly the state it exists to warn about, because e(cmd) is reghdfe there. The hypothesis that a failed wooldid destroys the caller's own estimates/matrices/Mata is FALSE - the epilogue drops only its own named tempname estimates (ado:90-97) and `matrix drop _all`/`clear mata` are reachable only through the opt-in cleanmatrices.

title: [aw=] and [pw=] leave no trace in e(), and e(vce) reads 'ols' under pweights although the standard errors ARE robust
surface: weights ([aw=]/[pw=]), e(wtype), e(wexp), e(vce), e(vcetype), the ereturn post at ado:4051
claim: wooldid posts neither e(wtype) nor e(wexp) on any weighted run, and under [pw=] it posts e(vce)='ols' with an empty e(vcetype) even though the standard errors it computes are identical to the robust ones, so nothing in e() records that the run was weighted or that its VCE is robust.
observed: Same data, att + esfixedbaseperiod esprelength(3) espostlength(3): [pw=pw] -> se(att)=0.210058487, e(vce)=ols, e(vcetype) empty, e(wtype) empty, e(wexp) empty; [aw=pw] robust -> se(att)=0.210058487 (identical to nine decimals), e(vce)=robust, e(vcetype)=Robust; [aw=pw] -> se=0.176744105, e(vce)=ols; unweighted -> se=0.167907539. [fw=] r(198) (documented refusal), [iw=] r(101). So the estimator is doing the right thing under pweights and only the e() labels are wrong. Cause: the single `ereturn post` at ado:4051 is `ereturn post `eb' `ev', esample(`esamp') depname(`y') obs(`N') dof(`df_r')` - no weight clause - and nothing later posts e(wtype)/e(wexp).
expected: e(wtype)/e(wexp) are the two entries every Stata estimation command posts to record its weights; esttab, estimates table and any replication script read them, so a stored .ster cannot currently tell a weighted run from an unweighted one. And [pw=] implies a robust VCE in every Stata command, so e(vce)='ols' misreports it - compare cluster(), which correctly posts e(vce)=cluster, e(vcetype)=Robust, e(clustvar) and e(N_clust). This is the exact push-on recon F6 left open ('pweights (imply robust - does e(vce) say so?)'); the answer is no.

title: The help names e(b) subgroup coefficients with a suffix the code never produces
surface: subgroups(), e(b)/e(V) column names, sthlp:1306
claim: sthlp:1301-1306 - the paragraph that tells users what esttab, coefplot, lincom and test address a coefficient by - ends 'Under subgroups() each subgroup's rows take the suffix _s#', but ado:4015 injects an infix _SG<value>_ instead, so the documented form errors r(111) while the undocumented form works, and the string '_SG' appears zero times anywhere in wooldid.sthlp.
observed: wooldid y id t ttre, att att_i att_it att_itime esfixedbaseperiod esprelength(3) espostlength(3) subgroups(sg) cluster(clu): `lincom main_att_s1` -> r(111); `lincom main_att_s0` -> r(111); `lincom main_SG1_att` -> rc 0, est 3.0590; `test main_SG1_att = main_SG0_att` -> rc 0. Every OTHER subgroup-keyed e() name DOES use the documented suffix: e(b_es_att_s1) (matrix), e(numpre_att_s1) (scalar), e(wdidsgresults_1), e(escomp_s1). `grep -o '_SG' wooldid.sthlp` returns nothing.
expected: The one sentence in the help that tells a user how to address a subgroup coefficient should match what ado:4015 builds. The single exception among otherwise-consistent _s# naming is what makes it easy to trip over. This confirms the seeded recon F2 with a one-line repro; the code form is the intended one (it appears in the project's own internal records), so the help sentence is the defect.

title: After any failed wooldid, `estimates restore` gives back a valid result set that wooldid then refuses to replay, with a false explanation
surface: the bare-wooldid replay guard (ado:26-46, 78-82), WOOLDID_LASTRC, estimates store/restore
claim: The replay-staleness refusal is keyed on a session global WOOLDID_LASTRC that no `estimates restore` can clear, so after a failed call a user who restores a stored good wooldid result (e(cmd)=wooldid, valid b/V) is refused with 'the stored results predate that failed call' - which is untrue of the restored results - even though sthlp:1299 states est restore/est save are compatible with wooldid.
observed: good wooldid -> estimates store GOODM -> `wooldid y id t ttre, att subgroups(nosuchvar)` r(111), $WOOLDID_LASTRC=111 -> `estimates restore GOODM` rc 0, e(cmd)=wooldid, K=16 -> $WOOLDID_LASTRC still 111 -> bare `wooldid` r(198) with the 'predate that failed call' message. Same after a post-regression failure: P1_FAIL_RC=322 with e(cmd)=reghdfe, restore brings back K=16, P3_REPLAY_AFTER_RESTORE_RC=198. For contrast, recon F4's macro-drop defeat is confirmed: after the parse-stage failure, `macro drop WOOLDID_LASTRC` then bare wooldid replays the STALE results rc 0 with the OLD e(cmdline). The marker survives `clear` and `discard`, and `macro drop _all` clears it.
expected: The guard should distinguish 'the e() you are looking at predates the failed call' from 'the e() you are looking at was deliberately restored'. Keying it on something estimates restore carries - e.g. comparing e(cmdline) with the failed call's - or clearing WOOLDID_LASTRC when wooldid-labelled results arrive from elsewhere would close it. As it stands the guard is simultaneously too strict (refuses a valid restored result) and defeatable (macro drop replays a genuinely stale one).

title: Missing subgroup values on PRE-treatment rows silently share-weight the pretreatment and pre-trend rows while main:att_i stays exact, so one unit is weighted 1.00 and 0.25 in two rows of the same printed table
surface: subgroups() x pretreatment:att_i / att_itime x missing subgroup values on pre-treatment rows
claim: w_per_i is grouped by (posttreatment, i), so the pre-treatment bucket carries its own denominator. When a unit's subgroup label is unknown only on its pre-treatment rows, main:att_i for that subgroup is exactly right while pretreatment:att_i and pretreatment:att_itime are share-weighted. The subgroup table then reports two different effective sets of units under one heading, with no caution and nothing in e() that records it -- and the distorted side is the one that feeds jointtests pre-trend tests, e(escomp_s#), e(numpre_att_s#) and the honestdid handoff.
observed: PART 2 of the repro. Three sg1 units with pre-window deviations 0.2, 1.0 and 3.0 at relative years -3 and -2; unit 3's subgroup label is unknown before t=8. Clean run: main:att_i = 5.0000000000, pretreatment:att = att_it = att_i = att_itime = 0.7000000000, ES_att:pre3 = ES_att:pre2 = 1.4. Label-missing run: main:att_i = 5.0000000000 (UNCHANGED, exact), but pretreatment:att_i = pretreatment:att_itime = 0.2666666667 and ES_att:pre3 = pre2 = 0.6. 0.2666666667 is exactly the share-weighted pre figure 0.6/2.25 -- unit 3 carries weight 0.25 in the pre bucket and 1.00 in the post bucket -- against an equal-unit pre target of 0.2000000000, a 33% error. No caution; header reports 0 obs dropped.
expected: Either the equal-unit pre-treatment average the estimand label names, or the same r(459)/caution the split-unit case already gets. At minimum, the same unit should not carry weight 1.00 in the main:att_i row and 0.25 in the pretreatment:att_i row of one printed table with nothing saying so: a user reading a subgroup table naturally assumes the pre-trend rows and the effect rows describe the same set of units. Same root cause as fpsg-01, but a different reported row, a different weight bucket in the code, and a different set of downstream consumers -- the original prober probed only the post-treatment side.

title: poisson + contreat() always trips the ppmlhdfe rc-3200 fallback, on a one-level fixed effect wooldid itself constructed, and the caution blames the user's fe()
surface: poisson + contreat() + contreatcontrols(basic|untreatedZero); the ppmlhdfe rc-3200 fallback caution at ado:1464-1467
claim: Whenever poisson is combined with contreat() and a contreatcontrols() set that reduces to the pooled ringer head (basic, or untreatedZero), wooldid puts i.<a variable identically equal to 1>##c.(ringer) inside ppmlhdfe's absorb(). ppmlhdfe fails r(3200) on that one-level factor EVERY time, so the rc-3200 fallback always fires: the user is shown a caution that attributes the failure to 'an absorbed categorical fixed effect with only 1 level' and closes by telling them to look at 'the fe() specified', when they specified no fe() at all and the one-level fixed effect is wooldid's own construction; every such run silently takes the slower explicit-regressor path the caution calls 'computationally less efficient'; and that path is the collinearity-drop-order-sensitive one, which is the mechanism behind fp-contreat-E on poisson.
observed: R9, four legs on the same generated count panel (720 rows, 6 cohort groups, staggered onsets, Poisson outcome). Leg A, poisson + contreat(dose) + contreatcontrols(basic) with a dose defined everywhere: 'Caution: initial estimation of ppmlhdfe failed, possibly due to inclusion of an absorbed categorical fixed effect with only 1 level. / Falling back to estimation with ppmlhdfe, but with any included time-trend controls, ccc_absorb controls, and/or continuous treatment controls pulled out of the absorb() statement and placed in the main regression. / In principle, this fallback solution should usually yield the same results, but will be computationally less efficient. / If estimation still fails, the issue could be either with the fe() specified or a result of having few cohorts/time-periods.' rc 0. Leg B, poisson + contreatcontrols(untreatedZero): same caution, rc 0. CONTROL leg C, poisson + contreatcontrols(basic byTime): no caution, rc 0. CONTROL leg D, plain binary poisson with no contreat(): no caution, rc 0. The same caution also appeared unprompted in R2's poisson legs on a different panel and a different seed.
expected: The two controls pin the cause to wooldid's own construction rather than to the data or the user's specification: ado:1301-1303 clears ccringerheadabs exactly when a byX has made ccringertail non-empty, which is precisely the leg (basic byTime) that does not fire, and a run with no contreat() at all never builds the head and also does not fire. So the condition is deterministic and internal, not 'possibly due to' anything the user did. A caution that names a construct the user cannot see, and that closes by sending them to inspect an option they did not specify, is a predictable mis-read; and the fact that it fires on every poisson continuous-treatment run with the most common contreatcontrols() choice means the absorbing poisson path is effectively dead code there, with the documented efficiency penalty paid every time. The reason it rises above cosmetic is that the fallback is what routes poisson + contreatcontrols(untreatedZero) onto the explicit-regressor path whose collinearity drop order produces the wrong number in fp-contreat-E.

title: The help's p-value MAP gives the wrong floor for permexact's default convention: it says 1/M, the measured floor is 2/M
surface: permute() + permexact, the help's p-value map (wooldid.sthlp line 607; secondary, line 608)
claim: sthlp:607, the 'permute() + permexact' row of the table the help introduces with 'This table is the map', under a column header reading 'convention, and the smallest p it can print', states 'Floor 1/M'. Under the default (equal-tailed 2 min(P_lo, P_hi)) convention -- the one in force unless the user names permabsp, permside() or permrawp -- the smallest p a permexact run can print is 2/M, not 1/M. The help's own prose (sthlp:512) and wooldid's own runtime caution (ado:7876) both state 2/M for the default; only the map row disagrees.
observed: 6 clusters, onsets 5,5,7,.,.,. -> M = 6!/(2!1!3!) = 60, with a large clean effect so the observed statistic is the extreme of its own enumeration and the reported p sits AT the floor. Default (no convention option): e(perm_p) main_att = .03333333333333330 = 2/60, with e(perm_p_hi) = .01666666666666670 = 1/60 (the one-sided share does reach 1/M; the reported two-sided p doubles it). permabsp: e(perm_p) = .01666666666666670 = 1/60. permside(right): = 1/60. permrawp: = 1/60. Corroborated on two other designs: M = 30 gives default att p = .0667 = 2/30 (r1b_px1.log) and M = 48 gives .0416667 = 2/48 (r4_oracle.py, matched by an independent Python oracle). Secondary instance in the same table: the 'permute(), joint and equality tests' row says add-one with floor 1/(n+1) unconditionally, while ado:16244 uses nex/n under permexact -- measured joint pre-trend p = 0.9833 = 59/60, a multiple of 1/M.
expected: The reported default p is min(1, 2 min(P_lo, P_hi)) on plain shares under permexact, and the observed assignment is a member of its own reference set, so min(P_lo, P_hi) >= 1/M and the reported p >= 2/M with 1/M unattainable. The help says so itself at sthlp:512 -- 'under permexact with M assignments it is 2/M under the default and 1/M under the absolute-value conventions' -- and wooldid PRINTS it: the incomplete-enumeration caution at ado:7876 reads 'the smallest attainable p is 2/n under the default convention (1/n under the absolute-value and one-sided conventions) rather than 2/`wdp_R''. Every other row of the map is convention-specific and states the right floor (default sampled 2/(n+1), permabsp 1/(n+1), permside 1/(n+1)); only the permexact row collapses the conventions and takes the absolute-value number. It matters because permexact is what wooldid's own runtime caution recommends when fewer than six clusters are ever treated (ado:6070, 'permexact enumerates the assignments and reports the exact floor'), i.e. exactly where M is small and the floor binds: at M = 30 the map promises a reachable .033 where the truth is .067, and the two straddle .05, so a user sizing a randomization-inference design is told it can reach significance when it cannot.

title: impvalues under-covers (0.82-0.86 at nominal 0.95) even at i = unit with cluster(unit), the geometry where Ibragimov-Muller is textbook-legitimate
surface: impvalues with i = unit and cluster(unit); the reported se/t/p/lb_*ci/ub_*ci on the att row
claim: The impvalues under-coverage is not confined to the finer-than-i geometry of mcci-01. With i = unit and cluster(unit) -- 45 treated clusters, each owning its own cohort-by-relative-period coefficients, so the per-cluster reads are 45 distinct numbers and no multiplicity exists -- the reported IM standard error is only ~0.66-0.70 of the estimator's actual sampling standard deviation and the nominal 95% interval covers 0.82-0.86. impvalues is therefore WORSE than the analytic path it is offered as an alternative to, in the commonest geometry an applied user will write down.
observed: 100-draw MC (p5_imunit.do): impvalues sd(b) 0.1249, mean(se) 0.0827, se/sd 0.662; 95% coverage 0.820 vs the att truth, 0.830 vs the cluster-equal-weighted truth, 0.840 around its own MC mean; e(df_r)=44. Analytic cluster(unit) on the same draws: sd(b) 0.1273, mean(se) 0.1153, se/sd 0.906, coverage 0.890. The self-contained repro on 80 draws: impvalues se/sd 0.702, coverage 0.850/0.863/0.863; analytic se/sd 0.967, coverage 0.900. 3 binomial SE at p=.95 is 0.065 (n=100) and 0.073 (n=80), so both coverage figures sit 4-6 SE below nominal. No caution is printed. Single-run corroboration (p4_mech.do B1/B2): impvalues se 0.069774 vs analytic 0.123567 on identical data.
expected: An interval reported at level(95) should cover about 95% of the time, and mean(se) should be within sampling error of sd(b). sthlp:257 and sthlp:1096-1097 present impvalues as the cross-cluster dispersion inference that 'remains valid' where the analytic path is not, and it is the only single-run alternative the help offers besides bootstrap/permute. The analytic arm's 0.890 here is the already-documented at-or-above-i understatement (known_bydesign section 1); what is new and undocumented is that the IM arm is worse still. The mechanism is HYPOTHESIZED, not measured: the 45 reads are distinct but plausibly positively correlated, since every treated unit's effect is measured against the same never-treated comparison group and the same estimated period effects, while IM's sd/sqrt(G) assumes independence across clusters. The finding stands on the coverage and se/sd numbers alone.

title: A cluster with no rows in the estimation sample counts toward every cluster-count screen, so both few-cluster cautions go silent on the run that most needs them
surface: bootstrap(standard) + cluster(); the cluster-count screens in wooldid_bootctl at ado:6459-6498 (two-cluster refusal, <10-cluster caution, <6-treated-cluster caution)
claim: wooldid_bootctl builds its own sample concept at ado:6459-6462 (((if)==1) & !missing(cluster), with no outcome/control/weight markout) and every cluster-count screen hangs off it: the two-cluster refusal (ado:6464), the 'fewer than 10 clusters' caution (ado:6479) and the 'fewer than 6 treated clusters' caution (ado:6498). A cluster whose rows are all dropped by the estimator therefore still counts, so padding the file with clusters that contribute nothing suppresses both cautions. A bootstrap that actually runs on 5 clusters is told nothing about it, while the identical estimation sample with the dead rows removed gets both warnings -- and in the same output the run prints 'N clusters = 5' beside a t(19) reference distribution.
observed: Block A (20 counties in the file, outcome collected in only 5; 80 plants, T=8; bootstrap(standard) cluster(county) reps(60) bootdf(clusters) bootdisplay(wald)): NEITHER caution is printed. The header reads 'N clusters = 5; N = 160 (480 obs dropped from initial sample)', e(N_clust)=5, e(df_r)=e(boot_df)=19. Block B, the control with the same estimation sample and the 15 dead counties physically dropped: BOTH cautions print -- 'Caution: only 5 clusters are available for the bootstrap; bootstrap inference is unreliable with very few clusters.' and 'Caution: only 5 treated cluster(s) are available for resampling ... with few treated clusters the literature finds this bootstrap badly sized (MacKinnon and Webb 2017, 2018) ...' -- and e(df_r)=e(boot_df)=4. Point estimates are identical between the two (att_i = 1.0836262589). Grep the log for 'clusters are available' to see the presence/absence directly.
expected: The cautions exist precisely to flag the setting the pairs cluster bootstrap is worst in, and the help's own bootstrap() entry says so at length ('Neither mode is a remedy for few treated clusters'). Which clusters are 'available for the bootstrap' should be the clusters that can contribute to a replication, i.e. the ones with rows in e(sample) -- the same count the run's own header prints as 'N clusters'. A cluster whose every row is dropped cannot contribute to any replication, so counting it toward a few-cluster screen inverts the screen's purpose: the more dead clusters the file carries, the quieter wooldid gets. Not tested and not claimed: whether the two-cluster refusal itself can be evaded this way (the df_r<1 guard at ado:1520 may catch that case first).

title: permute() builds its randomization design on the user-if universe too, so units with no estimable row are shuffled treatment onsets: 18 assignment slots for 12 estimation clusters
surface: permute(shuffle) / permsave() onset_ columns / permexact support count / the permutation shift interval
claim: Two runs with a bit-identical estimation sample (same e(N), same e(N_clust), same point estimate) get different permutation inference merely because units whose outcome is entirely missing are left in the data file: wooldid_permrun's cluster map is built from the raw user `if` alone (ado:7479-7488) with the ado:682/ado:704 markout never applied, so those units are clusters in the shuffle and receive treatment onsets that belong to data-bearing clusters. The reference distribution is therefore the randomization distribution of a systematically weaker design than the one the observed statistic came from.
observed: 12 real units (4 treated 2004, 4 treated 2006, 4 never) plus 6 units with y missing on every row (3 with onset 2004, 3 never). permute(shuffle), permreps(40), cluster(unit), permsave(). ARM A (extras in file): e(N)=120, e(N_clust)=12, att=+1.83bca602bfc4cX-001, but permsave writes 18 onset_ columns; onset_14 - a unit with no data - exists and is NON-MISSING, i.e. it was assigned a treatment onset, in 24 of the 40 replications. ARM B (extras deleted): e(N)=120, e(N_clust)=12, att identical, 12 onset_ columns, onset_14 absent (r(111)). The reported att interval moved with it: lb_95ci 0.2272 in ARM A vs 0.4141 in ARM B on the same estimate 0.75729865 and the same p_perm 0.049 (the null band's upper end 0.5301 vs 0.3432).
expected: 18 shuffle slots for 12 estimation clusters. 11 of the 18 clusters carry an onset, so in expectation 6 x 11/18 = 3.67 of the 11 treatment onsets land on a unit with no data in EVERY replication, leaving about 7.3 data-bearing treated clusters against the observed run's 8. That is a deterministic property of the design, not Monte Carlo: every replication's statistic is computed on a weaker design than the observed one, so the null distribution is not the randomization distribution of the design that produced the observed statistic. The support count wdp_npd that drives the 'only one possible assignment' refusal (ado:7547) and the permexact enumeration is computed over the same inflated cluster set, so permexact enumerates assignments that are duplicates as far as the data are concerned. Caveat I will not paper over: whether including a data-less unit in the shuffle is WRONG depends on whether that unit was part of the assignment mechanism (attrition -> arguably right) or is a junk row (-> wrong), and wooldid cannot know. What is not defensible is that it is undocumented and that it contradicts e(N_clust) in the same ereturn. I did not claim the 82% move in lb_95ci is all systematic: at permreps(40) a .975 quantile is nearly the maximum draw and the two arms run different RNG streams. The deterministic part is the 18-vs-12 universe and the 24/40 onsets assigned to a data-less unit.

title: permute()'s fast-mode default silently disables the only diagnostic wooldid owns for "this control has no within-cohort-period variation"
surface: permute() fast-mode default x interactivecontrols() reduction caution (ado:12706, ado:5414-5418, sthlp:1068)
claim: The interactivecontrols() reduction caution documented at sthlp:1068 and emitted at ado:12706 is suppressed on the permute() default path, because since 2026-09-05 the observed run under permute() takes the fastnose path unless permtstat/permanalyticse (ado:5414-5418) and the check does not run under fastnose. The user never typed fastnose, is not told the check was skipped, and loses it on exactly the path where a control with no within-cohort variation is most consequential -- under permonsetcohorts such a control goes live inside every replication.
observed: Same specification, three ways. (1) `wooldid y coh t onset, att cluster(state) interactivecontrols(cohbase)` prints 'Caution: every treated cohort-period slope term for the interactive control coh... was dropped for multicollinearity'. (2) The same command plus `permute(shuffle) permreps(20) permonsetcohorts` prints that caution NOWHERE in its output. (3) The same command plus `permanalyticse` prints it again. Verified in repro_NF1_iccaution.log at lines 202 (block 1), absent in block 2, and 379 (block 3). The consequence on the permute path is not cosmetic: on my panel the observed run collapses to controls(i.t#c.x) while every replication estimates the full interactive model, and the reference distribution changes accordingly -- null SD .5175 with the rebuild (cluster(state)) against .2555 without it (cluster(coh)), p .943 against .667.
expected: Either the caution fires whenever the reduction happens, or the run says the check was skipped. The expectation holds because the caution exists precisely to tell the user that the model they wrote is not the model that was estimated, and the permute() fast-mode default is a wooldid-internal optimisation the user did not ask for: sthlp:1068 scopes the suppression to an explicit `fastnose`, and the permute() help documents the fast-mode default in a different section, so nothing tells a reader that writing permute() removes a warning. Two separately documented facts compose into an undocumented one, and the composition removes the only warning in the package that names this exact condition.

title: The unclustered leg T2 opened returns standard errors ~36% too wide on a panel, and the revisit the ticket asked for was never done
surface: bootstrap(standard) + att_i/att_it/att_itime with no cluster() — the third refusal T2 deleted
claim: bootstrap(standard) with a cell-weighted estimand and no cluster() — refused r198 at old ado:6353 and legal since 2026-09-16 — resamples observations and produces se(att_i) about 36% larger than the true sampling SD on an ordinary panel, with no caution and nothing in the help about its calibration.
observed: 12 hospital systems x 5 hospitals, T=6, onset at system level, i = system, hospital random effect sd .8 plus iid sd 1, tau_s FIXED across the Monte Carlo. Oracle = MC SD of att_i over 60 redraws of the noise = 0.21252. bootstrap cluster(hosp) (the keep-i branch, cluster strictly below i): .21398 .20873 .27769, mean .23346, ratio 1.099. bootstrap with NO cluster(): .29362 .29409 .28238, mean .29003, ratio 1.365, and 1.33-1.38 on every one of the three datasets. n01_keepi_oracle.do corroborates on the same design: analytic cluster(hosp) mean .22913 (ratio 1.078), so the keep-i branch agrees with the legitimate analytic reference while the unclustered leg does not agree with either.
expected: A bootstrap standard error should approximate the sampling SD of the estimator; the keep-i branch does (within what 3 datasets and a 60-draw oracle can resolve) and the observation leg does not. The mechanism is the one the deleted refusal named at old ado:6353 — 'observation-level resampling cannot re-identify duplicated treatment cells' — observation draws fragment units and cells rather than redrawing them, which adds variance the real sampling process does not have. T2's own ticket text says of that refusal: 'Once weights are recomputed per replication, revisit whether that refusal is still necessary or can be relaxed to observation-level resampling.' It was relaxed; this is what the revisit measures. sthlp:241 states only the mechanism ('With no cluster() at all the resampling is observation-level') and nothing about calibration. Severity medium rather than high because the direction is conservative and the user did choose not to cluster; probable rather than certain because 3 datasets x reps(99) against a 60-draw oracle is a small measurement, though the +36% is consistent across all three and 8 sd outside the keep-i arm's scatter.

title: bootstrap()'s few-cluster and few-TREATED-cluster cautions are suppressed by a cluster that contributes no estimable row
surface: bootstrap() cluster-count cautions in wooldid_validate (ado:6460-6500), both bootstrap(standard) and bootstrap(bayes)
claim: wooldid_validate counts clusters for bootstrap()'s two count-based cautions over smp2 = ((if)==1) & !missing(cluster) (ado:6461), not over the estimation sample, so a cluster whose every row is discarded by markout inflates both counts and silences the caution. Two datasets with a bit-identical estimation sample and identical e(N)/e(N_clust) therefore differ in whether wooldid warns that the bootstrap is unreliable, and in particular whether it prints the few-treated-cluster warning the help itself calls the important one.
observed: e6_bootscreens.log. Arm A1, 9 real clusters (3 treated) plus one phantom never-treated cluster whose outcome is missing on every row: e(N)=216, e(N_clust)=9, and 'Caution: only 9 clusters are available for the bootstrap' is NOT printed. Arm A2, the phantom's rows dropped: same e(N)=216 and e(N_clust)=9, and the caution IS printed. Arm B1, 12 states of which 1-5 are treated with data and 6 is a treated phantom: e(N)=264, e(N_clust)=11, and the few-treated caution is NOT printed. Arm B2, the phantom's rows dropped: same e(N)=264, e(N_clust)=11, and 'Caution: only 5 treated cluster(s) are available for resampling. ... with few treated clusters the literature finds this bootstrap badly sized (MacKinnon and Webb 2017, 2018) ... Consider permute() ... or the wild cluster bootstrap-t' IS printed. e6b_controls.log repeats B with the phantom killed by a missing CONTROL instead of a missing outcome (controls(x1), x1 missing on every row of state 6): arm D1 prints no caution, arm D2 (rows dropped) prints 'only 5 treated cluster(s)'. All four pairs hold the estimation sample bit-identical.
expected: The two cautions describe what is available to the bootstrap engine, and what is available is the estimation sample: a cluster with no estimable row is never resampled into anything and contributes nothing to any replication. The expectation is also internal -- e(N_clust), which wooldid posts, already counts the right population (9 and 11 respectively), and the third screen in the same block, the two-cluster refusal, states its own population as 'in the estimation sample'. sthlp:430-431 documents the phantom-inclusive population for permute()'s randomization design and its possible-assignment count only; nothing in the bootstrap() entry extends it to these screens. The few-treated-cluster caution is the single warning that tells a user the pairs cluster bootstrap is badly sized in their design and redirects them to permute() or boottest; suppressing it leaves a user with exactly five estimable treated clusters reporting inference the help says is unreliable, with nothing in the output to hint at it.

title: semielasticity averages (dp/dx)/p over a subpopulation containing negative predictions and reports the result with se, t, p and a 95% interval, unscreened
surface: semielasticity (margins eydx) on the default linear path
claim: wooldid's semielasticity asks margins for eydx, which divides by the prediction, and wooldid never checks the sign of the divisor. On a panel where 14 of 720 fitted values are non-positive -- three of them inside the treated-and-post subpopulation the att is averaged over -- the run completes, prints 'Treatment Effects Presented as Semi-elasticities', and reports a point estimate with a standard error, t = 3.05, p = 0.003 and a 95% interval, with no caution of any kind. A '% change in y per unit change in x' is not defined at those rows, so the headline figure is contaminated to an extent the user is given no way to see.
observed: RF03 section A/C and R5b/R10 logs. Shift 2 of a plain 60x12 staggered panel: min(y) = -2.418, 30 of 720 raw values non-positive; refitting wooldid's own att-only specification gives min(fitted) = -1.362 with 14 non-positive fitted values, 3 of them inside the att subpopulation. wooldid returns rc 0 and prints `att | .23864029  .0783198  3.05  0.003  .08192275  .39535784` with no caution. Ladder across shifts 0..5: r(459), r(459), rc 0 (.23864029), rc 0 (.19509366), rc 0 (.16414207), rc 0 (.14149061); the non-positive fitted counts over the same shifts are 160/58/14/3/0/0 overall and 17/5/3/0/0/0 inside the subpopulation. Fitting att(c) = D/(m+c) to the ladder gives D = 1.0200, m = 2.2092 with every residual under 1.5%, so the contamination on this particular panel is a few percent -- but nothing bounds it, and the only thing between the user and an arbitrarily corrupted number is the point at which margins happens to give up with a bare error instead.
expected: wooldid screens comparable conditions and names them in its own words elsewhere -- the poisson perfect-separation message and the dose-slope screen -- and the cell-collapse eligibility caution that fires on THIS VERY RUN already says in as many words that 'semielasticity (and the contreat elasticity forms eyex and eydx) divide by the prediction'. Having identified the division, the run never looks at the sign of the divisor. The help's only hedge (sthlp:245) is that the option 'tends to require large samples and a y-variable that is not sparsely distributed'; nothing says the prediction must be strictly positive, and nothing warns that the estimate can be reported rather than refused when it is not.

title: A missing coefficient anywhere in the estimand vector costs the entire e(b): the run returns rc 0 having posted no coefficients, silently under fastnose and otherwise under a caution that says the opposite
surface: wooldid_worker's ereturn post fallback chain (ado:4051-4085) x fastnose
claim: ado:4051-4085 is a three-step post chain. `ereturn post eb ev` fails if any variance cell is missing; the partial-identification rescue is taken only when at least one variance is identified; `ereturn post eb` then fails if ANY COEFFICIENT is missing; and the last step, ado:4083, is a BARE `ereturn post` with no vector at all, which succeeds. The run therefore completes with rc 0 having posted no coefficients. Under fastnose the only caution on that path is gated off (`if evpostmiss > 0 & "`fastnose'" == ""`), so nothing is printed at all; otherwise the caution that does print says '...so no variance-covariance matrix e(V) was posted. Point estimates remain in e(b)', which is false precisely on the branch that just fired.
observed: R10 PART 2 demonstrates the PREMISE, not the full run: with B = (1.5, .) and V = I(2), `ereturn post B V` fails r(504) and `ereturn post B` fails r(504), while a bare `ereturn post` succeeds with rc 0 and leaves e(b) ABSENT (POST_bare_has_b=0). Reading the chain, that is exactly what ado:4082-4085 does. The end-to-end corroboration is the other agent's own log, probes/perm-interact/PX03_repro.log, which records precisely the state this path produces -- rc 0, e(cmd)=wooldid, a printed all-missing results table, and `matrix e(b) not found`. The author's own source comment at ado:5017 also names 'the data-dependent r(459)/missing-with-rc-0 behaviour' in passing. In 21 attempts on my own panels margins errored rather than returning missing, so I did not manufacture the missing coefficient myself. The designed fastnose path is intact and I verified it: with a non-missing b and an all-missing V, `ereturn post eb` succeeds, e(b) and e(b_es_att) and e(numpre_att) post, no e(V), no caution (R4_px01_sharp.log S3).
expected: A run that posted no coefficients should not return rc 0, and must not print a caution telling the reader the coefficients are in e(b). The caution's text should branch on which post actually succeeded, and the fastnose gate should suppress only the standard-error half of the sentence rather than the whole disclosure -- under fastnose, losing the coefficient vector is the one thing fast mode is NOT supposed to do, which is exactly why the silence there is the wrong default. semielasticity is only one way to get a missing coefficient into the vector; the `amevoid` case at ado:4026 is already special-cased by zeroing, which shows the author knows the hazard and has fixed exactly one instance of it.

title: Under the default cell collapse a plain wooldid run is not reproducible across a re-sort of the same data: the printed SEs, t, p and CI bounds move by up to 6.6e-06
surface: the default cell collapse (wooldid_fcol) x controls(); the pretreatment / event-study margins reads
claim: Running the identical default wooldid command twice on the identical dataset, changing only the order in which the rows are stored (sort unit t vs gsort -t -unit), changes the reported variance by 6.59e-06 relative on e(V) and 3.81e-06 on e(wdidmainresults), into the digits wooldid prints; the same two sorts under nofastcollapse agree to 2.45e-14. The cause is that the collapsed row keeps the cell's FIRST row's raw controls() value, so re-sorting changes which covariate value survives - verified by a one-line patched copy of the ado that carries the cell's weighted mean instead, after which the same permutation moves 1.38e-15.
observed: Two plain default runs, no option typed, same data, different sort order. RUN 1 pretreatment att se .11064425 lb -.24658272 ub .18749341; RUN 2 se .11064417 lb -.24658256 ub .18749324. RUN 1 pretreatment att_it se .11036045 ub .18727346; RUN 2 se .11036009 ub .18727275. Max relative move e(V) 6.59e-06, e(wdidmainresults) 3.81e-06. Same two sorts under nofastcollapse: 2.45e-14. Patched build (retained row carries the cell weighted mean of controls()): 1.38e-15.
expected: A run's reported standard errors must not depend on the storage order of the user's rows beyond machine precision - that is what the uncollapsed path delivers (2.45e-14), and the help's own calibration paragraph (sthlp:357) offers row-order sensitivity as a reassurance, telling the reader that permuting rows with the collapse OFF moves a near-zero coefficient about 19 times more than the collapse does. For variances under the default the ordering is reversed by eight to nine orders (6.59e-06 vs 1.32e-15). sthlp:350 also states that no digit wooldid displays is affected; the printed pretreatment standard errors and both confidence bounds differ between the two sorts. The project's indifference threshold is rtol 1e-10.

title: A COARSER cluster() can lower the reported standard error, reversing the conservatism every user expects from over-clustering
surface: cluster() on the default analytic path
claim: Applied practice treats 'cluster coarser than you need' as the safe direction. In wooldid, because the treated cohort-by-period dummies demean the residual across whatever sits inside the cell, a coarser cluster() puts FEWER clusters inside that cell and the reported standard error gets SMALLER. Nothing in the run or the help says so, and sthlp:255's 'cluster BELOW the level of i' does not distinguish 'below i' from 'as fine as the dependence actually is'.
observed: mc2_mech.do, 120 draws, on a DGP with no state-level dependence of any kind (units independent: unit RE + iid error; `state` is only a grouping label, so cluster(unit) is the correct level and cluster(state) is pure over-clustering). The two arms have identical point estimates, so the comparison of reported uncertainty is paired with no sampling-SD noise. mean SE with cluster(unit) vs cluster(state), and their ratio: main_att 0.1327 / 0.1170 = 0.882; ES_att_post0 0.1753 / 0.1519 = 0.867; post1 0.1699 / 0.1427 = 0.840; post2 0.1719 / 0.1547 = 0.900; post3 0.1723 / 0.1465 = 0.850; pre3 0.1719 / 0.1504 = 0.875; pre2 0.1780 / 0.1573 = 0.884. Mean ratio 0.871 against 0.853 predicted by sqrt(2/3)/sqrt(11/12). Coarsening from 160 clusters to 40 made every reported standard error 13% smaller.
expected: Moving to a coarser admissible cluster variable should never reduce a reported standard error; that is the direction users deliberately choose when unsure, and sthlp:255 reinforces it ('cluster BELOW the level of i'), which reads as 'anything below i is safe'. Honest scope: arm F is not itself well calibrated (1.136 of the sampling SD) because with i=coh the unit random effect is not absorbed and cluster(unit) picks it up in the scores although the estimator differences it out - both arms are miscalibrated in opposite directions and only the RATIO is a clean paired quantity, so the direction and the ~13% are established but the 0.853 constant is not precisely confirmed. mc2_noau.do is the clean control (same design with the unit random effect removed) and was still running when this was filed.

title: A stale $WOOLDID_LEVEL0 replaces the true return code with 198 and disarms the shell's rc-gated cleanup epilogue on every later parse-stage failure
surface: the WOOLDID_LEVEL0 restore in the wooldid shell (ado:68-71) and the rc-gated nobreak epilogue (ado:72-95)
claim: Once the wooldid shell's restore `set level $WOOLDID_LEVEL0` (ado:69) has failed once, the `macro drop WOOLDID_LEVEL0` on the next line is never reached, so the stale global persists; every subsequent wooldid call that fails BEFORE the worker's level block (ado:574-576) -- i.e. every parse-stage failure -- then re-runs the same failing, un-captured restore, which (a) replaces the call's true return code with 198 and (b) aborts the program before the rc-gated `nobreak` epilogue at ado:72-95, so the frame restore, the emptycells restore, the `est drop ___wooldidfullmodel` cleanup and the $WOOLDID_LASTRC update all fail to run.
observed: MEASURED (repro_SK_LEVEL.log, block 5): on a clean session `wooldid y uid t ttre, att robust cluster(nosuchvar)` returns rc=111 and sets LASTRC=[111]. After one poisoning call (`set level 99.9` then `wooldid ..., level(95)`, which leaves LEVEL0=[99.90000000000001]), the IDENTICAL bad-cluster call returns rc=198 and leaves LASTRC at the stale [111] and LEVEL0 still [99.90000000000001]. Both user messages still print ('variable nosuchvar not found' / '(error in option cluster())' then 'level() can have at most two digits after the decimal point'), so it is diagnosable, but the rc a caller's `if _rc == 111` branch sees is wrong. Also measured: a call that DOES reach the worker's level block refreshes the global and recovers (s4_level.log @@C2a-@@C2d, rc 0 each). INFERRED, not measured: the skipped `est drop ___wooldidfullmodel` and frame restore -- my parse-stage failures never created a fullmodel to leak, so I observed the epilogue skip only through the un-updated LASTRC; the rest follows from ado:72-95 lying past the point the aborted restore jumps from.
expected: ado:59-63 documents the shell as a thin wrapper that runs the worker under capture 'so that when a run fails midway, the caller's frame is restored and this run's scratch estimates are removed before the error is re-raised', and ado:64 states 'rc and error messages pass through exactly (exit, not error)'. Neither holds once LEVEL0 is stale: the rc does not pass through, and the epilogue that performs the B18/B22 cleanup never executes. ado:70's `macro drop WOOLDID_LEVEL0` is written as if the preceding `set level` cannot fail, and the restore at ado:69 is the one statement in the shell that is not under `capture`.

title: At i = unit the analytic ATT standard error degrades with the SIZE OF THE CONTROL POOL, reaching SE/SD 0.21 and 37% coverage at nominal 95%
surface: analytic clustered SEs at cluster() == i (att rows); interacts with safety()/si8 via the bootstrap remedy
claim: With the cohort variable i at the unit level and cluster(unit), wooldid's analytic ATT standard error is not merely 'understated at roughly 0.66 to 0.75 of the reference' as sthlp:251 states: the ratio is governed by the control-to-treated ratio and falls without bound as never-treated controls are added. Holding 20 treated units fixed and growing the panel from 60 to 300 units moves mean(SE)/SD(b) from 0.508 to 0.212 and 95% coverage from 0.733 to 0.367. No caution is printed on the att rows.
observed: 60 replications per arm, same DGP (y = 2 + 0.15*(t-1999) + unit effect + N(0,1) + 1.5*D, three staggered cohorts), truth 1.5, nominal 95%. ARM A (i=unit, cluster(unit), 20 treated of 300 units): SD(b)=0.193591, mean SE=0.041052, SE/SD=0.212, coverage 0.367. ARM D (same spec, 20 treated of 60 units; r8_calib.do block D): SD(b)=0.235697, mean SE=0.119794, SE/SD=0.508, coverage 0.733. ARM C (i=unit, robust, 20 of 300): SE/SD=0.646, coverage 0.783. ARM B (i=coarse cohort id + fe(unit), cluster(unit), 20 of 300 -- the help's intended practice of clustering below i): SE/SD=0.891, coverage 0.900. The point estimate is identical across arms A/B/C on the same draws (mean 1.493863), so only the variance is at issue. Nothing is printed on the att rows: the granular-i caution that does print concerns RUNTIME, and the SI-A1 caution fires only with jointtests.
expected: Arm B validates the harness at close to nominal, so the arm A number is wooldid's and not my Monte Carlo's. The mechanism makes the gradient predictable rather than fixture-specific: with i = unit every treated (unit, period) cell is a singleton carrying its own dummy, so its residual is exactly zero and the CRVE omits the treated-side variance entirely; what remains is the control-side time-FE variance, which shrinks as controls are added, while SD(b) stays pinned near 1/sqrt(treated observations). Arms D and A are that prediction measured. sthlp:251 gives 'roughly 0.66 to 0.75 of the reference on the diagnostic fixtures' and the project record pairs it with coverage 0.794-0.876 at G=40 -- arm C (robust) lands in that band, arm A is three times worse on SE/SD. The phenomenon is ruled (known_bydesign section 1) and I do not claim it as new; the contribution is the magnitude and its DRIVER in the few-treated / many-controls regime, which section 7 explicitly names as open ('the effect at a different cluster count'). Aggravating, and linking this to SAFETY-01: the help's first remedy, a finer cluster(), does not exist when i is already the unit, and the remaining remedy bootstrap() is itself refused r(907) by the si8 false positive on exactly the wide panel where the problem is worst.

title: saveplots() never got the pre-flight file-name check the author added to bootsave()/permsave(), so rerunning a do-file loses a completed run -- and under bootstrap() the whole replication loop
surface: saveplots() x makeplots / histogramcohorteffects / makecfxplots, interacting with replace; ado:2494, 12390, 13325, 13339 vs the pre-flight at ado:5866-5877 and 6276-6298; sthlp:696-697 and 700
claim: wooldid performs every saveplots() write (graph save at ado:2494/12390/13121/13325/13440, save at ado:13136/13339/13448) with no prior existence check, so a rerun of an unchanged do-file without `replace' raises r(602) and fails the whole wooldid call AFTER the estimation has succeeded; under bootstrap()/permute() the failure lands after the entire replication loop and its e() rewiring. permsave() (ado:5866-5877) and bootsave() (ado:6276-6298) were given exactly this pre-flight check on 2026-09-05, with the rationale stated in the code at ado:6276-6278: 'Until 2026-09-05 only wooldid_bootsave checked them, after the loop, so a name clash cost the whole run'. `grep -n "confirm file" wooldid.ado` returns only those four permsave/bootsave sites.
observed: On a plain 40-county x 8-year panel. (A) analytic run, `att esprelength(2) espostlength(2) makeplots saveplots(rrstem)': run 1 rc 0 and writes rrstem_ES_att.gph + rrstem_ES.dta; run 2, the identical line, prints the complete result table and then dies r(602) 'file rrstem_ES_att.gph already exists' (repro PART B; probeB B1). (B) `histogramcohorteffects saveplots(rrstem)': run 2 dies r(602) at ado:12390, reached from ado:1944 -- BEFORE the ereturn post at ado:4051 -- so e(cmd)=reghdfe, kb=82, e(N)=320, e(b)[1,1]=0 and the user's previous wooldid results (+1.b7fbc5505179aX+000) are gone (repro PART C; probeD D2). (C) `bootstrap(standard) reps(12) makeplots saveplots(pcstem)': run 2 completes all 12 replications AND the rewiring (e(boot_method)=standard, e(boot_reps)=12, colsof(e(b))=6), prints the bootstrap main table, and THEN dies r(602) at the plot save, before wooldid_display part(boot) (probeC C1). (D) control: both reruns return rc 0 with `replace' (repro PART D). On the help: sthlp:696-697 documents a soft failure -- 'If that write fails, typically because a file of the name already exists and replace was not given, the run is not lost' -- but read strictly that sentence is scoped to the _cfx.dta write named in the preceding clause (unmeasured by me; by code reading it is the cap noi wooldid_cfxplots ... dataonly at ado:517-524), and the help is SILENT that the event-study .gph/.dta and the histogram .gph writes hard-fail and lose the run.
expected: The author's own rule, written in the code at ado:6276-6278 and applied twice: a file-name clash is checked BEFORE the work runs so it cannot cost the whole run. saveplots() is the option most likely to hit that clash, because it writes on every ordinary rerun of a do-file, and it is the one option the rule was not applied to. This is NOT a claim that plot failures should not error -- ado:277-279 states plainly that 'A plot failure is an error of this call (its rc propagates, the caller's frame is restored and the replay marker is set), as it is on a plain run', and known_bydesign section 6 rules the WOOLDID_LASTRC machinery as design. The claim is only that the file-exists case is trivially pre-flightable and is not pre-flighted.

title: wooldid's estimand names are prefix-nested, so Stata's default varabbrev silently redirects _b[main_att] to main_att_i -- a 2.55x wrong number, sign-flipped under contreat()
surface: e(b)/e(V) column naming across the att / att_i / att_it / att_itime and ame families; _b[] / lincom / test; sthlp:1303-1307
claim: On a wooldid fit that posts exactly one member of an estimand name family, a reference to a DIFFERENT member of that family resolves silently to the one that is there and returns its number with rc 0, no message and no trace. main_att is a strict prefix of main_att_i / main_att_it / main_att_itime; pretreatment_att of pretreatment_att_i; main_ame of main_ame_i; main_SG1_att of main_SG1_att_i. Stata's `set varabbrev` (default ON) applies to coefficient names, so `di _b[main_att]` after `wooldid ..., att_i` returns the att_i estimate although no att estimand was requested or posted.
observed: Same 192-unit design in both runs. att alone: _b[main_att] = 0.47640617 (correct). att_i alone: _b[main_att] = 1.21489080 rc 0 -- that is main_att_i, ratio wrong/right = 2.55; _b[pretreatment_att] = -0.00952806 rc 0 (= pretreatment_att_i). att+contreat(dose): _b[main_ame] = +0.0772947 (correct). att_i+contreat(dose): _b[main_ame] = -0.02992339 rc 0 (= main_ame_i) -- OPPOSITE SIGN. att_i+subgroups(sg): _b[main_SG1_att] = 1.4232655 rc 0 (= main_SG1_att_i). `di _b[main_att]` / `scalar b = _b[main_att]` is completely silent; `lincom main_att` and `test main_att = 0` return rc 0 but echo the expanded name in their '( 1)  main_att_i = 0' line (a trace that is easy to miss and absent under quietly); `esttab ., keep(main_att)` errors 111. Fires ONLY when exactly one family member is posted: with att_i att_it together _b[main_att] is ambiguous and errors r(111); with att att_i together the exact match wins and returns the correct 0.47640617. MECHANISM (r6_varabbrev.do): `set varabbrev off` makes _b[main_att] and lincom main_att error r(111) while _b[main_att_i] still works; `confirm variable main_att` and `confirm variable main_att_i` are both r(111), so no dataset variable is involved.
expected: A coefficient reference that names an estimand the fit did not compute should not silently return a different estimand's number. Abbreviation is normally harmless because a prefix names the SAME object (pri -> price); wooldid is the unusual case where the prefix of one estimand's name is another ESTIMAND with a different weighting. sthlp:1305 presents main_att first as 'the headline average treatment effect on the treated' and then says the other estimands use 'the same names with att replaced by ...', which invites exactly the reference that misfires. known_bydesign.md s6 explicitly says 'a missing hidden twin is documented; a WRONG or COLLIDING name is not', so this class is in scope.

title: The only quantification on record for the analytic SE understatement at cluster()>=i (0.66-0.75) is the no-unit-heterogeneity case: the reported se is bitwise constant in cross-unit treatment-effect variation, and se/sd runs 0.93 to 0.36 as that variation grows
surface: analytic clustered standard errors for att at i = unit level with cluster() nesting i (sthlp:255's quantification)
claim: With i at the unit level and cluster() nesting i, the reported analytic standard error for att is bitwise invariant to cross-unit (and to per-cell) treatment-effect heterogeneity, so the '0.66 to 0.75' figure at sthlp:255 is a point on a curve rather than a range: it is what a DGP with no unit-level effect heterogeneity produces. The project's own measurement (review_process/se_coverage_2026-09-14/se_cov_mc.do) builds tau as a constant within cohort in both of its DGPs, which is why it landed there. Restore unit-level heterogeneity of ordinary size and the reported se does not move at all while se/true-sd falls to 0.358.
observed: r09_analytic_blind.do, one 28-state panel, four arms identical except for the effect heterogeneity. Reported analytic se(att): homogeneous +1.2e2d6dd8f2531X-003; unit-level effect shock sd 1.5 +1.2e2d6dd8f2531X-003 (BITWISE equal); unit-level shock sd 4.0 +1.2e2d6dd8f2531X-003 (BITWISE equal); per-CELL shock sd 1.5 +1.2e2d6dd8f252dX-003 (3 ulps). Over the same arms the point estimate moves 0.905 -> 1.463 and bootstrap(standard) se(att) moves 0.152361 -> 0.935422, a factor of 6.14. r10_sesd_het.do, 80 draws per arm, 30 states x 10 years: unit-effect sd 0.0 -> true sd 0.1515, mean reported se 0.1415, se/sd 0.933; unit-effect sd 0.5 -> true sd 0.1921, mean reported se 0.1415, se/sd 0.736; unit-effect sd 1.5 -> true sd 0.3956, mean reported se 0.1415, se/sd 0.358. The mean reported se is the SAME NUMBER in all three arms.
expected: sthlp:255 already says the analytic covariance at that level 'is the wrong object rather than a mis-scaled one', so I am not claiming the range was offered as a bound. What is missing is that the one number a user can act on - 'measured at roughly 0.66 to 0.75 of the reference on the diagnostic fixtures' - was produced by DGPs in which tau is constant within cohort (se_cov_mc.do: hom sets tau = 0.5 for every treated cell; stag sets tau = cond(ttre==5, 1.0, 0.4) + 0.05*rel, still constant within cohort), and a reader has no way to know that. My middle arm reproduces their number (0.736) and the outer arms bracket it at 0.933 and 0.358 - a nominal 95% interval with roughly the content of a 51% interval - purely by turning cross-unit treatment-effect heterogeneity on, which is the normal state of the world in a state-policy panel. This SHARPENS recon sec 1 rather than contradicting it; it is filed because the only quantification on record is off by a factor on ordinary data and because the exact bitwise invariance is not in the record.

title: contreatwithin + contreat() + esfixedbaseperiod on a panel with no usable pre-period burns a full reghdfe and then dies with a bare r(198) whose entire output is 'invalid syntax'
surface: contreatwithin + contreat(); esfixedbaseperiod; safety(); the pre/post estimability assert at ado:908
claim: ado:908's named r(459) refusal ('cannot find sufficient pre- and post-treatment periods for the treated units') gates on the working safety value that ado:4829 rewrites to off under contreatwithin + contreat(). With the screen skipped the run estimates its regression and then fails in the margins stage with a bare r(198) and no wooldid message at all, where the same command without contreatwithin gives the named r(459).
observed: r7_bare198.log, 40 units with the 30 treated ones carrying ttre == 1 so no treated unit has a usable pre-period. Leg 1 (default safety): r(459) 'Error: cannot find sufficient pre- and post-treatment periods for the treated units.' Leg 2 (+contreatwithin): r(198), and the command's entire output is the word 'invalid syntax'. Leg 3 (safety(off), no contreatwithin) and leg 4 (binary safety(off)): the same bare r(198), which pins the mechanism to the skipped ado:908 assert rather than to anything contreatwithin-specific. Leg 5 (contreatwithin + verbose) shows the run getting all the way through 'Wooldid is now estimating its regression', the full reghdfe line, 'Wooldid has finished regression estimation and is preparing to begin margins calculations', and only then 'invalid syntax'. The pooled (non-esfixedbaseperiod) path keeps its named r(459) under contreatwithin (r6_extra.log), so this is specific to the esfixedbaseperiod branch.
expected: The ado:908 refusal exists to convert this exact failure into a sentence the user can act on, and a panel whose treated units have no pre-period is one of the most common specification mistakes in staggered DiD. A user who typed contreatwithin asked to be excused the control-group requirement, not to be excused every diagnostic; the sthlp:1209 working-value family is enumerated as the collinearity family, the realized relative-time range asserts and the control-availability count, and it is at best ambiguous whether this refusal is meant to be in it. Under safety(off) the bare failure is an accepted cost of the option; under contreatwithin nobody asked.

title: Two differently-referenced "joint pre-trend test" p-values print in the same bootstrap run, and under boottstat the only one printed is the one the help says is never printed
surface: bootstrap() x jointtests x pretrendpower(); boottstat; wooldid_ptp display at ado:10620-10622; sthlp:532
claim: Under bootstrap() with jointtests and pretrendpower(), wooldid prints two joint tests of the same null on the same coefficients with no cross-reference - the valid bootstrap rank test and a normal-theory Wald on e(V) referred to F(k, G-1) - and under boottstat, where the rank test is structurally unavailable on a singleton-treated-cell panel, the only joint pre-trend p the user sees is the normal-theory Wald that sthlp:532 states is not printed.
observed: Design A (60 counties in 30 states, 16 periods, NO pre-trend in the DGP), reps(10): the jointtests line reads 'p-value for joint test that all pre-treatment att horizon estimates are 0: 0.0909' and, twenty lines later, the pretrendpower block reads 'joint pre-trend test: F(6, 29) = 8.5244, p = 0.0000' (r00_setup.log). On 40 states / 22 periods / 6 treated / esprelength(9) at reps(200): rank test .00995 vs ptp Wald .000814, a factor of 12 (r10b_attrit.log). Under boottstat at reps(60) (r11_boottstat.log): the run prints 'Caution: the bootstrapped joint_horiz joint test is unavailable (no usable replication statistic - rank-deficient replication covariances, or a horizon missing from the replications).', e(joint_horiz) is missing and e(boot_jt_family) = studentized, yet the pretrendpower block prints 'joint pre-trend test: F(6, 29) = .957282, p = 0.4708' - and a hand `test ES_att_pre7 ... ES_att_pre2` returns .4708198565 with df 6 and drop 0, identical to ten digits. The value is also bit-identical to the plain-bootstrap arm at the same seed, so boottstat's studentization never reaches it.
expected: sthlp:532 says of the bootstrap joint pre-trend tests: 'Neither is the Wald test on e(V) that a hand test reproduces; that one is a normal-theory test on the bootstrap covariance and is not printed.' It is printed, in the pretrendpower block, and it is the ONLY one printed once the studentized twin withdraws. Two p-values for the same null, four orders of magnitude apart in the reps(10) case, with no line telling the reader they are different tests, is a UX defect that will predictably cause a mis-read; and the help's own factual assertion is contradicted.

title: The Monte-Carlo component of the printed Roth slope, its CI, mdt_wald and the joint p is unrecorded, and at reps(50) it is about half the printed standard error
surface: bootstrap() x pretrendpower(); wooldid_ptp GLS block ado:10515-10545
claim: Under bootstrap(), the pretrendpower GLS quantities are functions of a drawn S, so re-running the same specification on the same data with a different rseed() moves the printed slope, CI, detectable-trend columns and joint p; e(roth_slope_se_att) contains only sampling uncertainty and nothing in e() or in the printed output records the replication component.
observed: One dataset (design A), four seeds, reps(50): slope .050479 / .019465 / .001135 / .010997 (across-seed SD ~ .021) against printed se .0287-.0425, and printed joint p .2712 / .7145 / .3994 / .6789. At reps(200): slope .027367 / .030265 / .020188 / .028359 (SD ~ .0044), p .4901 / .5829 / .5504 / .5415. Oracle coverage of the nominal-95% slope CI (r03_oracle.out): 92.8% at (k=6, n=50), 88.7% at (k=11, n=50), 84.3% at (k=6, n=20). The systematic part is E[S^-1] = Sigma^-1 (n-1)/(n-k-2), so the slope se and mdt_wald are understated by sqrt((n-k-2)/(n-1)) - 7.4% at (6,50), 13% at (11,50).
expected: A CI asked for at level(95) should have approximately 95% coverage, and a number a user will quote ("a pre-trend this size would have been caught 80% of the time") should not move by half its own standard error when the seed changes. Either the se should absorb the replication component, or a caution keyed on the draw count relative to the number of pre horizons should fire, in the way permreps() carries a hard floor of 20 for the same reason.

title: The singleton-treated-cell degeneracy reaches plain robust, rank-deficits the analytic event-study covariance by one with an exact unit correlation between two horizons, and cascades into pretrendpower() and the boottstat joint test with no caution about its cause
surface: analytic e(V_es_att) / wooldid_vsplice; pretrendpower() rank guard ado:10505-10510; boottstat joint_horiz availability
claim: On a panel where i is the unit (so every treated (i, relyr) cell is a single observation), the analytic pre-period block of e(V_es_att) is exactly rank-deficient under robust as well as under any cluster level - reporting corr(pre7, pre4) = 1 and Var(pre7)/Var(pre4) = 4 exactly while the point estimates are not in a 2:1 ratio - and the bootstrap contradicts it outright; wooldid's runtime caution attributes the problem to clustering at or above i, which is not the cause here.
observed: Design A, i = county, esfixedbaseperiod esprelength(6) (r12b_corr.log): under `robust` Var(pre7) = .0849489 and Var(pre4) = .0212372 (ratio exactly 4.000), corr(pre7,pre4) = 1 exactly, row 1 of the correlation matrix identical to row 4, smallest eigenvalue 2.90e-17; under cluster(state) and cluster(county) the same structure (smallest eigenvalue -2.55e-17); under iid full rank (smallest eigenvalue 5.98e-2). b_pre7 = -.2489177 and b_pre4 = -.0806095, not a 2:1 ratio. The bootstrap says that direction has ordinary variance: for v proportional to 2*pre4 - pre7, v'S_analytic v = -2.17e-17 while v'S_bootstrap v = 1.10e-01 (71% of the block's mean bootstrap variance), and SD(v'b_r) over 199 draws in e(bootdist) is 0.331 (r07_nulldir.log). DISCRIMINATOR (r13b_disc.do part A): same data with i coarsened to the onset cohort and fe(county), so the treated cells are no longer singletons - full rank under robust (eigenvalues 3.17e-2 .. 5.53e-1, max off-diagonal |corr| .691) and under cluster(state) (1.22e-2 .. 3.20e-1, max |corr| .709). Consequences: pretrendpower() prints its rank-deficiency caution and g-inverses that direction away, computing the analytic slope, CI, joint test and detectable-trend columns on 5 of 6 pre horizons; and under boottstat every replication inherits the degeneracy, so 'Caution: the bootstrapped joint_horiz joint test is unavailable' fires at every reps() and e(joint_horiz) is missing, leaving only the F(k,G-1) Wald (BX-N1).
