expected: The project's record documents singleton treated cells for ccc_absorb() and documents an all-zero covariance only on the continuous-treatment / cluster-at-or-above-i geometry (sthlp:1076); an all-zero e(V) under robust is explicitly listed as undocumented and reportable. Here the treatment is binary, the VCE is plain robust, the failure is partial (rank 5 of 6), `wooldid y unit t onset` with i = the unit is the default way the command is called, and no message names the cause. Either the caution should name singleton treated cells, or the analytic covariance should not assert a deterministic relation the coefficients do not have.

title: wooldid re-renders the confidence level at 16 significant digits and feeds it to set level, so ~13% of legal session levels make every call fail r(198) - and when it half-works it silently destroys c(level) and reports a successful, posted estimation as an error
surface: level() / c(level) round-trip (ado:5507, ado:575, ado:578, ado:69-71)
claim: wooldid fills an omitted level() from c(level) (ado:5507) and stores the caller's level as a macro (ado:575), both of which render at 16 significant digits, then hands the result to set level, which parses the literal text and refuses more than two decimals. Consequence A: with any such level in force in the session and NO level() option at all, every wooldid call fails r(198) with a message about level() digits the user never typed, while plain regress, reghdfe and margins run fine at the same session level. Consequence B: with such a session level and a legal level(95), the estimation succeeds and posts e(), the table prints, and the command still exits r(198) from the shell's restore - leaving c(level) silently at 95 instead of the user's value and leaking WOOLDID_LEVEL0.
observed: Limb B (REPRO_NEW_level_state.log): control at session level 90 with level(99) -> rc 0, e(level)=99, c(level) restored to 90. Defect: session level 99.9 with level(95) -> the table prints, e(cmd)=wooldid, e(N)=600, e(level)=95, and rc=198; c(level) afterwards is 95, not 99.9; WOOLDID_LEVEL0 leaked = [99.90000000000001]. Limb A (REPRO_F03_level.log): with set level 99.9 in force and no level() option, 'att robust' / 'att robust safety(off)' / 'att unconditionalse' / 'att robust fastnose' all return r(198) with 'level() can have at most two digits after the decimal point' printed twice, while regress and reghdfe at the same session level return rc 0; set level 95 restores service. set trace (pF_level_trace.log) pins both failing lines: ado:576 executes as 'set level 99.90000000000001' on a call with no level(), and ado:70 then fails identically. Mapped scope: 1152 of the 9000 two-decimal levels in [10,99.99] and 40 of the 100 one-decimal levels in [90,100) (90.1, 91.1, ..., 99.1, 99.4, 99.6, 99.9) have this property; an independent Python %.16g reproduction agrees exactly.
expected: An omitted level() should be a no-op, and a session-level setting that plain Stata accepts should never make an estimation command unusable; if a level truly cannot be honoured, wooldid should say so in its own words rather than emit Stata's message about digits the user never typed. A run whose estimation succeeded and posted e() should not return a nonzero rc, and no command should silently change c(level) behind the user's back - a caller's 'if _rc' guard will skip results that are in fact present, and every later Stata confidence interval in that session is computed at the wrong level.

title: cfxplottypes() token validation is gated behind makecfxplots, so the VAL-G13A fix does not apply without the parent and sthlp:974's unconditional rejection promise is false
surface: cfxplottypes(); wooldid.ado:5188 (VAL-G13A); wooldid.sthlp:974 vs sthlp:917
claim: The cfxplottypes() token validator sits inside `if "`makecfxplots'" != ""` (wooldid.ado:5188), so an invalid token is refused r(198) when makecfxplots is present and accepted rc 0 in silence when it is not - although sthlp:974 states the rejection with no parent qualifier, and the sibling entry sthlp:917 says of contreatpoly() that 'the value is validated whether or not contreat() is given'.
observed: Part 3 of the repro, identical data and identical options but for one word: `wooldid y unit t ttre, att robust contreat(dose) contreatcontrols(untreatedZero) cfxlattice(dose0) cfxplottypes(psot) safety(off)` returns rc 0 with no message; adding makecfxplots returns r(198) 'Error: cfxplottypes() contains an unrecognized entry: psot'. With no contreat() at all (r_f1_noparent.do), cfxplottypes(psot), cfxplottypes(1.5), cfxplottypes(nosuchvariable) and cfxplottypes(postpost 2post2) are all rc 0 and silent. The contrast option behaves as documented: contreatpoly(0) is r(198) whether or not contreat() is given.
expected: sthlp:974 says, with no makecfxplots qualifier, 'a token that is neither post nor pre must be a number, and one that is neither (postpost, 2post2, a variable name) stops the run with an error naming the entry, as does a numeric token that is missing or not an integer'. ado:5188's own VAL-G13A comment records that the old substring matching 'accepted garbage tokens (postpost counted as post, 2post2 became 2 2)' and that fractional entries 'fell through both cap'd window filters silently (rc 0, no plot, no message)' - the fix was placed inside the makecfxplots block, so without the parent the exact pre-fix behaviour the comment says was removed is still live. wooldid's stated convention for the sibling option is that a VALUE is validated regardless of whether its consumer is reached.

title: The maxvar preflight is not a lower bound and DOES fire falsely: si8demand adds the ABSORBED i and t levels, so an ordinary many-unit panel is refused although it estimates in seconds at that very maxvar
surface: safety() variable-count preflight (ado:1342-1374, si8demand at ado:1371) on the default reghdfe/ppmlhdfe estimation path (ado:1476); correct only on the reg/poisson path (ado:1490). Documented at sthlp:1167 and sthlp:1207.
claim: wooldid.ado:1371 computes si8demand = si8cells*(1 + (contreat!="")) + si8ilev + si8tlev + 200 and errors 907 when it exceeds c(maxvar). On the default estimation path (ado:1476, `reghdfe y ... i._i#i._t#i.targetflag ... , absorb(i.`i' i.`t' `fe')`) the i and t levels are ABSORBED and are never design-matrix columns, so si8ilev + si8tlev is additive slack that grows one-for-one with the number of NEVER-TREATED units. The documented zero-false-positive guarantee is therefore false: a realistic many-unit, few-treated-cohort panel is refused although the identical command estimates fine at the same maxvar. The 'lower bound' in the ado comment attaches to si8cells*(1+contreat) alone, not to si8demand.
observed: HEADLINE, at Stata's UNTOUCHED DEFAULT c(maxvar)=5000 (s2_falsepos_default.log): 5,200 units x 12 years, 20 treated (onsets 2012-2015), `wooldid y unit year ttre, att`. DEFAULT safety -> 'Error: this specification requires at least 5542 variables (about 130 treated cohort-by-period interaction terms) but maxvar is currently 5000, so estimation would fail with r(907).' rc 907, nothing estimated. IDENTICAL data, IDENTICAL maxvar, only safety(off) added -> rc 0 in 3.75 SECONDS, att = 1.3745078 (truth 1.5), N = 62400. CONTROLS (s3_controls.log): same spec, DEFAULT safety, set maxvar 8000 -> rc 0, att = 1.3745078, hex +1.5fdfbe7391aecX+000, bit-identical to the safety(off) run, so safety(off) changed nothing about the estimate and the refusal was purely the variable count. The wooldid-shaped design hand-built on the same data (`reghdfe y i._i#i._t#i.tf, absorb(i.unit i.year)`) reports F(220, 56969): 220 estimated columns of 240. Claimed 'at least 5542'. Overshoot >= 23x (the hand-build is a generous upper proxy: ado:928-929 and ado:1009 set _i=0 and _t=0 outside post-treatment cells, so wooldid's own design is smaller still). CONTROLLED CONTRAST: the 2,200-unit and 5,200-unit panels carry the SAME 20 treated units, si8cells = 130 on both, same design matrix; si8demand moves 2542 -> 5542, exactly the 3000-unit change in si8ilev. The deciding term costs zero columns. BE CEILING (s1_falsepos.log), maxvar 2048 which Stata/BE fixes and a BE user cannot raise: 2,200 units -> 'requires at least 2542 variables (about 130 ...)' rc 907; safety(off) at the same 2048 -> rc 0 in 1.91 s, att = 1.4700209. CONTINUOUS PATH (s8_zip_contreat.log), default maxvar: 5,000 ZIP codes x 12 years, 60 exposed, `att contreat(exposure) contreatcontrols(basic)`, no lattice/poly/interactive controls -> 'requires at least 5992 variables (about 390 treated cohort-by-period interaction terms)' rc 907; identical + safety(off) at the same maxvar -> rc 0 in 68.18 s, estimate .63452766 (truth .60), N = 60000; true demand about 390*2+1 = 781 columns, overshoot ~7.7x. Formula validated exactly on four panels: 130+2200+12+200=2542; 130+5200+12+200=5542; 390*2+5000+12+200=5992; 1200*2+3143+18+200=5761. SELF-CONTRADICTION: one line above the refusal the same block prints 'a granular unit can dominate runtime long before it approaches Stata's variable limits', then refuses on the variable limit a run that takes 3.75 s.
expected: Four project documents assert the invariant this violates: ado:1342-1348 ('a lower bound on the regression's variable demand, so an early refusal can only fire when the late r(907) was certain anyway'); review_process/open_defects.md:74-79 ('The design accepts false negatives ... in order to guarantee zero false positives, because a false positive would refuse a specification that would actually have estimated fine'); known_bydesign.md section 5; review_process/research_2026-09-16/guard_failure_modes.json:59 ('it cannot convert a would-be-successful run into a refusal'). Grepping guard_cost_2026-09-16.md for ilev/absorb/over-pred/false positive returns only the UNDER-prediction direction (line 342) and a restatement of the invariant (line 406) -- the over-prediction direction is nowhere in the project record. The precise statement: si8ilev + si8tlev ARE real columns on the reg/poisson path (ado:1490, under unconditionalse/customvce()), where the formula is correct; they are absorbed on the reghdfe/ppmlhdfe path (ado:1476), which is the path essentially every run takes. Beyond the false refusal, the message's named remedy ('swap i to a coarser level of aggregation') changes what is estimated -- for att_i/att_it/att_itime the cells are redefined so the estimand changes outright, and for att the within-cell weighting changes -- so a spurious refusal pushes the user off the quantity they asked for. On Stata/BE maxvar is fixed at 2048 and cannot be raised at all, so the only escape there is safety(off), which disables roughly sixty other checks.

title: One coefficient, three standard errors: printed, e(V), and e(V_es_att) - and the footer points honestdid at the wrong matrix
surface: bootstrap(standard) + subgroups() / e(V) vs e(V_es_att) / footer ado:11790 / sthlp:1560-1567
claim: On a bootstrap run with subgroups(), the same event-study coefficient carries materially different standard errors in the printed table, in e(V) (what esttab/coefplot/lincom/test read) and in e(V_es_att) (what the package's own honestdid recipe reads), because the two stored matrices are listwise covariances over different column sets; the bootstrap footer nevertheless groups esttab, coefplot and honestdid as tools that read e(V).
observed: Run A (36 states, subgroups(reg), reps(60), rseed 6201, e(boot_N_V)=16): ES_att_post9 printed se .150121, sqrt(diag(e(V))) .096468, sqrt(diag(e(V_es_att))) .150121 - a 56% spread between the two stored matrices for one coefficient; ES_att_pre6 .111737 / .082039 / .117609. Mechanism pinned: run A's e(V_es_att) equals run B's (no-subgroups) whole e(V) to the six digits printed for every ES coefficient, i.e. the family subblock keeps the replications the full matrix loses. e(V_boot) is identical to e(V) coefficient by coefficient. The help's honestdid recipe is verbatim `matrix b = e(b_es_att)` / `matrix V = e(V_es_att)` / `honestdid, numpre(...) b(b) vcov(V) ...` (sthlp:1560-1567), and ado:10068 calls e(V_es_*) 'the honestdid entry point', while the run-time footer says '...the tools that read e(V) without being asked: esttab, coefplot and honestdid export the standard-deviation family'.
expected: A run should not carry two stored covariances that disagree by 56% on the same coefficient without saying so, and the footer that tells the user which tools read which family should agree with the help's own handoff recipe. Secondary note for a maintainer: sthlp:1318 ('since 2026-09-07 the same blocks are spliced into e(V)') and the PS-62 description of e(V) as carrying the event-study blocks are written for the analytic state; under bootstrap e(wdid_vcvstate) reads 'bootstrap' and e(V)'s ES block is a different matrix from e(V_es_att).

title: A zero survey weight mints a phantom bootstrap cluster the same way
surface: bootstrap() with aweight/pweight; bootdf(clusters); the few-cluster cautions
claim: Rows with w == 0 are removed from the estimation sample at ado:686 (`replace ifvar = 0 if ... w <= 0`) but remain in the bootstrap map frame, so a cluster whose every row carries a zero weight is counted in G and inflates e(boot_df).
observed: r7_novel.do section B: 14 states x 2 units x 12 years, states 2 and 5 carrying w == 0 on every row, run with [aw=w] cluster(state) bootstrap(standard). e(N)=288 and e(N_clust)=12 with and without those rows; e(boot_df)=e(df_r)=13 with them, 11 without.
expected: 11 either way, because the estimation sample is the same either way. Zero-weight records are routine in weighted administrative and survey extracts (a record retained for structure but given no analytic weight), so this fires on ordinary weighted data with no missing values at all.

title: permstrata() strata are built on the same unscreened cluster set
surface: permute() + permstrata(); the reported possible-assignment count
claim: The stratified permutation design counts clusters that contribute no rows to e(sample), so the reported number of possible assignments under permstrata() is overstated in the same way and by a larger factor, because the inflation compounds within strata.
observed: r7_novel.do section E: 16 states, region 1 = states 1-8 (all treated), region 2 = states 9-16 (all never treated), states 1-4 report no outcome. permute(shuffle) permstrata(region): reported possible assignments 560 (full) vs 12 (dead rows deleted), with e(N)=288 on both sides.
expected: The design size should describe the assignments the analysis admits. A stratum that is half made of clusters carrying no data is exactly the situation permstrata() exists to let the user reason about.

title: The worker's own onset-uniqueness screen IS markout-aware, so wooldid contradicts itself about which sample a screen should use - and the pattern for the fix is already in the codebase
surface: the worker's ttre-uniqueness screen vs wooldid_permctl's cluster-onset nesting screen
claim: wooldid's worker-level 'exactly one treatment onset per group defined by i' screen evaluates on the internally screened sample: the identical stray record trips r(459) when it carries an outcome and passes silently when it does not. wooldid_permctl's structurally identical cluster-onset nesting screen evaluates on the unscreened sample and refuses in both cases. The two screens disagree about what 'in-sample' means.
observed: r2_nest.log:336-349. One appended record for unit 19 carrying an onset different from unit 19's own: with y present the run stops with r(459) 'wooldid requires exactly one treatment onset per group defined by unit ... offending unit: 19', listing remedies; with y missing (r2b_nest.do, same record) the run completes normally with e(N)=480. Contrast r3b_perm.do C1: a y-missing stray record with a different onset makes permute() refuse r(459) and calls the row 'in-sample observation(s)', while the ordinary run on the same file succeeds with e(N)=160, identical to the run with the row deleted.
expected: Both screens describe the same kind of precondition and should agree on the sample. The worker's version shows that a markout-aware screen of this exact shape is already implemented and shipped, which removes the 'it would be hard' objection to fixing wooldid_permctl and wooldid_bootctl. I found this accidentally, as a self-inflicted bug in an earlier fixture, which is why it is worth stating: nothing in the help or the code comments flags the asymmetry.

title: The boottstat simultaneous critical value has no guard against a near-zero replication standard error, and the printed band can be 1e14 wide with no caution
surface: simultaneousbands + boottstat + cluster() (wooldid_bootband, ado:16776)
claim: wooldid_bootband's studentized path drops a replication only when a horizon's standard error is missing or non-positive; a tiny POSITIVE one passes and sends |b_r - b_obs|/se_r to infinity, so at cluster() == i the level() quantile of the sup comes back an order of magnitude or more above the nominal ~2.5 and the printed simultaneous band is vacuous, with nothing in the output saying so.
observed: repro_sk02_bandcrit.do arm A (15 states, log-normal errors sigma 1.3, 5 horizons, cluster(state), reps 299, boottstat simultaneousbands): A_CRIT = 1.17727e+14 with nband=293, and the printed band endpoints are A_BAND pre3 [-23018976972227, 23018976972227], A_BAND post0 [-62463216459926, 62463216459928] -- no caution. Arm B, GAUSSIAN errors at G=20, same shape: B_CRIT = 13.799, band half-widths 3.22-4.74, roughly five times the pointwise intervals. Sweep (r08_bandsweep.log cells 1-6): e(esband_crit_att) = 30.92, 1.17727e+14, 13.80, 4.64, 15.17, 6.77. The 95th percentile being 1.18e14 at nband=293 means roughly 15 complete replications had a horizon standard error near machine zero.
expected: sthlp:528 describes this band as 'a genuine percentile-t, on the same scale as the pointwise intervals printed beside it'. A percentile-t sup band over five horizons should carry a critical value of roughly 2.5-3.5, and the printed band should be readable beside the pointwise rows. Every other degenerate-denominator site in the package (the boottstat cell p, the AMESE R1 scrub, wooldid_sgdeg) either withholds the object or prints a named caution; this one does neither. The code path is ado:16776-16876: the only screen is `if (S[r, sel[j]] >= . | S[r, sel[j]] <= 0) mx = 0`.

title: The printed bootstrap standard error and e(V) are built on different completeness masks, so under bootdisplay(wald) lincom does not reproduce the printed row -- by up to 20 percent, concentrated in the subgroup block
surface: bootstrap() + subgroups() + bootdisplay(wald); e(V) / test / lincom (wooldid_bootwire ado:9606-9625)
claim: Column 2 of e(wdidmainresults)/e(wdidsgresults_*) is exactly the PER-COLUMN standard deviation of the bootstrap draws, while sqrt(diag(e(V))) is exactly the LISTWISE-complete one. Under bootdisplay(wald) -- the display the help singles out as the one where the standard error, statistic, p-value and interval all reproduce one another and where a hand test or lincom reproduces the printed p -- the two disagree, by up to 20 percent, and the large gaps sit in the subgroup block that wooldid_bootwire's own comment flags as an unguarded walk.
observed: repro_sk03_vdiag.do (24 states, 2-4 units each, 9 years, subgroups(sg3) with three levels, cluster(state), reps 399, bootdisplay(wald); 368 of 399 replications complete over all 24 coefficients): WORST_PCT_V_VS_PRINTED = 19.84125. Worst coefficient pretreatment_SG0_att -- printed se 0.269231486, sqrt(V_kk) 0.215812605, and `lincom _b[pretreatment_SG0_att]` returns se .2158126, t 0.81, p 0.427, 95% CI [-.2720803, .6208045]. Second worst ES_att_SG0_pre1: printed .324726026 vs sqrt(V_kk) .293179186 (9.71 percent). All 24 coefficients differ (0.38 to 19.84 percent); the six MAIN-table rows are all within 0.38-1.60 percent and BOTH large gaps are in the SG0 block. r10_sdrule.do identifies the two rules exactly: WORST_PCTDIFF_PERCOL = 0.00000 (printed se == per-column SD) and WORST_PCTDIFF_LISTWISE = 24.75244, while sqrt(diag(e(V))) matches the listwise SD to 0.00000 percent on all 24. This is not a column shift -- I tested every coefficient against both neighbours' recomputed SDs and no neighbour equality exists.
expected: sthlp:554, verbatim: 'Under every setting {it:e(df_r)} is aligned with the reference distribution actually reported ... so a {cmd:test} or {cmd:lincom} run by hand afterwards reproduces the reported p-values rather than diverging from them - {bf:this holds under} {cmd:bootdisplay(wald)}{bf:, which is what} {it:e(V)} {bf:and} {it:e(df_r)} {bf:always carry}.' The run footer additionally states that e(V) holds the bootstrap covariance '(complete-replication listwise, e(boot_N_...))'. Under bootdisplay(wald) the printed interval is b +/- crit*se, so if the printed se is not sqrt(V_kk) the promise fails on its own terms.

title: The no-pre-period drop is per-unit against that unit's own first observed period, not against the start of the sample, and the help says otherwise
surface: pooled (default) reference regime; wooldid_reltime nopre screen; sthlp:73
claim: wooldid_reltime (ado:12047-12055) drops every unit with ttre <= mint, where mint is THAT UNIT's first in-sample period. So a unit that enters the panel late and whose onset falls comfortably inside the sample window is dropped too. sthlp:73 describes the screen only as 'cohorts treated before the sample begins are dropped', which does not cover that case, and no caution names the cause -- while the anticipation-driven version of this same screen both prints a caution and is documented as printing one (sthlp:824).
observed: Design C spans t=1..8. Six units have ttre=3 -- inside the window -- and are first observed at t=3 (run11.log:230-246). They are dropped entirely: e(N)=240 of 276 rows, e(N_dropped)=36 (run3.log:1755-1761). The header does report the count -- 'N = 240 (36 obs dropped from initial sample)' -- but states no cause, and the only printed caution concerns a different rule ('reference period for some units forced ...'). The same data under anticipation(3) DOES print 'Caution: anticipation(3) places the effective onset of 9 unit(s) at or before their first usable pre-period; those unit(s) and their N observations are dropped from the sample' (repro_nopre_silent.log:513). In the repro those six cohorts carry a true effect of 3 against the others' 1, so the reported att is an estimand over a different population than the user specified.
expected: Either sthlp:73 should say 'at or before their first observed period' rather than 'before the sample begins', or the unconditional screen should print the caution its anticipation twin already prints. NOTE: this finding was narrowed and downgraded during review -- my first draft claimed no message at all and no documentation, and both halves were partly false (the header prints a count; sthlp:73 documents the always-treated case). What survives is the per-unit-vs-per-sample gap and the missing cause.
refuter_did: Read ado:12047-12055 (mint = min(t) by i; nopre = max(ttre <= mint) by i -- the screen is per-unit against that unit's own first observed period) and built my own panel: t=1..8, 30 units, units 11-16 with ttre=4 (comfortably inside the window) but first observed at t=4. They are dropped: e(N)=192 of 222 rows, e(N_dropped)=30, and grepping the whole arm for 'Caution' returns NOTHING -- only the header line 'N = 192 (30 obs dropped from initial sample)', which names no cause. Rebuilt with the same units observed from t=3 (one pre period): nothing dropped, e(N)=228. Because those six carry a true effect of 6 against the others' 2, the reported att moves 2.1609926 -> 3.9429456, so the run silently estimates over a different population. Checked the documentation side as well: grepped the whole sthlp for 'first observed', 'no pre-treatment', 'without a pre' and 'first usable' -- the only 'at or before their first usable period' sentence is sthlp:824, which is the anticipation() twin of the same screen, and that twin DOES print a caution (ado:12036-12046). So the per-unit-vs-per-sample gap really is undocumented and the unconditional screen really is silent about the cause. Dropping the unit is correct behaviour (no within-unit pre-period exists), so this stays a doc/UX low, exactly as the seeded finding's own narrowed version says.

title: The att_it/att_i/att_itime weight formulas in the help omit customweightmultiplier(), while still calling the result a simple unweighted mean
surface: customweightmultiplier() x att_it / att_i / att_itime; sthlp:220-236
claim: The seeded worry -- that cwm entering the numerator of all four estimand weights and the denominator of none silently breaks the documented estimand -- is NOT confirmed: the code is coherent and sthlp:1107 authorises it ('the weights normally used to produce the requested type of treatment effect (ATT, ATT_i, etc.) will be multiplied by this variable'), which is exactly w_item*cwm. What remains is a documentation gap: the three phang entries at sthlp:220-236 spell the weights out as w/W_it, w/W_ipre|post and w/(W_it*T_iprepost) with no cwm factor and keep describing the result as 'the simple, unweighted mean', which under cwm it is not.
observed: My from-scratch oracle reproduces all four estimands, both pretreatment rows and every event-study horizon under customweightmultiplier() to 2.75e-13 using the CODE's formula (w*cwm/W_it etc.), on both a unit-level design (cmpA.py runs A4 and A6) and a multi-row-per-cell design (cmpBC.py run B4). A second oracle built from the help's literal formulas (simple mean over cells / over cohorts) matches wooldid everywhere EXCEPT under cwm, where it differs by 1.5-2.5% (cmpBC.out:113-115). In a one-row-per-cell panel w_att_it = cwm exactly, so att_it becomes the cwm-weighted mean of cell effects -- which is the only placement under which cwm does anything at all for that estimand, and is therefore evidently the intent.
expected: The three phang formulas should carry the cwm factor, or say that cwm multiplies each of them and that the result is then a cwm-weighted rather than simple mean. A reader who takes the printed formulas literally will mis-predict the number.
refuter_note: One nuance the seeded write-up's own title omits although its body is consistent with it: the att phang at sthlp:220 ALREADY names cwm explicitly ('multiplied by the customweightmultiplier() variable if one is specified - that multiplier enters the margins weights only and is deliberately not folded into the regression weight'). So the gap is exactly the THREE cell-weighted phangs (att_it, att_i, att_itime), not the estimand block as a whole.
refuter_did: Read sthlp:220-236 and sthlp:1107 directly, then checked the number moves. sthlp:222-236 spells att_it / att_i / att_itime as w/W_it, w/W_ipre|post and w/(W_it*T_iprepost) with no cwm factor and calls each 'the simple, unweighted mean'; sthlp:1107 authorises the multiplication generally. Numeric confirmation on my own one-row-per-cell panel (30 units, 9 periods, unit-level cwm = 1+mod(i,5), heterogeneous effects): att_it = 4.552181151 without cwm and 4.548217942 with it, on identical data -- so what is reported under cwm is demonstrably not the simple unweighted mean of the cell effects those three entries describe. I did not re-derive the exact weight formula; nothing I saw contradicts the seeded oracle's conclusion that the CODE is coherent and only the printed formulas are short.

title: e(perm_sd) silently switches denominator inside one permexact table
surface: permexact + an element some enumerated assignments cannot estimate; e(perm_sd), e(perm_sd_est), footer 'SD of the permutation distribution'
claim: Under permexact, e(perm_sd) is the population SD (divisor n) for elements estimable in all M enumerated assignments and the sample SD (divisor n-1) for elements that lost assignments - same run, same table, no marker - although the p-value convention printed beside it was deliberately moved off completeness and onto membership (BS-23).
observed: 8 clusters, 2 treated, M=28, a subgroup level on two clusters. main_att (n=28) posted +1.85227db25c93dX-001 == population SD (1/n); main_SG0_att (n=27) posted +1.6a5103d115142X-001 == sample SD (1/(n-1)); main_SG1_att (n=13) posted +1.771507ea81bbbX+000 == sample SD. The n=13 rows are inflated by sqrt(13/12) = 4.1% relative to the convention the n=28 rows in the same table use. Source: wooldid_permtail at ado:15968, out[6] = (exact ? population : sample) where `exact' is the completeness flag.
expected: One SD convention per table, or a documented switch. The help describes e(perm_sd) only as 'SD of the permutation distribution' (sthlp:1345) with no denominator and no statement that it changes within a run. The switch also contradicts the reasoning the project adopted alongside it: BS-23 (author ruling 2026-09-07) moved the SHARE convention from completeness to MEMBERSHIP precisely because an element whose reference set contains the observed statistic is exactly enumerated over the assignments that completed - and this run confirms the p-values follow that rule (2/27 and 2/13 exactly, e(perm_p_se)/e(perm_p_ci) withheld, e(perm_incomplete) naming the elements, e(perm_addone) empty). The same reference set is therefore treated as a population for its p and as a sample for its SD. e(perm_sd) is descriptive and feeds no p-value or interval, so nothing downstream moves.
refuter_note: The finding is right; three scoping corrections. (1) 'no marker' is overstated: e(perm_incomplete) names the elements that lost assignments and e(perm_n) gives each element's n, so a user CAN tell which branch an element took. What is missing is the DOCUMENTED RULE (sthlp:1345 says only 'SD of the permutation distribution'). (2) Do not attack the general rule: 'sampled draws -> sample SD, complete enumeration -> population SD' is defensible. The defect is precisely that an INCOMPLETE ENUMERATION falls to the SAMPLED branch for its SD while BS-23 puts it in the EXACT branch for its p. (3) 'e(perm_sd) is descriptive and feeds no p-value or interval, so nothing downstream moves' is right about inference but understates visibility: the same kernel row 6 is also posted as the legacy scalar e(perm_sd_<est>) (ado:222), which is PRINTED in the run footer (ado:11734). Honest limit: whether a POOLED estimand can be incomplete while other elements are not was NOT established here -- under permexact a whole-row failure costs every element the same rows, so exk=0 everywhere and the table is uniformly sample-SD with no switch. Second site, source read only: wooldid_permstep (ado:16294) carries the same completeness-tied population rescale on the PRINTED t_obs row of e(perm_stepdown) while its p rows use (exk | memb); there exk is one flag per stepdown table, so the switch is across tables in a run rather than within one, and ranks/p are unaffected because it is a common scalar per column.
refuter_did: Independent data and independent geometry (theirs: 8 clusters, 2 treated, M=28, subgroup on 2 units, n=27/13). Mine: 9 counties 2010-2019, 3 treated in 2015, subgroups(big) on 3 counties, permute(shuffle) permexact -> M = C(9,3) = 84, completed 84, failed 0; the SG0 family loses the single assignment that puts all three treated inside the big group, so n=83. Compared every posted e(perm_sd) entry bit-for-bit (%21x) against both the population SD (divisor n) and the sample SD (divisor n-1) recomputed from e(permdist_b), and simultaneously classified each column's p against the exact share and the add-one share. Result: every COMPLETE column (n=84=M) posts the population SD; every INCOMPLETE column (n=83) posts the sample SD; EVERY column's p is the exact share, complete and incomplete alike, with e(perm_addone) empty and e(perm_incomplete) naming exactly the SG0 family. Ratio samp/pop = 1.006 in my geometry (their n=13 case gives 4.1%). Also verified e(perm_sd_att) (the printed footer scalar) equals the matrix entry for main_att bit for bit.

title: permstepdown's p_raw/p_singlestep/p_stepdown are documented and printed as add-one shares, but permexact computes plain exact shares
surface: permstepdown + permexact (footer ado:11700, help sthlp:514, kernel ado:16290-16320)
claim: Under a complete `permexact` enumeration the step-down kernel `wooldid_permstep` (ado:16302, 16310, 16320) computes `nex/n` — the plain exact share — for all three of its p rows, while the runtime footer (ado:11700) and the help (sthlp:514) describe that row unconditionally as "the two-sided |t| share, add-one". The two conventions differ by roughly a factor of two at the floor (1/M vs 2/(M+1)) and, in the repro, straddle 0.05.
observed: M = 30 enumerated assignments, 30/30 completed. e(perm_stepdown) reports p_raw = p_singlestep = p_stepdown = 0.033333333333333 for ES_att_post0/post1/post2, i.e. exactly 1/30 = the plain share. The add-one value the footer and help promise, with one exceedance, is (1+1)/(30+1) = 0.0645161. The same run prints: "... p_raw is the two-sided |t| share (add-one) in the step-down's own metric, not the table's convention ...". Every step-down number in the run is a multiple of 1/30 and none of 1/31 (e(perm_stepdown_pre): p_raw 0.900 = 27/30 and 0.400 = 12/30; p_singlestep 0.966666… = 29/30 and 0.700 = 21/30). Code: `out[2,h] = (exk | memb ? nex/n : (1 + nex)/(n + 1))` with `exk = (M < . & n == M)`.
expected: The label should be exactness-aware, as its own siblings already are: the coefficient-p footer at ado:11681 branches on `e(perm_exact)` and says "the p-values are exact shares with no Monte-Carlo error"; sthlp:503 says of the equality tests "with the same add-one form for sampled draws and plain shares under permexact"; sthlp:452 says the joint tests use "under a complete permexact enumeration the enumerated assignments alone"; and sthlp:654 states the general rule, "permexact needs no add-one while sampled draws do". Only the permstepdown sentence and its footer were not updated. The arithmetic is the right one for an enumeration, so the defect is in the two descriptions. The stated convention is what a reader uses to judge resolution and to compare the step-down column with the table: a user told the row is add-one concludes its floor is 1/(n+1) and that it cannot coincide with the table's convention, and under permexact both conclusions are wrong.
refuter_note: The claim and its EXPECTED are right; its OBSERVED framing is misleading in two places and should not be carried into a ticket. (1) 'The add-one value the footer and help promise ... is (1+1)/(30+1) = 0.0645161' is the number the code would print if the branch flipped, not a target: under a complete enumeration the observed assignment is one of the M draws, so nex already counts it and (1+nex)/(n+1) would count it twice. 1/30 is the statistically correct exact p, as the kernel's own comment at ado:16290 says. (2) 'The two conventions differ by roughly a factor of two at the floor ... and straddle 0.05' overstates the reader-facing gap: a reader told 'add-one' infers the generic add-one floor 1/(n+1) = 1/31 = .0323 against an actual 1/30 = .0333, a 3% gap, not 2x. Also worth noting in mitigation: the governing rule is printed FOUR lines above the offending sentence in the same footer ('The assignments are enumerated rather than sampled, so the p-values are exact shares with no Monte-Carlo error', verified in r1b_px1.log), and stated generally at sthlp:654 and sthlp:512. The defect is exactly what the prober's EXPECTED says -- an unqualified label whose siblings are exactness-aware -- and low is the right severity.
refuter_did: Built my own 5-cluster staggered panel (onsets 4,4,6,.,. -> M = 5!/(2!1!2!) = 30) and ran the same design twice: permute(shuffle) permexact permstepdown, and permute(shuffle) permreps(199) permstepdown. Under permexact the three p rows of e(perm_stepdown) are .06666666666666669 and .03333333333333330, i.e. exact multiples of 1/30 (p*30 = 2.0000000000 and 1.0000000000; p*31 = 2.0667 and 1.0333) -- the plain share. Under permreps(199) the same rows are .045 and .015, exact multiples of 1/200 (p*200 = 9.000 and 3.000; p*199 = 8.955 and 2.985) -- the add-one form. The permexact run's own footer printed, verbatim, '... where p_raw is the two-sided |t| share (add-one) in the step-down's own metric, not the table's convention ...', and sthlp:514 says 'the two-sided |t| share, add-one'. So the convention really does switch with permexact and the sentence really is unqualified: the claim is true. I also read the kernel: the branch is (exk | memb) and wooldid_permmemb returns 0 whenever M >= . (sampled draws), so the prober's scoping of the divergence to permexact is right.

title: customvce() can never reach a permutation replication: the customvce forwarding line in the permute rep string (ado:128) is dead code, and the seeded twin-asymmetry has no behavioural consequence
surface: permute() x customvce()
claim: The seeded lead says the twins are asymmetric because permute() forwards customvce() to its replications while bootstrap() refuses it. The source asymmetry is real (ado:128 emits customvce(...) into wdp_ro; ado:6414 refuses it under bootstrap()), but permute()+customvce() is UNREACHABLE, so ado:128 can never execute and no user is affected.
observed: PX02_repro.log and p03_refuse.log/p11_gaps.log. With cluster(): r(198), "Error: customvce() is not compatible with robust and cluster(). You must manually specify the contents of reg's vce() statement in this case." (ado:4667, which runs before wooldid_permctl). Without cluster(): r(198), "Error: permute() requires cluster() with a single variable - the unit whose treatment-onset assignment is randomized." Both customvce(cluster unit) and customvce(robust) behave the same way. permute() admits exactly one cluster variable, so there is no third case. For contrast, the bootstrap twin refuses it explicitly: "Error: bootstrap() may not be combined with customvce(); the reported standard errors would be bootstrap-based, contradicting the custom-VCE request."
expected: Either the line should not be there, or — if the customvce+cluster guard is ever relaxed — permute() should carry the same explicit refusal bootstrap() carries, since the bootstrap's reasoning ("the reported standard errors would be bootstrap-based, contradicting the custom-VCE request") applies verbatim to a permutation run, where the reported inference is the permutation distribution's and under the fast-mode default no VCE is computed at all. Filed at low severity because it is dead code today; filed at all because the coordinator note asks for contradictions of the record, and because relaxing either guard would silently switch the line on.
refuter_note: The factual claim is right and I could not break it. As a defect it is dead code with no user-visible consequence, which is the brief's lowest category -- arguably severity 'none'. I keep it at low only because it is a correct correction of a seeded lead and because relaxing either guard would silently switch the line on.
refuter_did: Tried to REACH permute()+customvce() five ways on my own data rather than take the unreachability claim on trust: cluster(firm)+customvce(cluster firm) -> r(198) 'customvce() is not compatible with robust and cluster()' (ado:4667); no cluster()+customvce(cluster firm) -> r(198) 'permute() requires cluster() with a single variable' (ado:5947); cluster(firm)+customvce(robust)+safety(off) -> r(198), the same customvce message, so that guard is NOT safety-gated; multi-way cluster(firm year)+customvce -> r(198); customvce() empty and customvce( ) a single space -> rc 0, parsed as absent, so ado:128 is still not emitted. I also closed the one loophole they did not: an INTERNAL assignment that could make the macro non-empty without the user typing it. grep shows `customvce` is never assigned anywhere in the file -- the only occurrences outside the syntax and forwarding lines are two `subinstr ... local customvce` reads at ado:1418 and ado:1539.

title: Without cluster(), the count leg and the re-identification leg draw DIFFERENT resamples at the same rseed(), so att's reported SE moves when a second estimand is added
surface: bootstrap(standard) without cluster(), att vs att+att_i
claim: `bootstrap(standard) att` and `bootstrap(standard) att att_i` at one rseed() produce different replicate draws and a different att standard error when no cluster() is given. The re-identification leg's own comment at ado:9340 asserts 'same-seed draws equal the count path's'; that is true with cluster() and false without it.
observed: repro_br3.log (40 units x 8 periods, reps(200), rseed(12345)): UNCLUSTERED att (count leg) se_att = 0.235921 vs att att_i (reid leg) se_att = 0.231988, with replicate draws differing by up to 3.82e-01 relative. CLUSTERED att vs att att_i: se_att = 0.169566 both, draws differing by 2.61e-14. probe1.log/cmp1.log confirm the clustered w_* cluster-multiplicity columns are BIT-IDENTICAL between the legs (max abs diff 0 over 60 columns x 30 reps). probe8.log settles whether the unclustered gap is more than Monte Carlo: at reps(300), count seed A 0.081208 / count seed B 0.075653 (7.3% same-leg spread) and reid seed A 0.077783 / reid seed B 0.078920, so the cross-leg gap at a common seed (4.4% and 4.3%) sits inside the same-leg seed-to-seed spread.
expected: A user rerunning a specification with a second estimand added, at the same rseed(), should get the same att column; nothing in the help says the seed stops being comparable across estimand lists, and the code comment says the opposite. The fix is already in the file: the physical-expansion leg at ado:9238 draws with `bsample, cluster(<row id>) idcluster(...)` on exactly this unclustered geometry, and probe5.log shows that leg's draws coincide with the count leg's to 3 ulps (se 1.27ddc7e86ca7cX-004 vs 1.27ddc7e86ca7fX-004). Only the re-identification leg at ado:9345 uses a plain `bsample`. The two legs are the same estimator - the effect is Monte Carlo, not bias - so this is a reproducibility/UX defect and a false code comment, not a wrong number.
refuter_did: Compared e(bootdist) (the replication coefficient draws), column main_att, between `att` and `att att_i` at one rseed(20260917), reps(120), on my own 40x8 panel. UNCLUSTERED: mreldif on the att column = 0.4505, se_att 0.182665 (count leg) vs 0.158003 (re-id leg), rep-by-rep e.g. 0.87470193 vs 0.49623578. CLUSTERED: mreldif = 1.58e-15, se_att agrees to 2 ulps. Verified the leg selection at ado:378: wdb_reid fires for any cell-weighted estimand regardless of cluster(), so `att att_i` unclustered takes the re-identification leg and `att` alone takes the count leg. The mechanism is the author's own note: the count path at ado:9295-9301 says 'map-frame draws == full-data draws under the cluster()+idcluster() form, measured; plain bsample diverges - A17', and the unclustered branch of the re-id leg at ado:9345 is exactly `if "`clus'" == "" bsample` - the diverging form. The false comment they cite as ado:9340 is actually the sentence at ado:9322, inside the same block; immaterial. On 'Monte Carlo, not bias': I reproduced the mechanism, the clustered agreement and a gap magnitude consistent with MC noise (13.5% at reps(120), where the noise on the difference of two SDs is ~9%), but my single seed cannot discriminate MC from bias - the discriminating same-leg seed-to-seed spread test is the original prober's probe8, which I read and did NOT re-run. I accept their conclusion as consistent with my numbers rather than as my own evidence.

title: permsave() has no comma check and silently writes a file literally named "<name>, replace.dta"
surface: permsave()
claim: bootsave() was given a comma check on 2026-09-13 (RF-6, ado:6282-6289) precisely because bootsave(name, replace) was 'swallowed whole and wrote a file literally called name, replace.dta at rc 0'. permsave() (parse check ado:5866-5881, writer ado:8837) never got that check and still does exactly that.
observed: repro_br1.log: `bootsave(brtest, replace)` -> r(198) with the RF-6 message 'Error: bootsave() takes a plain file name and no comma; replace is a separate option of wooldid...'. `permsave(brtest, replace)` -> rc 0, the run prints 'file brtest, replace.dta saved', and `confirm file "brtest, replace.dta"` returns 0 while `confirm file "brtest.dta"` returns 601. probe2.log reproduces the same on a different dataset (junkp).
expected: permsave() should refuse the comma with the same message. sthlp:495 and sthlp:700 document permsave()'s name rules AS bootsave()'s, so this is also a documented-vs-actual divergence, and the failure mode is silent: the user believes the file is named as they wrote it.
refuter_did: On my own 40x10 panel: `bootsave(skboot, replace)` -> r(198) with the RF-6 message. `permsave(skperm, replace)` -> rc 0, the run prints 'file skperm, replace.dta saved', `confirm file "skperm, replace.dta"` returns 0 and the file holds 21 rows (20 replications plus the rep-0 row), while `confirm file "skperm.dta"` returns 601. Control arm `permsave(skperm2)` writes skperm2.dta normally. Read the source: bootsave's comma check is at ado:6282-6289, permsave's parse block at ado:5866-5881 has no equivalent, and ado:5866 asserts 'permsave(): the name rules are bootsave()'s'. surface: e(gteffects) weight columns; ado:1643 and 1758-1762; gteffects help parenthetical
claim: The gteffects help says the weight columns are "missing for estimands not requested". Requesting att_i alone, or att_itime alone, returns a fully populated w_att_it column although att_it was not requested, because ado:1643 generates w_att_it whenever ANY of att_it / att_itime / att_i is asked for and the builder (ado:1758-1762) fills a column for every weight variable that exists.

title: the replay-staleness guard is self-poisoning: a bare `wooldid` typed when another command owns e() errors about a missing varlist AND records itself as a failed wooldid call, after which a valid stored model cannot be replayed

title: bootsave() under bootalpha(size) writes 1/(rows in the user-if sample) on the observed row where the help promises 1/(estimation sample)

The same effect on a second dataset (p13_docsample.do): 437 rows, e(N)=375, observed row = 1/437; and sum_c n_all_c*w_c = 1.0000000000000000 while sum_c n_estimated_c*w_c = 0.8595794591351535.

Either the divisor or the sentence should change. Secondary, and reported for completeness rather than as the substance: the same map-frame count is the Dirichlet SHAPE alpha_c under bootalpha(size), so a cluster with more item nonresponse carries more concentration than its contribution to the estimate warrants - the replication MEAN is unaffected (expected surviving mass stays proportional to the cluster's estimated row count, so the draws remain centred) and only the dispersion moves, by about sqrt(n_estimated/n_rows) per cluster, roughly 7% here.

Their secondary point (the Gamma shape is also the map-frame count, so per-cluster concentration is mismatched by ~sqrt(n_est/n_rows)) is arithmetically right and leaves the replication mean unbiased, and it is a footnote on an option the help already calls unsound for panel data.

title: bootalpha(size): the Dirichlet concentration is read off the unscreened frame, understating the bootstrap SE by a further sqrt(live fraction)
surface: bootstrap(bayes) + bootalpha(size)
claim: Under bootstrap(bayes) bootalpha(size) the Gamma shape and the row divisor are both __wdbn (ado:8946), the cluster's row count in the UNSCREENED map frame. With a fraction f of a cluster's rows outside e(sample) the cluster-weight CV-squared shrinks by f, so the reported bootstrap standard error is sqrt(f) times what a bootstrap of the estimation sample gives - an undocumented shrinkage on top of the one sthlp:548 already warns about.
observed: Section B: 14 states x 2 units x 12 years, y missing at random for half the cells (no cluster is wholly dead). e(N)=164 and estimate .64896714 identical on both sides. SE .0309309 (full) vs .04522715 (dead rows dropped); ratio .6839 against the predicted sqrt(164/336)=.6986, MC noise on the ratio about 5% at reps(400). The reported SE is 32% too small.
expected: The Dirichlet concentration should be the cluster's count of rows the estimator will actually use. sthlp:548 documents only the n_c-vs-G shrinkage as the reason size 'is not a sound default for panel data'; the extra factor here scales with how unbalanced the panel is and appears nowhere in the output. CAVEAT: bayesboot is not installed on this machine, so I could not check whether bayesboot's id() also counts unscreened rows. If it does, wooldid preserves the advertised parity and the correct reading is 'the understatement on an unbalanced panel is worse than documented'; if it does not, wooldid also diverges from the command it claims parity with. The measured 32% stands either way.
refuter_note: The mechanism and the ~32% magnitude are right; the severity is not high. (i) It is confined to bootalpha(size); bootalpha(equal), the default, is bit-identical with and without the dead rows. (ii) sthlp:548 already calls bootalpha(size) 'not a sound default for panel data' with 'badly understated' standard errors, and its stated purpose is exact comparison against bayesboot. More pointedly, the help's own stated magnitude - 'roughly the square root of the mean cluster size' - already describes FRAME counting: frame n_c = 24 gives sqrt(24)=4.9 and the measured standard/size ratio is 5.3, whereas the live mean 11.4 would give 3.4. So the documented magnitude matches the code; what is imprecise is the phrase 'observation count'. (iii) bayesboot draws its Dirichlet shape from the rows an id() holds IN MEMORY and cannot know what the estimation command drops, so frame counting is most likely the advertised parity (I could not verify - bayesboot is not installed here and is not at the usual SSC path). This is a documentation-precision gap on an option already documented as unsound.
refuter_did: Built my own 14-state x 2-unit x 12-year panel with y missing at random on half the rows (no cluster wholly dead): frame 336 rows, live 160, e(N)=160 both sides, att bit-identical (+1.603ab04740d61X-001). bootalpha(size) se .0270485748 (full) vs .0400620885 (dead rows deleted), ratio .6752 against the predicted sqrt(160/336)=.6901. Then ran the control the probe did not: bootalpha(equal), the DEFAULT, on the same two datasets - se +1.efeac239772daX-004 on BOTH, bit-identical, which is what Dirichlet aggregation requires and which isolates the effect entirely to bootalpha(size). Also measured standard=.1428631773 and equal=.1210734927 on the same data.

title: bootdisplay(bca): the delete-one-cluster jackknife runs one fit per FRAME cluster, so dead clusters enter the acceleration
surface: bootstrap() + bootdisplay(bca)
claim: The BCa jackknife loop is `forval g = 1/wdb_C` (ado:9493) over the unscreened cluster count, so deleting a cluster with no rows in e(sample) reproduces the full estimate exactly. Because the standard acceleration is built from deviations about the MEAN of the leave-one-out estimates, those duplicate points shift the mean and change the acceleration.
observed: Section C: 18 states of which 5 report no outcome. The full-data footer says 'The BCa acceleration comes from a delete-one-cluster jackknife (18 fits)' when only 13 clusters can influence anything. att: full p 0.007, CI [.07633539, .64459309]; oracle p 0.021, CI [.07277344, .55503347]; se .13672789 vs .12282744.
expected: The jackknife should run 13 fits. I do NOT claim the size of the interval difference: those two runs also have different draw streams (different cluster counts shift the bsample sequence), so the measured gap is confounded with Monte-Carlo variation at reps(300). What is established is structural - the acceleration is computed over the wrong set and five of eighteen influence points are exact duplicates of the full fit. An isolating run (comparing the BCa-minus-percentile offset within each run) would settle the magnitude; I did not do it.
refuter_note: The mechanism is confirmed and the confidence should rise from uncertain to certain - e(boot_jk_completed)=18 with e(N_clust)=13 is hard evidence in e(), not prose. But the numerical worry the probe raised (p 0.007 vs 0.021, CI [.076,.645] vs [.073,.555]) is REFUTED: measured Monte-Carlo-free, the acceleration moves by 0.26%. The interval and p gaps they saw were draw-stream confounding, exactly as they honestly flagged. Deleting a dead cluster reproduces the full estimate, which sits near the mean of the leave-one-out values, so the duplicate points contribute almost nothing to d2 or d3 and the ratio largely cancels. The real cost is five wasted refits and a footer that overstates the jackknife.
refuter_did: Built my own 18-state panel with 5 states reporting no outcome, bootdisplay(bca). title: SEEDED CLAIM: facts confirmed, stated mechanism REFUTED — rank tracks the draw count, not the `ereturn repost` bypass

Additionally, the demonstration test is on POST-treatment coefficients with large TRUE effects, so its tiny p is a correct rejection and is not evidence of a wrong number; and Stata's `test` DOES announce 'Constraint N dropped' when q exceeds the rank, so 'no constraint dropped' at q=3 against rank 7 is correct behaviour, not a missing signal.

MECHANISM, measured: pA2_lean.log varies only reps() on a fixed K=20 spec — reps 4/8/15/30/60 give boot_N_V 4/8/15/30/60 and rank 3/7/10/10/10, i.e. rank = min(distinct column space, boot_N_V−1). claim: ado:10044-10049, ado:14556-14560 and ado:16956-16961 all state that `ereturn post` would trip on, or wholesale-zero, the matrices wooldid produces, and that using `ereturn repost` is what avoids it. No user-visible number is wrong because of this — the route chosen works — but a maintainer refactoring this code is being told a barrier exists where there is none, and told that repost protects against nonsymmetry when it does not. refuter_did: Ran the post cases at the top level (r1b_post.do) and the repost cases inside an eclass program (r1c_repost.do; `ereturn repost` returns rc 152 outside one, which is a harness fact about my first attempt, not a defect). title: Requesting event-study horizons silently moves the headline att and inflates its confidence interval by up to 60%
surface: esprelength() / espostlength() interaction with the reported att estimate and its interval; the reference-normalization pool
claim: On one unchanged dataset, adding esprelength()/espostlength() changes the reported `att` point estimate and widens its analytic standard error by up to 60%, with no message. The mechanism is that the reference-normalization pool is `relyr < -esprelength` plus each treated unit's forced first in-sample observation, so requested pre-horizons are removed from the reference pool. This IS documented -- but only in the Stored Results entry for e(escomp_refN), not in the esprelength() option entry where a user would look, and nothing is printed at run time.
observed: probeI.log, ESOPT block, one dataset (fixI.dta, 40 units, i=cg, cluster(unit)). e(N)=320 and e(df_r)=39 are IDENTICAL in all four runs -- the load-bearing observation, since it rules out any change of sample or degrees of freedom. (none): att=1.093400346 se=0.132401198; esprelength(1) espostlength(1): att=1.117099722 se=0.158879296 (+20%); esprelength(2) espostlength(2): att=1.132362929 se=0.173433656 (+31%); esprelength(3) espostlength(3): att=1.065211265 se=0.211200984 (+60%).
expected: A user who adds esprelength(3) only to draw an event-study plot should not silently get a different ATT and a 60%-wider confidence interval. All four estimates remain consistent for the same truth (1.0 in this DGP), so this is efficiency rather than bias -- hence low severity -- but it is exactly what makes two runs of "the same" specification disagree, and the option's own help entry does not mention it. This also explains an apparent inconsistency between two of my own MC arms (sd(b)=0.183 with esprelength(2) vs 0.125 without on otherwise-similar designs), recorded so nobody else burns time on it.
refuter_note: The behaviour, the stated reference-pool mechanism and the doc-gap are all real -- e(escomp_refN) falling 270 -> 180 -> 135 confirms the pool shrinks exactly as claimed, and there is no runtime message. Two things in the claim are wrong. (1) The title and claim say 'adding esprelength()/espostlength()', implicating espostlength(). It moves nothing: espostlength(2) reproduces the no-ES att AND se to the last digit. The mover is esprelength() alone, which is what the stated mechanism implies but the headline contradicts. (2) 'inflates its confidence interval by up to 60%' is their dataset's number, not a property of the option: the same option at the same setting gives +21% on mine. The finding should read 'esprelength() > 0 silently re-bases the headline att and widens its interval by an amount that depends on how much of the pre-history the request consumes'.

title: The i-keyed-covariate convention is documented and cautioned for the bootstrap re-id leg, and neither documented nor cautioned for the permonsetcohorts rebuild
surface: permute() + permonsetcohorts documentation and cautions
claim: wooldid warns and documents when a covariate names the i variable under the bootstrap's re-identification leg (ado:403-414 prints the A10 caution; sthlp:532 spells out the convention), but the permonsetcohorts rebuild, which performs the same kind of per-replication re-identification of i with strictly greater exposure, prints no caution and the help's permonsetcohorts text (sthlp:68, 255, 431, 1240, 1352) says nothing about covariates at all -- including when the user literally writes fe(<the i variable>).
observed: `wooldid y coh t onset, att cluster(state) permute(shuffle) permexact permonsetcohorts fe(coh)` runs to completion with no message of any kind about fe() naming i; the only cautions printed are the unrelated 'only 4 of the resampling clusters are ever treated' one. The p-value moves from .04444444 to .02222222 relative to the same run without fe(coh). The bootstrap path on the same kind of specification prints 'Caution: a covariate specification names the i variable ...'.
expected: Either the same caution the bootstrap leg prints, or help text under permonsetcohorts saying what happens to i-keyed covariates inside a replication. The asymmetry is a documented-vs-actual divergence in the sense that the help's only statement of this convention (sthlp:532) is scoped to bootstrap() and so implicitly tells a reader that permute() does not have the issue -- when in fact permute() under permonsetcohorts has a worse version of it (FP-1).
refuter_note: Every factual assertion is true and reproduces, but it is not a separate defect and it is not a documented-vs-actual divergence. (1) It is FP-1's remedy restated -- everything it asks for is what fixing FP-1 produces. (2) Row D shows the bootstrap 'convention' is a NAME-EQUALITY tripwire, not coverage of the class FP-1 describes: a covariate merely constant within i gets no caution on the bootstrap leg either. So the honest statement is 'neither engine says anything about a covariate constant within i; the bootstrap has a narrow tripwire for the literal fe(i) spelling', not 'documented and cautioned for the bootstrap, silent for permute'. FP-2 overstates the bootstrap side's coverage. (3) The load-bearing inference -- that sthlp:532 'implicitly tells a reader that permute() does not have the issue' -- is inference about a reader, not a promise the help makes; brief category 5 needs the help to promise X while the code does Y, and here the help simply says nothing. (4) known_bydesign.md section 6 already carries 'No display line for the permonsetcohorts rebuild of i -- e(perm_irebuilt) is the record. Ruled 2026-09-16, Not to be reopened.' That is adjacent rather than identical (it is about announcing the rebuild, not about covariates), but it is the author already declining to print on this path. Verified-true core: on the exact fe(<the i variable>) spelling the asymmetry between the two engines is real.
refuter_did: Ran the five comparisons non-quietly on my own panel and grepped for 'names the i variable': (A) permute(shuffle) permonsetcohorts fe(coh) -> NO caution; (B) permute + controls(cohbase) -> NO caution; (C) bootstrap(standard) cluster(coh)==i att_i fe(coh) -> 'Caution: a covariate specification names the i variable coh; under resampling, ...' PRINTED; (D) same but controls(cohbase), constant within i but not NAMED i -> NOT printed; (E) bootstrap cluster(state) finer than i, fe(coh) -> NOT printed (the wdb_nest gate). Also read ado:403-414 and the full sthlp:532 sentence, and re-read known_bydesign.md.

title: e(permdist_b) and e(perm_jointW)/e(perm_advW) are not row-aligned when replications fail
surface: permute() stored results: e(permdist_b), e(permdist), e(perm_jointW), e(perm_advW), permsave()
claim: In one permute() run, e(permdist_b) and e(permdist) are compacted to the completed replications while e(perm_jointW) and e(perm_advW) keep the full requested length with missing rows, so row r of one is a different replication from row r of the other and neither is indexed by permsave's _rep. The help states this for the bootstrap side and says nothing for the permutation side.
observed: requested=120, completed=111, failed=9 gives e(permdist_b) 111x6, e(permdist) 111x1, e(perm_jointW) 120x1 (111 non-missing), e(perm_advW) 120x1, permsave file 121 rows. Source: wooldid_bootdist() at ado:14644 selects rows with any non-missing coefficient, while wooldid_permqf/permadv write Wr = J(rows(A),1,.) at full accumulator length.
expected: One row basis for every replication-indexed object of a run, or a statement of the difference. The same help file carries that statement for the bootstrap twins: bootsave() says 'a replication that failed keeps its row with every value missing, so _rep indexes the draws exactly as e(bootdist) does after its missing rows are dropped', and e(bootdist_se) is 'on the same row mask as e(bootdist)'. The permutation paragraph (sthlp:1348) says only 'the draw matrices e(permdist_b)' and calls e(perm_jointW)/e(perm_advW) 'the replication statistics behind the joint, equality and adversarial p-values', while advertising this surface as the reconstruction route ('the p is reconstructable from the pair'). No printed number is wrong; select() on the mismatched pair errors loudly, so the quiet failure shapes are a positional loop over rows and a by-row merge of e(permdist_b) onto the permsave file. Sharper case: applying the help's own formula (1+#{W_r>=W_obs})/(n+1) to the full-length e(perm_jointW) without dropping its missing rows over-counts by exactly e(perm_failed), because Mata's :>= treats missing as +infinity - here (1+9+nex)/121 instead of (1+nex)/112.
refuter_note: The claim's own words -- 'neither is indexed by permsave's _rep' -- are FALSE for the jointW/advW pair, which is the half that matters because that pair is the help's advertised reconstruction route. wooldid_bootsavemk (ado:14871) does st_addobs(R+1), _rep = 0::R, st_store(., idx, B[1,k] \ A[.,k]): the file IS the whole accumulator, and wooldid_permqf/permadv write Wr = J(rows(A),1,.) on that same accumulator, so e(perm_jointW) and e(perm_advW) are precisely _rep-indexed. e(permdist_b) is recoverable from the same file by dropping the all-missing coefficient rows (maxabsdiff 0). The run therefore DOES supply one row basis for everything -- the permsave file -- and it reconciles the two e() bases. The correct framing is a documentation gap about missing rows: sthlp:1348-1349 advertises 'the p is reconstructable from the pair' and never says e(perm_jointW) is at the full REQUESTED length with missing rows while e(permdist_b) beside it is compacted. Mata's :>= ranks missing above every finite value, so the naive reconstruction silently over-counts by e(perm_failed). Additionally (source read only, not measured): the gap is engine-agnostic, not permutation-specific -- sthlp:1340 describes e(boot_jointW) with no missing-rows statement either and wooldid_bootqf writes Wr = J(rows(A),1,.) identically; the prober's bootstrap contrast is about bootsave()/e(bootdist_se), a different object.
refuter_did: Built my own failure mechanism instead of theirs (they used permprobs with a 14% chance of drawing zero treated clusters; contrived). Mine is administrative attrition: 10 districts, 2 adopt in 2017, 3 stop reporting after 2014, so a shuffle landing both onsets on early leavers leaves no treated observation and the replication fails; P = C(3,2)/C(10,2) = 3/45. Measured requested=100, completed=93, FAILED=7. Confirmed the two row bases: e(permdist_b) 93x6 and e(permdist) 93x1 compacted, e(perm_jointW)/e(perm_advW) 100x1 with 7 missing rows, permsave file 101 rows. Then tested the part I doubted ROW BY ROW rather than by counts: the missing rows of e(perm_jointW) are EXACTLY the _rep rows of the permsave file whose coefficient columns are all missing (PB_ALIGN agree=100 of 100), and e(permdist_b) equals the compacted permsave coefficient block with maxabsdiff = 0. Also reproduced their 'sharper case' exactly: applying (1+#{W_r>=W_obs})/(n+1) to the full-length e(perm_jointW) without dropping missing rows gives p=0.51485 against the posted/correct 0.47872, an over-count of 7 = e(perm_failed) exactly. Controls pB_rowalign.do and pB2_rowalign.do (realistic unbalanced panels, late reporters, early leavers, singleton cohorts) completed every replication: with zero failures there is zero misalignment.

Nothing in e() gives the correct denominator for that test, and — the part no prior agent saw — e(perm_failed)=0 together with row counts that match e(permdist_b) does NOT mean there are no missing rows to drop: a replication that merely loses a tested event-study horizon on an unbalanced administrative panel leaves a missing W row on a run that reports every replication as completed and prints no caution.

title: The permexact add-one caution describes a branch the code does not take: at complete-enumeration-but-not-a-member the share is plain and the p can be 0
surface: permexact + wooldid_permtail share branch (ado:15992) vs the wdp_addone caution (ado:8297, flag at ado:16147)
claim: `wooldid_permtail` selects the plain share on `exact | memb` (ado:15992), where `exact` is COMPLETENESS of the enumeration, but `wooldid_permstat` flags an element into `wdp_addone` on `!memb` alone (ado:16147) and the caution the caller prints (ado:8297) asserts the add-one form is in use. For an element with exact=1 and memb=0 the caution is false and the add-one floor of 1/(n+1) is not applied, so the reported p can be exactly 0 over a reference set that the caution itself says does not contain the observed statistic.
observed: Kernels extracted verbatim from the pinned build (sed -n '15908,15915p;15937,15943p;15945,16062p', md5 7b878e5b1e4484a0527f855ec6a65154) and called directly with 30 complete draws and an observed statistic one ulp below all of them: exact=1 memb=0 gives p = 0 (default convention) and p = 0 under permside(left), with p_lo = 0, p_hi = 1, and the Monte-Carlo se left missing (i.e. the share is treated as exact); the add-one branch exact=0 memb=0 gives 0.064516129 and 0.032258065 respectively. The caution that fires in exactly this situation reads "...their p-values use the add-one form (1 + count)/(n + 1) rather than an exact share". The same shape is in wooldid_permqf (ado:16221-16249), wooldid_permstep (ado:16293-16320) and wooldid_permpw.
expected: Either the share branch should key on membership alone for a flagged element, or the caution should say what actually happens. As written the run promises a floor of 1/(n+1) while reporting 0, and known_bydesign §2 explicitly ranks a p of 0 on a non-permrawp permutation p as reportable. REACHABILITY IS UNPROVEN, which is why this is filed uncertain: I could not drive wooldid into exact=1 with memb=0 from the command line. memb was TRUE for every one of 54+30+16+1 permuted elements across six designs, because the rep-0 comparator and the identity replication are the same fit; and the two estimation paths the review brief names as not bit-reproducible run-to-run (unconditionalse, customvce(cluster ...)) are refused by permute() with r(198) (p07b_edges.do cases E10-E12), which removes the obvious trigger. The contradiction between the branch and the message that documents it is nevertheless demonstrated.
refuter_note: The code-level contradiction is real and I confirm it; the runtime defect it predicts is not reachable, and the prober's evidence does not show that it is. Their OBSERVED is a unit test of kernels extracted with sed and called with inputs (an observed statistic one ulp below all 30 draws, exact=1, memb=0) that wooldid does not produce -- legitimate evidence about the kernel, none about the command. More importantly, I closed BY MEASUREMENT (r6_guard.do) the one structural route that would have reached it and that the prober did not try: if a cluster carried more than one onset, the identity replication (which writes one cluster-level onset to every row of the cluster) would fit different data from the rep-0 comparator (which fits ttrevar as given), giving exk=1 with memb=0. On cluster(state) with two units of one state at onsets 4 and 6 wooldid exits r(459) 'permute() requires clusters to be subsets of treatment-onset groups' under default safety AND under safety(off) (an onset-homogeneous control on the same data runs, M=6). So the state is latent: a three-way inconsistency between ado:15992, ado:16130 and the ado:8297 caution that no user input demonstrated so far can exercise. Keep it as a code-hygiene item; do not describe it as a p-value that can print 0, because nothing shows it can.
refuter_did: Split the claim into its textual half and its reachability half. TEXTUAL (confirmed by reading, no run needed, and stronger than the prober put it): ado:15992 takes the plain share on (exact | memb); ado:16127 sets exk = (M < . & sum(s :< .) == M), i.e. COMPLETENESS; ado:16130 flags wdp_addone on !memb ALONE; ado:8297 then asserts the add-one form is in use -- and ado:15974-15979's own comment says "`memb' is MEMBERSHIP ... which is what the SHARE convention turns on", so the code ORs in a flag its own comment says should not govern. REACHABILITY (my own runs, r2_px2.do): three further designs beyond the prober's six. T1 permonsetcohorts + permexact with cluster strictly finer than i, i rebuilt in every replication (e(perm_irebuilt)=1, M=60): the rep-0 comparator statistic occurs bitwise exactly once among the 60 draws for every element, so memb=1. T2 permtstat + permexact, where b and se reach s = b/se by separate paths: hits = 1 for every element. T3 unbalanced panel (M=20, two horizons estimable in only 16 assignments): exk=0 with memb=1 is reached, the incomplete-enumeration caution fires, and the plain share is correctly taken over the reduced set -- the reachable half of the OR. The wdp_addone caution printed ZERO times in any run in this directory. Separately, r4_oracle.py recomputed every reported permexact quantity from the saved draws and matched to 1e-14, which is what a broken membership test would have shown up in.

title: The 149/150 over-coverage at cluster()==i is an ADDED cohort-composition term, not the effect the record names
surface: bootstrap(standard) at cluster() == i, att_i (the nesting re-id leg)
claim: The recorded att_i over-coverage of 149/150 = .9933 at cluster()==i (c8c4e2c, reported and unexplained) is caused by the nesting re-id leg injecting a cohort-composition component Var_s(tau_s)/S_treated into the bootstrap distribution, which the Monte Carlo cannot contain because its DGP holds tau_s fixed. The explanation on the record - 'at or above the i level the covariance stops seeing the treated cells' own variation' - names an effect measured at SE/SD 0.66-0.75 that makes intervals too NARROW, so it cannot produce over-coverage; my HOM arm shows that effect is indeed present (ratio 0.913) and is simply overwhelmed.
observed: Re-implementation of the published dgpE (40 states, T=6, unit RE + AR(1)), HET (tau .4/1.2, Var_s = .16) vs HOM (tau .8 for all, Var_s = 0), identical truth att_i = 0.8, identical noise draws, b(att_i) bit-identical between arms. With the noise scaled to 2% so the true sampling SD is ~0.003: cluster(state)==i se(att_i) = 0.0868634699692049 (HET) vs 0.0019218211999355 (HOM), a 45x gap; predicted composition SE sqrt(.16/20) = 0.0894. Keep-i arm on the same data: 0.0244 (HET) vs 0.0022 (HOM). At full noise, MC sampling SD of att_i = 0.13328 over 70 draws; cluster(state)==i boot RMS SE = 0.15501 (HET, ratio 1.163) and 0.12167 (HOM, ratio 0.913); cluster(unit) keep-i boot RMS SE = 0.12830 (HET, ratio 0.963). Paired implied composition SEs: .0903 .1343 .0675 .0655 .1053.
expected: Those ratios predict BOTH published numbers: ratio 1.163 gives 2*Phi(1.96*1.163)-1 = .977 against the observed P5 149/150 = .9933 (+1.3 sd on Binomial(150,.977)), and ratio 0.963 gives .941 against the observed P4 142/150 = .9467 (-0.4 sd). Also correcting the record: P4's nominal coverage is NOT evidence the keep-i branch is correct - on that design a treated state with 2 units goes entirely undrawn with probability e^-2 = .135, so keep-i carries about 28% of the composition SE and the total happened to land near the fixed-cohort sampling SD. Whether the composition term belongs in att_i's SE (superpopulation of cohorts vs the cohorts in the data) is an estimand ruling for the author; what is measured here is that the two regimes estimate different variances and nothing reports which ran.
refuter_note: The composition mechanism is real and I measured it precisely: HET se(att_i) = .0886, .0946, .0899, .0969 against HOM .0044, .0041, .0057 — a factor of ~20 on data whose idiosyncratic noise is 2% of the effect — with the predicted composition SE sqrt(.16/20) = .0894. That is genuine added value and it is the measurement of the §7 'unexplained' over-coverage. But three things in the claim are wrong. (1) THE RECORD ALREADY MADE THEIR CORRECTION. test/suite/PREREG_FEATURE_FINECLUS_2026-09-16.md, F3/F4 amendment 3, carries a section headed 'A wrong analogy, retracted here so it does not propagate': 'That passage documents the ANALYTIC cluster-robust covariance at or above i and its direction is anti-conservative ... This measurement is the BOOTSTRAP and its direction is conservative. Same location in the design, different estimator, opposite sign. Do not cite that passage for this finding.' FCW-03's entire 'the explanation on the record cannot produce over-coverage' argument was made by the author on the same day he recorded the number. (2) The record also already states the mechanism, as a hypothesis: 'conservatism of the percentile cluster bootstrap where every cohort is its own resampling cluster'. (3) The attribution 'the nesting RE-ID LEG injecting a cohort-composition component' is wrong. r03b measures se(att) at cluster(state)==i as .0709192322 on the re-id leg (att att_i) and .0709192322 on the count path (att alone) — bit-identical. The composition term is a property of resampling cohorts as clusters, present on both legs and independent of the unit rule, which is also why the project's own att control over-covered 149/150 on the same arm while att is invariant to that rule (their own se(att) ratio 1.0029, mine 1.0091). Severity high -> low: it measures a number the project recorded, explained as a hypothesis, and ruled 'recorded, not fixed' on 2026-09-16.
refuter_did: Two things. (1) Measured the mechanism cheaply and decisively instead of re-running a 150-draw MC: 40 states, T=6, cluster(state)==i, noise sd .02, HET (tau .4/1.2, Var_s = .16) vs HOM (tau .8 everywhere, Var_s = 0), identical noise draws, reps(199), two dataset seeds x two rseeds. (2) Tested their ATTRIBUTION with r03b_whichleg.do: wdb_reid is set only for a cell-weighted estimand or boottstat+cluster (ado:378), so a run asking for `att` alone at cluster()==i never enters the re-id leg. (3) Read the project's own record of the 149/150 number rather than taking their quotation of it on trust.

title: Regression: the reps() p-value-resolution caution is unreachable without cluster(), on a path T2 just opened
surface: bootstrap() reps() cautions in wooldid_bootctl
claim: RF-2 (commit 813c414, 2026-09-13) moved the `if reps > 0` resolution-caution block from an unconditional site into the body of `if "clus" != "" {` (pinned build: block opens ado:6459, caution at ado:6473-6478, closes ado:6501). An unclustered bootstrap therefore prints no caution about the p-value grid, and T2 made unclustered + cell-weighted estimands newly legal on 2026-09-16.
observed: Three paired runs, one dataset, reps(10) throughout. RUN1 `att att_i att_it bootstrap(standard) reps(10)` with no cluster(): rc 0, NO caution. RUN2 the same plus cluster(unit): rc 0, prints 'Caution: with reps(10) the coefficient p-values fall on a grid of 0.200 (2/reps) ...'. RUN3 `att` only, no cluster(): rc 0, NO caution. Source confirmed with `git show 813c414`, which deletes the block at old :6011 and re-inserts it inside the cluster-conditioned block.
expected: The caution's content - that a printed p of 0 is the resolution floor rather than evidence - has nothing to do with clustering; it is about reps(). The commit message says only that it was 'moved below every aborting validation', which was the intent; landing inside the cluster block was not. The unclustered leg is otherwise treated carefully (bootdf(clusters) is refused there at ado:6328-6331 precisely because the resampling unit is the observation), so the omission reads as accidental.
refuter_note: The structural claim is right and the gate is WIDER than they said: RUN1 (att att_i att_it, no cluster) rc 0 no caution, RUN2 (same + cluster) caution prints, RUN3 (att only, no cluster) none, RUN4 (bootdisplay(wald), no cluster) none, RUN5 (boottstat, no cluster) none, RUN6 (bootstrap(bayes), no cluster) none. The git move is confirmed: 813c414 deletes the block from a top-level site (the 22 preceding lines are the CS-20 rationale comment and the 'bootstrap() requires reps(#)' error, no cluster gate) and re-inserts it inside `if "`clus'" != "" {`. BUT the information loss is much smaller than the claim implies. The disclosure footer at ado:11784-11785 is NOT cluster-gated: RUN1 and RUN3 still print, unprompted, 'The rank-based coefficient p-values have resolution 2/10 = 0.200: a p printed as 0 means p below that (no completed replication on the far side of the null)' plus the below-table note 'p = 0 above means p < 0.200', and RUN5 prints the studentized analogue 'their resolution and their smallest attainable value are both 2/(n + 1) = 0.182'.
