The only leg with no coverage at all is bootdisplay(wald), because ado:11785 opens `else if "`wdbdsp'" != "wald"`; I tried to exhibit harm there (r04b: jointtests + wald + reps(10), no cluster) and could not — at reps low enough to trigger the caution the joint tests were absent ('no usable replication statistic'), so no unfloored joint p was actually printed. Severity medium -> low. Medium would be defensible on the ground that CS-20 was an author ruling (2026-09-07) that this caution should exist and RF-2 silently removed it for a whole class of runs; I put it at low because I could not construct a run where a user is actually left uninformed.
refuter_did: Ran six paired runs at reps(10) on my own 12-county panel covering all three caution variants plus bayes, not just the percentile one they tested; then read the FULL output of the unclustered runs rather than only grepping for the caution; then verified the regression in git myself (git show -U25 813c414) rather than taking their git reading on trust; then built r04b_waldleg.do to test whether the one leg with no footer coverage actually harms anyone.

title: Nothing in e(), the table or bootsave() records which bootstrap regime ran
surface: e() postings for bootstrap(standard) under the two-regime unit rule
claim: wdb_nest is computed in wooldid_bootrun (ado:8987-8998), c_local-ed to the shell, and used only at ado:407 to decide whether to print the A10 covariate caution. It is not posted to e(), not displayed, and not saved by bootsave(), so a user cannot tell which of two variance concepts - differing by 23% in FCW-01/FCW-02 - produced their standard error.
observed: grep of the pinned build: wdb_nest appears at ado:407, 8987, 8993, 8998, 9348 and nowhere else; no `ereturn` of it exists. The probe1d and probe1c logs show two runs on near-identical data producing se(att_i) 0.4349 and 0.3308 with no difference in any printed line or stored result other than the SE itself.
expected: T1's exactly analogous regime switch IS recorded: e(perm_irebuilt) (ado:195, sthlp:1352) was kept expressly as 'the record' when the author declined a display line for the permonsetcohorts rebuild on 2026-09-16 ('Not to be reopened'). The bootstrap's two-regime rule, shipped the same day and with a larger numerical consequence, got no equivalent. This is what makes FCW-01 and FCW-02 silent rather than merely surprising.
refuter_note: The claim holds empirically: diff r05_A.txt r05_B.txt is EMPTY — every e() scalar and macro is identical across the two regimes — while se(att_i) moves from +1.0db021a8e5c64X-002 to +1.a9dfa55549169X-003, a ratio of 0.7896. wdb_nest is indeed never ereturn'd (only ado:406-407, 8969-8998, 9323, 9348). title: A cluster whose outcome is missing on every row stays in the permutation design, so rows the estimator discards change the p-value and the interval
surface: permute() design population (wooldid_permrun ado:7481-7490; wooldid_permctl ado:5959-5964); shared with bootstrap() (wooldid_bootrun ado:8912-8923)
claim: Under permute(), the randomization design population is ((if)==1) & !missing(cluster) and does NOT require a row to be usable for estimation. A cluster all of whose rows have a missing outcome therefore enters the map frame, is handed an onset in every replication's shuffle and enlarges the reference set, while contributing nothing to any fit. Two datasets with a bit-identical estimation sample and bit-identical point estimates consequently report different permutation p-values and different confidence intervals, with no caution. Removing the same cluster by setting its CLUSTER value to missing, or by the user's `if`, DOES remove it from the design, so the three exclusion routes disagree with one another.
observed: 40 counties in 10 states, state 5 a 2006 adopter, 30 replications, rseed(20260917). A = state 5's outcome set to missing with its rows kept; B = state 5's rows dropped. e(N)=360 and e(N_clust)=9 in BOTH; the att point estimate is bit-identical (+1.82acfb38ea209X-001 in both, `identical = 1`). But e(perm_npossible) is 16800 (A) vs 5040 (B); p(pretreatment att) 0.516129 vs 0.322581; p(ES_att pre1) 0.580645 vs 0.451613; the 95% interval for att [0.4452, 1.4635] vs [0.2666, 1.4431]. Setting state 5's cluster value to missing (C) and `if state != 5` (D) both give 5040 and reproduce B. On a second panel (probeH) the same contrast gives p(pretreatment att) 0.645 vs 0.452 and the att interval [0.636, 2.019] vs [0.293, 1.948]. Sharper instance (probeE2 J0/J1/J2): when the phantom is the SOLE carrier of an onset level (state 7, the only 2008 adopter), the estimation sample contains no 2008 cohort at all, yet a data-carrying cluster received the 2008 onset in 29 of 30 replications; e(perm_npossible) 16800 vs 1680. Nothing fails: e(perm_failed)=0, e(perm_blank)=0, identical column sets - the mechanism is a different design, not broken replications. Partial missingness inside a surviving cluster is neutral (H4partial == H4bdrop). wooldid_bootrun uses the identical predicate (ado:8912-8923), so bootstrap() shares the design population.
expected: Rows that cannot enter any fit should not change an inference surface. The randomization distribution wooldid reports is meant to be the distribution of the realized statistic under reassignment of the estimable design; a cluster that can never carry information consumes one of the onset labels in the replications that hand it a treated onset, and in the sharpest case puts into the reference set statistics from cohort structures the observed data cannot produce. The expectation is also internal: a missing CLUSTER value removes a cluster from the design, the user's `if` removes it, wooldid records that the rows left (e(N_dropped)=40 on the kept-rows run), and sthlp:61 states only that the `if` rule applies identically to the estimation sample and the randomization design - nothing says a missing outcome is treated differently from a missing cluster id. e(perm_npossible)=16800 is the correct count for the design wooldid uses; the defect is that the design silently differs from the estimable one and that the three exclusion routes are inconsistent.
refuter_note: The observations are correct and reproduce harder than PI-1 showed them, but the behaviour is not undocumented and is not a defect. wooldid.sthlp lines 430-431, inside the permute() entry, specify it verbatim and name missing outcomes as the example: 'the randomization design consists of the clusters having at least one row where the if expression evaluates to exactly 1 with a nonmissing cluster value; rows wooldid later removes by its deterministic markout, e.g. missing outcomes or zero weights, still count toward the design and its possible-assignment count'. That one sentence supplies the design predicate PI-1 reports, the asymmetry between the three exclusion routes, the rule that markout-dead rows stay in, the outcome as the named example, and the fact that the possible-assignment count is what moves. PI-1's EXPECTED rests on 'sthlp:61 states only that the if rule applies identically ... nothing says a missing outcome is treated differently from a missing cluster id' -- that is false; PI-1 cited sthlp:61 and missed sthlp:430. The run-time footer also prints the design size ('56 of 56 replications completed; 56 possible assignments'), which a reader can compare against e(N_clust)=7. So there is no doc-vs-code divergence, no silently wrong number, and no inference path failing what it documents. What remains is a legitimate design question for the author -- should the randomization population be the estimable design or the assignable one -- not a defect, and 'medium' overstates it. Two sub-claims should also be struck: 'with no caution' is literally true but misleading given the help text and the printed assignment count; and the bootstrap extension ('wooldid_bootrun uses the identical predicate, so bootstrap() shares the design population') is true at the predicate level but has no measurable consequence -- measured, bootstrap SEs move by 0.1% (bayes), 0.7% (standard, att) and 0.55% (standard, att_i), all inside Monte-Carlo noise, because aweights are scale-free and the normalized weight sub-vector over the clusters that carry rows has the same distribution with or without the phantom.
refuter_did: Wrote my own repro from the claim on my own panel (8 states x 3 counties x 8 years, state 1 = 2004, state 2 = 2006, rest never, state 8 = the phantom) and replaced PI-1's 30 sampled replications with permexact, which enumerates every distinct assignment and removes the RNG entirely -- PI-1's contrast was confounded, since 10 clusters shuffle differently than 9, so a p gap at 30 draws was not by itself evidence that the reference distribution moved. Under exact enumeration it is: e(N)=168, e(N_clust)=7 and att bit-identical (+1.a7c7591ced275X-001) in every arm, while e(perm_npossible) is 56 with the phantom against 42 without, exact p .07142857 against .04761905 -- crossing .05 -- and the 95% shift interval [-.5312,.8277] against [-.5130,.5876]. B (rows dropped), C (cluster value set missing) and D (if state != 8) agree bit-for-bit, so the three exclusion routes really do split 1-vs-2. I added two arms PI-1 did not have: the cluster can equally be killed by a missing CONTROL rather than a missing outcome (56 vs 42, same p gap), and I reproduced PI-1's sharpest J case (phantom the sole 2008 adopter: 336 vs 42). I then checked every arm's npossible against the combinatorial count for the documented population and they all match. Separately I measured PI-1's unmeasured bootstrap extension (e5_boot.do, e7_physleg.do). Finally I read the permute() entry of the help end to end, which PI-1 did not.

title: With cluster() at or above i, every subgroups() row's analytic standard error is numerically identical to the pooled one (and so is e(boot_ase_obs), the boottstat studentization denominator)

claim: Under a clustered VCE at or above the level of `i`, the standard error wooldid reports for each `subgroups()` level equals the pooled standard error to 15 significant digits, on the att row and on essentially every event-study row, even though the subgroup estimates differ and separate subgroup-restricted runs give clearly different standard errors. The subgroup standard errors therefore carry no subgroup-specific information.

repro_sgse_clusteri.do (24 states, i = state, cluster(state), subgroups(mod(state,2))):
  main att b=1.567921674  se=0.126889554  (+1.03deab9e44e73X-003)
  sg0  att b=1.496542253  se=0.126889554  (+1.03deab9e44e75X-003)
  sg1  att b=1.639301096  se=0.126889554  (+1.03deab9e44e74X-003)
  ratios to pooled 1.00000000000 / 1.00000000000; 5 of 6 table rows identical.
CONTROL, same data, `robust` instead of cluster(): 0.226363662 / 0.267818831 / 0.244313253 (ratios 1.183, 1.079).
CONTROL, two separate runs restricted to each subgroup with cluster(state): b=1.465722071 se=0.221480605 and b=1.670121277 se=0.132589734.
p13_sgse2.do, cluster STRICTLY ABOVE i (i = district, 60 cohorts, cluster(state), 30 states):
  main 1.153391171 se=+1.644d7ae0eb146X-004 ; sg0 1.169219231 se=+1.644d7ae0eb141X-004 ; sg1 1.137563111 se=+1.644d7ae0eb14aX-004 ; ratios 1.00000000000.
expected: Two subgroups holding different cohorts, with different point estimates and (as the separate runs show) genuinely different sampling variability, cannot share a standard error to the last two bits. The `robust` control uses the SAME margins weight vectors and returns three different numbers, so the collapse is a property of the clustered e(V), not of the estimand's weights. This sits on the boottstat surface because wooldid_bootwire's first walk (ado:9606-9625) fills `aseobs` from column 2 of e(wdidmainresults)/e(wdidsgresults_*) -- exactly these numbers -- and `aseobs` is e(boot_ase_obs), the percentile-t studentization denominator and the multiplier in the printed interval b - q*se_obs. known_bydesign section 1 rules that analytic SEs are UNDERSTATED (0.66-0.75 coverage) in this regime; that is a statement about the LEVEL of the pooled SE and does not say the subgroup SEs become the same number. refuter_note: The exact identity is a PERFECTLY-BALANCED-PANEL artifact, not a property of cluster() >= i. On any ragged panel -- which is what administrative data look like -- it is simply false. And where it DOES hold, it is mathematically the same statement as a behaviour wooldid already detects, documents and withholds: with a PSD covariance, d'Vd = 0 for the difference direction forces Vd = 0, so 'the contrast SE is zero' and 'each subgroup SE equals the pooled SE' are one fact. wooldid_sgdeg (ado:11092, ruled BS-15) measures the implied correlation, blanks the contrast, and the run the prober himself executed PRINTED the caution naming it ('largest implied correlation between two subgroups' estimates 0.9961 ... cancellation residue rather than an estimated variance ... use bootstrap() WITHOUT boottstat'). HOWEVER: the investigation of this surface turned up the real defect beside it, filed as SK-01 at critical.

title: The simultaneous band's critical value never sees bootdf(), so under bootdisplay(wald) -- where the pointwise interval IS symmetric -- the band still sits inside it
surface: simultaneousbands + bootdisplay(wald) + bootdf()
claim: wooldid.sthlp:525 scopes its non-nesting caveat to displays 'where the printed pointwise interval is a rank interval and not symmetric ... bootdisplay(percentile), bootdisplay(bc) or bootdisplay(bca)'. Under bootdisplay(wald) the pointwise interval is the symmetric b +/- invt(G-1,.975)*sd, so on the help's own logic the band must nest it; at modest cluster counts it does not, because the band's critical value carries no degrees-of-freedom correction and is computed on a different replication subset.
observed:
repro_band_ignores_bootdf.do (8 clusters, 2 horizons, reps(999), bootdisplay(wald), simultaneousbands):
  e(boot_df)=7 ; pointwise critical value invt(7,.975)=2.364624 ; e(esband_crit_att)=2.199558 ; band critical value is SMALLER = 1 ; HORIZONS_WITH_BAND_INSIDE_POINTWISE=2 ; FAIL=1 (both sides, both horizons).
Sweep p11_banddf.do: W_G8_M1 zc=2.364624 vs bandcrit=2.108943, 2 violations; W_G12_M1 (p09 K3) bandcrit 2.1738 vs invt(11,.975)=2.2010, both sides, both horizons.
Second, independent mechanism, p11 cell W_G8_M3: bandcrit 2.382340 > zc 2.364624, yet 4 of 6 horizons still violate -- because the band's sd_h is computed on the LISTWISE-complete replications while the table's se_h is computed per column.
expected: A simultaneous band at level() must be at least as wide as the pointwise interval at level(); and on the help's own stated scoping the wald display is the one case where the two are supposed to agree endpoint for endpoint up to the band's larger critical value. zc is taken from wdbdf at ado:9576, while wooldid_esband (ado:10879) passes only level() to wooldid_bootband, whose critical value is wooldid_bootqs(M, lev/100) (ado:16866) -- no df correction and no shared replication mask. (sthlp:554 does say bootdf() leaves quantile-based objects unaffected, so the band's insensitivity to bootdf() may be intended; the divergence is the under-scoped caveat at sthlp:525 plus the fact that the resulting band is not simultaneous at level().)
refuter_note: The claim fires but its stated SCOPE is wrong. It is not 'at modest cluster counts': the driver is the NUMBER OF HORIZONS in the family, because q_lev(max_h |t|) inflates with m while invt(G-1,.975) does not. At G=8 the same design violates at m=2 and does not at m=4. Across my eight cells the band critical value ranged 2.138-2.696 against invt(G-1) 2.201-2.365 -- the two sit within about ten percent of each other and the ordering is not systematic, so this is close to a coin flip rather than a direction. Second, 'the band's critical value carries no degrees-of-freedom correction' is DOCUMENTED at sthlp:554, as the finding itself concedes in its last sentence. Third, their independent second mechanism (listwise band sd vs per-column table se producing violations even when bandcrit is the larger) did NOT reproduce: in every cell where bandcrit exceeded the pointwise critical value, no horizon violated. Fourth, 'the resulting band is not simultaneous at level()' is unmeasured on both sides. Medium -> low; it is BT-01's doc-scoping defect seen in a corner.

But cell B (G=10,m=4) 2.42613 vs 2.26216, r08 BCELL9 (G=8,m=4) 2.42834 vs 2.36462, BCELL10 (G=12,m=2) 2.31140 vs 2.20099, r03 S3 (G=10,m=4) 2.63837 vs 2.26216 and S5 (bootdf(normal)) 2.69181 vs 1.95996 do NOT.

title: customweightmultiplier() silently turns att_it / att_i / att_itime from the documented simple means into weighted means
surface: customweightmultiplier() x {att_it, att_i, att_itime}; ado:1619-1620 vs 1631/1637/1650; sthlp att_it/att_i paragraphs vs sthlp:1107
claim: With customweightmultiplier(v) the cell and cohort weight masses stop being 1: the numerator carries the multiplier (w*v, ado:1631/1637/1650) while the normaliser does not (W_it / W_ipost = total(esamp*w), ado:1619-1620). So att_it is no longer "the simple, unweighted mean of all of the cohort-period-specific estimates" and att_i is no longer "the simple, unweighted mean of the cohort-specific treatment effects"; each cell/cohort enters weighted by its own mean of v. Nothing at runtime says so, and the cwm help paragraph (sthlp:1107) describes only the numerator, so the two help paragraphs disagree.
observed: repro_cwm.log, with a multiplier CONSTANT WITHIN each cohort-by-year cell (so within-cell variation cannot be blamed): (A) no multiplier -> per-cell w_att_it min=max=1, per-cohort w_att_i min=max=1. (B) with customweightmultiplier(pop) -> per-cell w_att_it runs 1.43606887 to 4.9238679 (ratio 3.43), per-cohort w_att_i runs 2.62936131 to 4.75544236. No caution is printed. p04_options.log arm F16 gives the same picture independently (cells 1.2420-3.2259, cohorts 1.5440-2.4191).
expected: The att_it and att_i help paragraphs state a SIMPLE, UNWEIGHTED mean without any "unless customweightmultiplier()" qualifier, and the cwm paragraph says only that the estimand's usual weights are multiplied by the variable. Under those two sentences every number above should be exactly 1, as it is in arm (A). Honest caveat: cross-cell reweighting is the only thing a multiplier CAN do to att_it (the cell derivative is constant within the cell), so this is plausibly the designed 'bespoke treatment effect' and the defect is a missing qualifier rather than a wrong computation. In the code's favour, e(gteffects) is the ONLY surface on which a user can see this at all - the weighted-mean identity still holds exactly, and the weight columns expose the distortion.
refuter_note: The stated mechanism is right but the framing is wrong in a way that matters for the fix. The code matches the customweightmultiplier() paragraph (sthlp:1107) LITERALLY -- 'the weights normally used to produce the requested type of treatment effect (ATT, ATT_i, etc.) will be multiplied by this variable' is exactly w*v/W_it. There is no disagreement between the code and that paragraph. The real gap is an asymmetry INSIDE the help: the att paragraph (sthlp:217) carries the qualifier 'multiplied by the customweightmultiplier() variable if one is specified', while the att_it / att_i / att_itime paragraphs (sthlp:221/227/234) say 'simple, unweighted mean' with no such qualifier. The remedy is one clause added to three paragraphs, not a computation change. The prober's own honest caveat already reaches this conclusion; the finding should be restated as 'three help paragraphs are missing the qualifier the fourth one has'.
refuter_did: Block A of r01_low4.do on my own 90-unit 3-cohort panel with a multiplier held CONSTANT within each (i,t) cell (pop = 1 + 0.5*coh + 0.2*(t-1999), i = coh). Without the multiplier the per-cell w_att_it mass is min=max=1.00000000 and the per-cohort w_att_i mass is 0.16666667-0.33333333 (exactly 1/6 and 1/3, one unit of mass per cohort). With customweightmultiplier(pop) the per-cell mass runs 2.50000000-4.00000000 and the per-cohort mass 0.41666667-1.33333333. I then pinned the mechanism numerically: max over post-treatment rows of |cell mass of w_att_it - the cell's own value of pop| = 2.2204e-15, i.e. the cell mass is exactly the cell's multiplier value, precisely as w*v/W_it with W_it = total(esamp*w) predicts. So the arithmetic in the claim is right.

With 8 completed replications the 95th percentile IS the maximum of 8 numbers, so the band is structurally too narrow — a confidence band that is not at level(). e(esband_n_att) records the draw count but no caution is keyed on it; only the generic 2/reps p-value-grid caution mentions reps at all.
observed: 40 states x 20 periods, esprelength(6) espostlength(6), simultaneousbands: analytic simulated critical value 2.6504 (e(esband_engine) = analytic-simulated); bootstrap reps(8) 2.0712 with e(esband_n_att) = 8 (22% narrower); reps(12) 2.4471. On the other design (11 pre coefficients, p09_calib.log) analytic 2.6920 vs reps(60) 2.7353 — by reps(60) the band is fine. The reps(2000) reference arm of p03_conseq.do was killed for slot budget, so the large-reps limit on the first design was not obtained.
expected: A band asked for at level(95) should have approximately 95% simultaneous coverage; a quantile taken at the maximum of 8 draws cannot. Either a floor on the draw count for the band, or a caution keyed on e(esband_n_*), or a finite-sample-adjusted quantile.
refuter_note: The arithmetic is right - at level 95 wooldid_bootqs returns the MAXIMUM for every n <= 19 - but 'therefore the band is structurally too narrow' needs two corrections. (a) Being the maximum is not itself the defect: the expected coverage of the r-th of n order statistics is r/(n+1), so n = 19 (max of 19) gives EXACTLY .95, while n = 8 gives .889 and n = 20 (mean of the 19th and 20th) gives .929. The rule is slightly low at every n: .939 at 40, .946 at 100, .949 at 400 - at most 1.1 coverage points at any reps a user runs. (b) On my data the reps(8) critical value came out LARGER than the reps(40) one (2.4543 vs 2.3535, against 2.6211 at reps 100, 2.6646 at reps 400 and 2.6038 analytic-simulated), so the narrowing is an expectation, not something visible in a run. Their claim that 'no caution is keyed on the draw count; only the generic 2/reps caution mentions reps at all' is half true - that generic caution DID fire at reps(8) and reps(20) on my runs and not at 40+. Severity low, as filed.
refuter_did: Read the quantile kernel wooldid_bootqs, computed the expected coverage of the order statistic it returns (E[F(X_(r))] = r/(n+1)), and measured e(esband_crit_att) and e(esband_n_att) on my own 40-state panel with simultaneousbands at analytic and at reps 8/20/40/100/400.

title: replay drops the cautions that disown the numbers it reprints, including the runtime half of two shipped rulings (PS-64/BS-9 and AMESE R1)
surface: replay (bare `wooldid`) / wooldid_display vs wooldid_worker and the wooldid shell
claim: A bare `wooldid` replay reprints the tables byte-for-byte but never prints the estimation-time cautions that describe the REPORTED RESULTS rather than the estimation run — so a replayed table shows a joint-test p-value the live run explicitly disowned as uncalibrated, permutation/bootstrap p-values the live run said were at their resolution floor, and blank ame cells the live run explained as structurally unidentified. sthlp:1458's justification for dropping them ('which describe the estimation run, not the results') is factually false for at least seven cautions, and wooldid_display already replays other results-describing cautions, so this is an omission rather than a policy.
observed: r01 (`att att_it att_i att_itime cluster(i) espre(3) espost(3) jointtests adversarial`): live 92 lines, replay 72; the 20 missing lines are exactly the caution block, and everything from the header down is byte-identical. Lost cautions measured: (1) 'jointtests was combined with analytic clustered SEs clustered at the level of the cohort variable i or above ... its p-value should not be read as a calibrated test' (r01); (2) 'with permreps(25) the smallest attainable per-coefficient permutation p-value is 0.077 ... a p-value printed at that floor is the resolution limit rather than evidence' (r08); (3) 'with reps(25) the coefficient p-values fall on a grid of 0.080 ... the only value below .05 this run can produce is exactly 0 - which records that no completed replication reached the far side of the null' (r10, h01); (4) contreat() with a cohort-constant dose: 'the within-cell average marginal effects (ame) ... are NOT IDENTIFIED in this design - the regression's ame entries are structural zeros, not estimates - so wooldid is reporting the ame results as missing' plus 'standard errors were not identified for 6 of 12 reported estimates' — on replay the blanks appear with no explanation at all (p7 r03); (5) the permute() cluster()==i exchangeability caution (r08); (6) 'the adversarial pre-trend p-value requires esfixedbaseperiod ...; the fitted line is reported without a p-value' (r01); (7) 'histogram outputs are drawn from the ANALYTIC covariance ...; the reported tables ... are bootstrap-based / permutation-based' (h01, h02). Caution sites by program: 21 in wooldid_worker, 15 in wooldid_validate, 5 in the wooldid shell (ado:299, 511), only 8 in wooldid_display.
expected: sthlp:1458-1459 promises the results are redisplayed 'byte-for-byte as originally shown' and justifies dropping cautions on the ground that they 'describe the estimation run, not the results'. Items 1-4 describe the results: they tell the reader that a specific number or blank in the replayed table must not be read at face value. Items 1 and 4 are the runtime halves of shipped rulings — known_bydesign §1 records PS-64/BS-9 as 'Computed anyway with a NAMED CAUTION' and AMESE R1 (7054878) as 'scrubbed to missing with a NAMED CAUTION' — so on the documented redisplay path those rulings are not in force. That the project intends results-describing cautions to be replayed is visible in wooldid_display itself, which reconstructs the subgroup withheld-pre-row caution from e(wdid_sgnopre)/wdid_sgnoprewhy/wdid_sgnoprerow (ado:4431-4437) and the Roth rank-deficiency and interrupted-pass cautions from e(roth_*) (ado:11447-11477).
refuter_note: The behaviour is confirmed but the framing is wrong in two ways. (1) What makes the drop a POLICY rather than an omission is simply that sthlp:1458 documents it explicitly ('does not repeat estimation-time Caution messages'); the prober's argument that it must be an omission does not survive that sentence. (2) The sgnopre / roth precedent the prober cites does not transfer: wooldid_display can rebuild those cautions because e(wdid_sgnopre*) and e(roth_*) carry the state, and no analogous state exists for the jointtests or ame cautions -- so the remedy is new e() postings, a substantially larger change than the 'wooldid_display already does this elsewhere' argument implies. What genuinely survives is narrower: sthlp:1458's JUSTIFICATION ('which describe the estimation run, not the results') is factually inaccurate for at least five cautions I measured, and the replayed contreat table shows blank ame cells with no reason given. Severity medium -> low: the behaviour is documented, no number changes, and the harm is bounded to a reader of a replayed log.
refuter_did: Wrote my own live/replay pair harness (`qui log using` around the live call and around the bare `wooldid`, so the two text files are a literal byte comparison) on my own data, for four specifications. Confirmed the behaviour independently: RJ (att, cluster(uid), jointtests, espre/espost 3) loses exactly the 6-line 'its p-value should not be read as a calibrated test' caution, with all 33 remaining lines byte-identical; RP (permute(shuffle) permreps(25) cluster(uid)) loses the 12-line permreps resolution-floor caution plus the permute exchangeability caution; RC (contreat(dose) with a cohort-constant dose, cluster(uid)) loses 24 lines including 'the within-cell average marginal effects (ame) ... are NOT IDENTIFIED in this design' and 'standard errors were not identified for 1 of 2 reported estimates' -- and the replayed table then prints `ame | . . . . . . .` with no explanation at all. So the core claim is TRUE. I then ran the discriminator the claim rests on and it fails: I dumped the full e() surface of the contreat run (`: e(macros)` / `: e(scalars)`, s7_more.log) and there is NO macro or scalar recording the ame-not-identified condition, and none recording the jointtests-uncalibrated condition. The e(wdid_*) macros present are wdid_replayv, wdid_esrel, wdid_espre, wdid_suppressjt, wdid_cetype, wdid_fcol, wdid_semielas, wdid_estimands, wdid_contreat, wdid_vcespec, wdid_vcvstate and the scalar wdid_fcncell.

title: pweights produce a robust covariance but the run is labelled OLS: e(vce)="ols" and e(vcetype) unposted, contradicting wooldid's own stated contract at ado:4283
surface: pweight + e(vce)/e(vcetype)/header (ado:4283-4301)
claim: With [pw=w] and no vce option, wooldid's e(V) is bitwise the robust covariance, but ado:4301's fallthrough `else ereturn local vce = cond("`poisson'" == "poisson", "oim", "ols")` never looks at the weight type, so e(vce) is posted as "ols" and e(vcetype) is not posted at all. The comment two lines above, at ado:4283, states the contract being broken: "e(vce) and e(vcetype) name what e(V) IS". This is wooldid's own doing, not inherited: reghdfe on the identical pweighted fit posts e(vce)="robust", e(vcetype)="Robust".
observed: [pw=svywt]: se 0.0919359312, e(vce)=[ols], e(vcetype)=[.], header "Standard Errors: " (blank). [aw=svywt] robust: se 0.0919359312, e(vce)=[robust], e(vcetype)=[Robust]. [aw=svywt] iid: se 0.0817970344, e(vce)=[ols], e(vcetype)=[.]. se(pw)==se(aw,robust) exactly, |diff| 0.0000e+00; se(pw)!=se(aw,iid), |diff| 1.0139e-02. Whole-matrix check in probe7: e(V) under [pw=k] vs [aw=k] robust differ by 0.000e+00; vs [aw=k] iid by 1.862e-01 relative. reghdfe y post [pw=svywt], absorb(i t) -> e(vce)=[robust], e(vcetype)=[Robust].
expected: e(vce)="robust" and e(vcetype)="Robust", because that is what e(V) is (bitwise), because sthlp:268 states pweights imply robust standard errors, and because ado:4283 declares that those two macros name what e(V) is. estout/esttab and outreg2 read e(vcetype) to decide whether to print "Robust standard errors" beneath a table, so a pweighted wooldid result is published labelled OLS. This is distinct from the ruled PS-33 cosmetic (an absent label on the genuine iid default); here a machine-readable macro makes a false positive claim about a non-iid covariance.
refuter_note: The claim is true and I reproduced it bitwise; what is wrong is the stated consequence, which is the whole basis for calling it medium. The finding says 'estout/esttab read e(vcetype) to decide whether to print "Robust standard errors" beneath a table, so a pweighted wooldid result is published labelled OLS'. Measured in p7_esttab.do with SINGLE-model tables (so a mixed-vcetype table cannot confound it): esttab on a cluster(state) model with e(vcetype)=="Robust" prints 'Standard errors in parentheses'; so does the robust model; so does the iid model. esttab's default footer does not read e(vcetype) at all. What does surface it is an explicit request -- `estout rrob, stats(vcetype N)' prints a 'vcetype Robust' row. So the false machine-readable label is real and does contradict ado:4283's own stated contract, and a user who asks for the vce row, reads `ereturn list', or writes code keying on it gets 'ols' for a covariance that is bitwise robust; but the automatic 'published labelled OLS' harm does not happen. Low, not medium.
refuter_did: Rebuilt on my own 30-state x 12-year x 8-county panel. [pw=pop] with no vce option: se 0.10884885, e(vce)=[ols], e(vcetype)=[.], header 'Standard Errors: ' blank. Whole-matrix check: mreldif(e(V) under [pw=pop], e(V) under [aw=pop] robust) = EXACTLY 0 (+0.0X-3ff); vs [aw=pop] iid = 4.5e-03 (the pw se is 1.2738x the iid se). reghdfe y post [pw=pop], absorb(i t) -> e(vce)=[robust]/e(vcetype)=[Robust]; regress ... [pw=pop] -> the same. So it is wooldid's own posting, as claimed, and the mechanism at ado:1448 (vcespecifier is left EMPTY under a bare pweight, so reghdfe makes its own robust V) plus ado:4291-4301 (the label ladder never inspects the weight type) is exactly right. Distinctness from PS-33/PS-1 verified in the repo record: rulings_2026-09-07.md:68 rules only 'the iid default and the unlabelled header stand', and the project's own PS-1 audit note says e(vce)=="ols" is posted for estout-class consumers on a BARE UNCLUSTERED run -- neither covers a run whose e(V) is not iid. grep confirms wooldid never reads e(vce)/e(vcetype) itself. Then I tested the stated downstream harm twice: once in p4 (confounded, mixed-vcetype table) and again properly in p7_esttab.do with single-model tables.

title: The fweight refusal prescribes aweights or pweights, neither of which reproduces fweight inference on collapsed data, and neither the message nor the help says so
surface: fweight refusal message (ado:628-632) + help coverage of weight types (sthlp:57)
claim: [fw=n] is refused at ado:628-632 with "Specify aweights or pweights." On the canonical case that motivates frequency weights - individual microdata collapsed to cells with a headcount - the substitute reproduces the point estimate exactly but not the inference: the standard error is wrong in both directions depending on the vce, e(N) reports the cell count rather than the analysis sample, and nothing in the output or the help (sthlp:57 documents only [aw/pw=weights] and never mentions frequency weights or count data) warns the user.
observed: 30 states x 12 years x ~25 people = 8941 microdata rows collapsed to 360 (state,year) cells with mean outcome and headcount n. microdata cluster(state): b .38464638 se 0.02936881 N 8941. [fw=n] on cells: r(198). [aw=n] on cells cluster(state): b .38464638 se 0.03673877 N 360, se ratio 1.2509. [pw=n]: identical, ratio 1.2509. Under the default iid vce: microdata se 0.04260507, [aw=n] se 0.03885874 (ratio 0.9121), [pw=n] se 0.04068764 (ratio 0.9550). Point-estimate reldiff aw vs microdata: 0.0000e+00.
expected: Either the fweight is accepted, or the refusal names a remedy that reproduces it, or the message states what changes. The standard error is 25% too large clustered and 9% too small iid, and e(N)=360 where the analysis sample is 8941. The point estimate being exact is the metamorphic identity this whole probe verified (expand n on the cells frame reproduces the microdata answer exactly), which is precisely why the SE gap is invisible: everything a user would sanity-check agrees.
refuter_note: The core fact survives -- the substitute reproduces the point estimate exactly and not the clustered SE, and neither the message nor the help (sthlp:57 documents only [aw/pw=weights]) says so. Three corrections. (1) THE IID LEG IS ATTRIBUTED TO THE WRONG THING. The finding presents 'se 9% too small iid' as a failure of the aw/pw substitute, implying fweights would have fixed it. They would not: [fw=n] on cell means is 0.1927 of the microdata iid SE -- a factor of 5 too small, because fw treats each cell mean as n identical observations and destroys the within-cell SSR -- while [aw=n] is 1.0064, nearly exact. Under iid the prescribed remedy is the RIGHT one and fweights are the disastrous one. Whatever the finding measured under iid is a cells-vs-microdata artefact of its DGP, not an aw-vs-fw gap. (2) THE CLUSTERED GAP IS ENTIRELY STATA'S SMALL-SAMPLE MULTIPLIER, not a difference in the estimated variance: meat and bread coincide (x is cell-constant, so the per-cluster score sums agree), and the observed 1.060009592 equals sqrt([(360-1)/(360-42)] / [(8717-1)/(8717-42)]) = 1.060009... to 7 digits, i.e. pure (N-1)/(N-k) with k=42. This is generic Stata aweight behaviour in every command, not anything wooldid does. wooldid's larger 1.2589 is the same phenomenon with reghdfe's much larger K at N=360 (an implied K=137 reproduces 1.25887 to 5 digits; I solved for K, so treat that as a consistency check, not a proof). (3) e(N)=360 IS NOT A DEFECT -- every Stata command reports the observation count under aweights. What is left is a message/help gap: the refusal names a substitute without saying inference changes, and the help never mentions frequency weights. Low.
refuter_did: Built my own collapsed-admin case: 30 states x 12 years x 15-34 people = 8717 microdata rows collapsed to 360 (state,year) cells with a mean outcome and a headcount n. Then ran the leg the finding never ran -- WOULD [fw=n] have reproduced the microdata answer? Plain-regress oracle, SE relative to the microdata SE: [fw=n] cells cluster(state) 1.000000000; [aw=n] cells cluster(state) 1.060009592; [fw=n] cells iid 0.192690664; [aw=n] cells iid 1.006426015; b agrees to ~2e-14 on every leg. wooldid legs: [fw=n] -> r(198) 'Error: wooldid does not accept fweights. Specify aweights or pweights.'; [aw=n]==[pw=n] bitwise; att b matches the microdata wooldid run to ~1e-14; att se ratio cells/micro under cluster(state) = 1.258867.

title: An outcome missing on every never-treated row is refused as a DESIGN failure, and the remedy the message names substitutes a different sample with no caution
surface: safety() / the r(459) estimability screen / missing-value handling
claim: When the outcome (or i, t, or the weight) is missing on every never-treated row, wooldid exits r(459) saying "you have no never-treated control group and no not-yet-treated control group whose treatment falls outside the sample window / To ignore this error, specify safety(off) or modify the sample window manually". The refusal is correct but the diagnosis is not: nothing in the message mentions missing data, the sample window is fine, and safety(off) - the first remedy it names - then proceeds silently on a different sample and estimand (half the rows, 9 of 12 clusters, identified off not-yet-treated comparisons only) and reports it with no caution about the absent control group.
observed: 60-unit x 12-year staggered panel, 15 never-treated units (180 rows), outcome set missing on exactly those rows, nothing else changed. LEG1 (outcome intact): rc 0, e(N)=720, att=.251427121182, se=.100824299164. LEG2: r(459) with the message above, preceded only by "Caution: estimability checks found time periods exist in sample without a control unit, causing them to be dropped". LEG3 (safety(off)): rc 0, N clusters = 9, e(N)=360, e(N_dropped)=360, att=.182200591071, se=.0610866413393, p=.0175291582039, and NO caution of any kind. LEG4 (drop the outcome-missing rows by hand): r(459), the honest answer. On the richer DGP used by p09_misc.do / p15b_safetyoff.do (same shape plus a dynamic effect) the same three legs give att=.795871565626 intact vs att=.415533924404 under safety(off) - a 48% move, reported at p=.000137. Partial missingness is handled well: 30% of control rows missing -> rc 0, e(N)=667, e(N_dropped)=53; one whole calendar year missing -> rc 0, e(N)=660, e(N_dropped)=60.
expected: The message should name the cause the user can act on. wooldid already has the number: the markout at ado:683 (`qui replace ifvar = 0 if i >= . | t >= . | y >= . | w >= . | w <= 0') zeroes every control row long BEFORE the control-group screen at ado:952 (`qui count if ttre == . & ifstatement' -> 0 -> error 459) ever looks, so by then wooldid has removed the controls itself. The help states that missing-value drops surface "in the header's dropped-observation count" (sthlp:898, 927, 1411) - but that count is only printed at ~ado:1497, after the regression, so on this failure path the documented disclosure never happens. As written, both remedies the message offers are wrong for this data, and the one it names first produces an estimate for a sample the user did not ask for.
refuter_note: Only the message-wording half survives: the r(459) text does not mention that rows were removed for missing y/i/t/weight before the control-group check. That is a low-severity UX nit. The load-bearing half of the finding is false. (a) safety(off) is not silent - it prints the dropped count for half the dataset in its header, and suppressing CAUTIONS is the explicit documented contract of the option the user typed (sthlp:1159: 'Specifying safety(off) removes them ... suppressed along with everything else'). (b) safety(off) does not substitute an estimate of its own invention - it is bit-identical to hand-deleting the missing-outcome rows, and equals the 'truncate the window' remedy. (c) 'both remedies the message offers are wrong for this data' is false: the second remedy works and restores a real never-treated control group. The r(459) itself is by-design per the brief. Severity medium -> low.
refuter_did: Rebuilt the claim on my own 40-state x 12-year panel (cohorts 2009/2011/2013, 10 never-treated), eight legs, never running the prober's script. LEG A2 (y missing on every never-treated row) reproduces r(459) with the quoted message - but LEG A4, which DELETES those rows outright, produces the IDENTICAL r(459) and the IDENTICAL message, so the message is not a mis-diagnosis: it is the same accurate statement a genuinely control-less design gets, and it is preceded by 'Caution: estimability checks found time periods exist in sample without a control unit, causing them to be dropped.' LEG A3 (safety(off)) is NOT silent: its header reads 'N clusters = 30; N = 240 (240 obs dropped from initial sample)' on a 480-row dataset, which is exactly the dropped-observation disclosure the help promises at sthlp:898/927/1411. In rB_verbose_and_remedy.do I compared e(wdidmainresults) from safety(off)-on-missing-y against safety(off)-on-the-hand-cleaned-dataset: max|diff| = exactly 0, BIT-IDENTICAL - safety(off) returns precisely the honest answer, not a wrong number. I also ran the message's SECOND remedy, which the prober called wrong: 'wooldid y st yr onset if yr <= 2012' returns rc 0, N=240, N_dropped=80, att=.21855514, the 2013 cohort supplying the control group, and a hand-restricted dataset gives the identical table. All four routes land on the same number and the same e(N)=240, because the control-less-period screen at ado:830-836 is not gated on safety() (only the caution at ado:838 is), so safety(off) lands on exactly the window the second remedy names. Legs A7 (zero weight on never-treated) and A8 (missing i on never-treated) give the same r(459), so this is the general markout-then-screen ordering, not an outcome-specific bug; leg A6 (30% of control rows missing) runs cleanly at N=436, N_dropped=44. Finally, 'the documented disclosure never happens on this path' is trivially true of any failed run - a command that errors prints no results header.

title: `verbose` adds a variable to the user's dataset and leaves it there
surface: verbose
claim: A `verbose` run leaves `_est____wooldidfullmodel` (byte, variable label "esample() from estimates store") in the user's data: c(k) goes 12 -> 13 and the datasignature changes. A plain run leaves nothing, because ado:4539 (`if "`verbose''" != "verbose" ... qui est drop `wdfm''`) drops the stored estimate and the marker variable with it. The help documents the retained ESTIMATE (sthlp:1132) but never the variable, so a user who saves, exports, or loops `foreach v of varlist _all` after a verbose run ships a column they did not create.
observed: repro_verbose_leaves_variable.log: PLAIN_LEFT_A_VARIABLE=0, VERBOSE_LEFT_A_VARIABLE=1. From the full session snapshot (p16_snapdiff.do arm s3, `diff snap_s3_pre.txt snap_s3_post.txt'): [C] k 12 -> 13; [D] nvars 12 -> 13; + [VAR] _est____wooldidfullmodel | byte | %8.0g | vl= | lbl=esample() from estimates store; [D] datasignature 720:12(95947):1438951675:2824387038 -> 720:13(90315):3721695459:2080210338. `frames dir` correspondingly reports `default 720 x 13`. The plain arm s1 shows no variable added.
expected: A command should not change the shape of the caller's dataset without saying so. Either drop the marker variable when the run ends (keeping the estimate is what `estimates store` is for, and the variable can be re-created), or document it in the verbose entry alongside the retained ___wooldidfullmodel, as sthlp:712 already does for _ppmlhdfe_d under poisson. The grep `_est_` returns zero hits in wooldid.sthlp.
refuter_note: True as an observation, wrong as a 'leak'. The variable is the unavoidable storage Stata's estimates system requires for the estimate that verbose deliberately retains and that sthlp:1132 documents; it is removed by the documented cleanup ('est drop'), removed by the next plain run, and does not grow across repeated verbose runs. The proposed remedy is destructive: it silently empties e(sample) of the retained model while leaving 'est restore' returning rc 0. The residue is a one-clause documentation nit in the verbose entry, mirroring sthlp:712's treatment of _ppmlhdfe_d, not a state leak.
refuter_did: Confirmed the observation on my own data: plain run c(k) 8 -> 8 with no _est_ variable and an empty estimates dir; verbose run c(k) 8 -> 9 with _est____wooldidfullmodel present and estimates dir = ___wooldidfullmodel. Then I attacked the framing. (1) I TESTED THE PROBER'S PROPOSED REMEDY: after a verbose run whose marker marks 480 rows, 'drop _est____wooldidfullmodel' then 'est restore ___wooldidfullmodel' returns rc 0 and 'estimates describe' returns rc 0, but 'count if e(sample)' returns N = 0 (was 480). Dropping the marker silently empties e(sample) of the very model sthlp:1132 tells users to restore, so 'the variable can be re-created' is false - the marker is Stata's own estimates-system storage, not something wooldid invented. (2) It self-heals through the documented object: 'est drop ___wooldidfullmodel' removes the variable too (c(k) back to 8), and a subsequent PLAIN wooldid run removes it via ado:4539 (c(k) back to 8). (3) It does not accumulate: three back-to-back verbose runs leave c(k) = 9, 9, 9. (4) I verified the prober's cited precedent: sthlp:712 does document the analogous _ppmlhdfe_d retention under verbose, so the one-clause help addition they ask for is a fair, and the only, actionable item.

title: At cluster()==i the bayes percentile interval for att missed 7 of 30 at nominal 95% where bootstrap(standard) missed 2 on the same panels at equal width; and bayes att_i's reported SE is only 0.62 of the true sampling sd
surface: bootstrap(bayes) interval coverage at cluster() == i (percentile and wald families)
claim: In a 30-panel Monte Carlo at cluster() == i with a known homogeneous true effect, (a) every reported standard error - analytic, bootstrap(standard) and bootstrap(bayes) - lies below the true sampling standard deviation of the estimate, and bootstrap(bayes) for the cell-weighted att_i is the WORST of the five at 0.621, worse than the analytic SE a user would be turning to the bootstrap to escape; and (b) on the same 30 panels bootstrap(bayes)'s percentile interval for att covered 23/30 at nominal 95% where bootstrap(standard) covered 28/30, with mean percentile widths within 2% of each other and identical point estimates, all five discordances in the same direction.
observed: 30 simulated 30-cluster panels, 10 periods, true att = 1, homogeneous effects, cluster(st) with i = st, reps(79), nominal 95%. arm/est/n/covered(percentile)/covered(wald)/mean se/true sd/ratio: analytic att 30 / - / 26 / .12554 / .17784 / .706 ; analytic att_i 30 / - / 25 / .14698 / .17942 / .819 ; bayes att 30 / 23 / 28 / .14392 / .17784 / .809 ; bayes att_i 30 / 24 / 24 / .11138 / .17942 / .621 ; standard att 30 / 28 / 29 / .15078 / .17784 / .848. Mean percentile widths: bayes 0.60283, standard 0.61461 (ratio 0.981). Paired discordances (p21_covdetail.do): standard covers and bayes misses on 5 panels, bayes covers and standard misses on 0. The bayes interval is shifted, not narrower - on draw 11, b = 1.2474, bayes gives [1.0038, 1.5676] and standard [0.9259, 1.4658]. bayes's misses are asymmetric: 5 low-side, 2 high-side.
expected: A nominal 95% interval should cover about 28-29 of 30. Part (a) is certain and is F1 expressed as coverage - it also extends the project's documented analytic-SE understatement at cluster() at-or-above i (recon note section 1) to the bootstrap families in that configuration, which is new. Part (b) is marked uncertain: 30 panels give a +/-13pp band on a coverage proportion, and I did not diagnose why the two percentile intervals sit at different locations when both replication distributions are centred within 0.16 bootstrap-sd of the estimate. It is reported because it sits in the recon note's section 7 hunting ground ('any arm that FAILS coverage', 'the effect at a different cluster count'), because it is the OPPOSITE direction from the open, unruled bootstrap(standard) over-coverage result recorded there (att_i 149/150 = .9933), and because 5/5 same-direction discordances on paired data is a sign-test p of 0.031.
refuter_note: Part (a) reproduces for att (all three se/true-sd ratios below 1, bayes lowest) but is not new: the analytic leg is recon sec 1, and the BOOTSTRAP legs are printed in the help - sthlp:532 reports a 24-cluster staggered simulation with 'standard error 0.967 of the truth' under bootstrap(standard) and '0.877' under bootstrap(bayes), a documented ratio of 0.907 against my 0.935. I did not independently re-measure their att_i figure of 0.621; that is bb-01's collapse expressed as a coverage number, and by my r02 design B it is a nesting-regime number, since with cluster() finer than i the bayes/standard ratio on the cell-weighted estimand is 0.965. Part (b): the DIRECTION reproduces but the magnitude does not. Their 16.7pp gap (23/30 vs 28/30) and 5/5 one-directional discordance become a 3.3pp gap and a 3-1 discordance (sign test p = .31) on 60 paired panels, where a 16.7pp gap would have been unmissable. And their stated mechanism is wrong: 'the bayes interval is shifted, not narrower' does not hold on my panels - the width ratio is 0.931 in the MC and 0.96/0.87 at reps(999), with both distributions centred. Part of their gap is the reps(79) choice, where the 2.5% endpoint is essentially the second order statistic and the Dirichlet's lighter weight tails bite hardest. Their 'opposite direction from sec 7' argument also fails: sec 7's over-coverage result is bootstrap(standard) on att_i, while bb-03(b) is att.
refuter_did: Two attacks. (i) Mechanism first, no Monte Carlo needed: r04_tailshape.do runs both engines at reps(999) and reps(79) on three panels of their stated design and dumps e(bootdist). At 999 reps BOTH replication distributions are centred on the estimate and near-symmetric (P1: standard (repmean-b)/sd -0.0023 skew -0.042; bayes +0.0029 skew +0.015) and the bayes percentile interval is simply NARROWER (width 0.7547 vs 0.7862, ratio 0.960; P2 0.5518 vs 0.6328, ratio 0.872). The same panel at reps(79) shows bayes skew +0.486 and (repmean-b)/sd -0.188 - reps(79) noise, not an engine property. (ii) My own paired coverage MC (r06_a/b/c.do, 60 panels, 30 clusters, 10 periods, true att=1, homogeneous, cluster(st) with i=st, reps(79), same panel and same rseed for both engines, aggregated by agg.py): standard percentile 56/60 = .933, bayes 54/60 = .900; mean widths 0.64209 vs 0.59762; mean se/true sd standard .907, bayes .848, analytic .850; discordance standard-covers-bayes-misses 3, the reverse 1.

title: The onset-commensurability bypass silently relabels the onset year as pre-treatment and manufactures a 14-sigma pre-trend
surface: safety(off) / onset-commensurability screen (ado:5340-5366)
claim: Under safety(off), a fractional onset (a mid-year effective date on an annual panel) does not merely proceed: wooldid silently adopts the round-up convention, folding the true onset year into the pre-treatment window, and the run reports a large, highly significant pre-treatment att on a DGP whose pre-trend is exactly zero. Nothing is printed. This is the failure mode sthlp:73 names as the PRE-fix behaviour ("silently mislabeled the onset period as pre-treatment"), restored by the documented bypass without any statement of the convention adopted.
observed: 60-unit clean panel, esprelength(2) espostlength(2). With the correct integer ttre: att = 1.1373096, pre-period att = -0.00211341 (t = -0.04, p = 0.965). With ttre+0.5 under safety(off): att = 1.096691, pre-period att = 0.68206619 (t = 14.39, p = 0.000) - bit-for-bit the answer of the honest ttre+1 recode (att 1.096691, pre-att 0.68206619). Default safety refuses with r(459) "t minus ttre takes non-integer values...". Note that refusal message never mentions safety(off) as an escape; only the help does (sthlp:73, sthlp:1207).
expected: Either the refusal (the default) or, at minimum, a line stating which rounding convention was adopted. The issue is not which convention is correct - both are defensible for a mid-year effective date - but that one is chosen silently and the chosen one produces a spurious pre-trend that a researcher would read as a failure of parallel trends. The user most likely to hit it is one who set safety(off) for the runtime reason sthlp:1167 actively recommends ("saves roughly two to four percent of runtime ... worth having once a specification is settled") and later merged in a fractional onset. Reachability caveat: I tested esprelength(2); with the default esprelength(0) the shifted _t stays fractional and the run is expected to die r(452) instead - untested.
refuter_note: Both load-bearing words in the claim are wrong. (1) NOT SILENT: the event-study rows are LABELLED with the fractional horizons. My ttre+0.5 run under safety(off) prints rows 'pre1.5 / pre.5 / post.5'; e(b_es_att)'s column names are ES_att_pre1.5, ES_att_pre.5, ES_att_post.5; and the relyr entries in e(wdidmainresults) are -1.5, -0.5, +0.5. A half-integer relative-time grid on an annual panel is announced in three places. (2) NO ROUND-UP CONVENTION IS ADOPTED: there is no rounding anywhere. _t = t - ttre exactly (ado:12081), and the ttre+0.7 arm proves it -- its rows come out 'pre1.7 / pre.7 / post.3' (colnames ES_att_pre1.700000047683716 etc.), not pre2/pre1/post0. The bit-for-bit coincidence with an honest ttre+1 recode is a pure RELABELLING IDENTITY that holds for any offset in (0,1): adding a constant to ttre shifts every row's horizon by the same constant, so the window cut (_t < -esprelength) and the pre/post split (t >= ttre) partition exactly the same rows. No convention was chosen, silently or otherwise. (3) The classification of the onset calendar year as pre-treatment is exactly 't >= ttre', which is what the help says the treatment indicator means, and sthlp:73 documents this precise failure mode and names safety(off) as the bypass, while sthlp:1207 lists it under 'refuses, and safety(off) proceeds'. What survives is only the residual UX point: the pretreatment att row does pick up the onset-period effect (0.739 against -0.157 on the correct onset, on a zero-pre-trend DGP) and nothing flags that as a hazard. That is a caution-wording suggestion behind a documented bypass, hence low.
refuter_did: Own 60-unit, 8-year panel with a DGP whose effect switches on at the integer onset and whose pre-trend is exactly zero. Seven legs: integer ttre under default safety (att 1.4085652, pretreatment att -0.1570145, ES rows pre2/pre1/post0/post1); ttre+0.5 under default safety (r(459) as documented); ttre+0.5 under safety(off) (att 1.4943905, pretreatment att 0.7393189, ES rows pre1.5/pre.5/post.5); the honest ttre+1 recode under default safety (bit-identical hex +1.7e90609ae3a27X+000 on att and +1.7a88027ebfe5eX-001 on the pretreatment att, ES rows pre2/pre1/post0); ttre+0.7 under safety(off) -- THE DISCRIMINATING LEG, which returns the same numbers under the labels pre1.7/pre.7/post.3; ttre+0.3 under safety(off); and ttre+0.5 at the default esprelength(0). Confirmed their untested caveat: esprelength(0) dies r(452). Found additionally that offset +0.3 also dies r(452) at esprelength(2) while +0.5 and +0.7 run, because the shifted _t must land on exact binary integers -- the bypass path is a floating-point lottery.

title: The esfixedbaseperiod pre/post refusal degrades to a bare Stata r(2001) under safety(off)
surface: safety(off) / esfixedbaseperiod pre-post screen (ado:908)
claim: The named r(459) at ado:908 ("cannot find sufficient pre- and post-treatment periods for the treated units") is gated on the working safety value; with safety(off) the whole block is skipped and the run dies later with Stata's generic "insufficient observations", r(2001), naming no wooldid concept.
observed: Block (B): every treated unit's onset set to its first observed period. Default safety -> "Error: cannot find sufficient pre- and post-treatment periods for the treated units." r(459). Same call with safety(off) -> "insufficient observations", r(2001).
expected: A crash rather than a wrong number, so low severity; recorded because the assignment asks what each bypass actually unlocks, and here it is an uninformative error rather than the informative one. sthlp:1209 lists "the realized relative-time range asserts" under "skips a check entirely" without saying what the skip produces.
refuter_note: The substance holds -- the named r(459) does degrade to a bare Stata error under safety(off) -- but the stated rc is wrong, and it is not a single rc. On my panel the degradation lands on r(198) 'invalid syntax' with esprelength(2) espostlength(2) or esprelength(1) espostlength(1), and on r(461) 'no observations in subpop() subpopulation' with no ES window options at all; the report's r(2001) is a third variant. The rc therefore depends on the options rather than on the bypassed guard, so 'degrades to r(2001)' should not be written into a ticket. Worth noting that r(198) 'invalid syntax' is materially worse than either r(2001) or r(461): it tells the user their syntactically valid command is mistyped and sends them hunting through their own do-file for a typo that does not exist. Severity stays low -- it is a crash, not a wrong number.
refuter_did: Own 60-unit panel with every treated unit's onset set to its first observed period, run under esfixedbaseperiod. Four legs: default safety with esprelength(2) espostlength(2) -> named r(459) 'cannot find sufficient pre- and post-treatment periods for the treated units'; same call + safety(off) -> r(198) 'invalid syntax'; default safety with no ES window options -> the same named r(459); same + safety(off) -> r(461) 'no observations in subpop() subpopulation'. A fifth leg with esprelength(1) espostlength(1) + safety(off) also gave r(198).

title: The replay-staleness guard is unreachable for exactly the failure class it was written for, and the user gets an error about a command line they never typed
surface: replay branch ado:26-46 (WOOLDID_LASTRC / NFRPL-01/02) interacting with post-regression failures
claim: The replay branch at ado:26 is gated on `if `"`0'"' == "" & "`e(cmd)'" == "wooldid"`. A post-regression failure sets e(cmd)=reghdfe, which falsifies the guard's own gate, so the designed staleness refusal (NFRPL-01/02, documented in the 20-line comment block at ado:27-46) fires ONLY after failures that did not damage e(), and never after the failures that did. This contradicts the design that comment states.
observed: Same rc, two different diagnoses, and the user cannot tell the classes apart. After a PARSE-stage failure (`wooldid y unit year onset, attt`), typing bare `wooldid` gives the designed message: 'Error: the last wooldid call failed with r(198); the stored results predate that failed call. Refit wooldid before replaying.' (r198). After a POST-REGRESSION failure (`contreat(dosep) contreatcontrols(untreatedZero)`, r322), typing bare `wooldid` instead falls through to the worker and gives 'Error: command line input should feature all of y i t ttre; too few variables specified.' -- r(198) about a command line the user did not type, at the moment when the stored results have actually been destroyed. The designed message only becomes reachable again after a manual `est restore` of a pre-stored good run (verified: replay then prints 'the last wooldid call failed with r(322); ... Refit wooldid before replaying.').
expected: The staleness marker WOOLDID_LASTRC is a shell-level global set on EVERY failed invocation (ado:81), so the branch could be gated on it alone. The author's own comment says the guard exists because 'while it is set, the stored e() results predate the user's latest (failed) attempt, so redisplaying them silently would be misleading' -- a premise that is strictly more true, not less, when e() has been overwritten by reghdfe. The guard should therefore be reachable at least as often in that case.
refuter_note: The three measured facts are true (gate is empty-line AND e(cmd)=='wooldid'; a post-regression failure sets e(cmd)=reghdfe; the designed message therefore fires only after failures that left e() alone). The FRAMING, the SEVERITY and the proposed REMEDY are all wrong. (a) It does not contradict the design the comment states. The branch is a REPLAY branch and its job is to refuse a misleading REDISPLAY. With e(cmd)=reghdfe there is nothing to redisplay -- entering the branch would print a reghdfe model as a wooldid table, which is what the gate exists to stop. The guard is not 'unreachable for exactly the class it was written for'; it is moot in a state where its function cannot arise. (b) 'An error about a command line they never typed' is not a misdiagnosis: SEC4d shows a bare `wooldid' in a virgin state, with no marker and no wooldid result ever, returns the identical r(198) 'too few variables specified'. It is the generic invalid-call error, identical in a fresh session. (c) The remedy they propose -- gate on WOOLDID_LASTRC alone -- is wrong, and SEC4e pins the state that breaks it: with e(cmd)=regress (results the user deliberately put there) and the marker set from any earlier failed wooldid, a marker-only gate would answer bare `wooldid' with 'the stored results predate that failed call' about a regress model, and would hijack the generic invalid-syntax error for every later bare `wooldid' in that session. (d) It is not an independent defect but a symptom of HV-EPOST-01, demonstrated directly by SEC4c: put valid wooldid results back into e() and the gate fires with the designed message carrying the post-regression rc. Fix HV-EPOST-01's hold/restore and HV-EPOST-02 disappears. Severity low: one less-informative error message at a moment when an error is already the correct response. Note also that the guard's real message defect runs in the OPPOSITE direction -- see NF-SKEP-02, where it calls complete, valid results 'stale'.
refuter_did: probeA sections SEC4, SEC4b, SEC4c, SEC4d, SEC4e on my own panel. SEC4: after a post-regression r(322), bare `wooldid' -> 'Error: command line input should feature all of y i t ttre; too few variables specified.' r(198) -- reproduces. SEC4b: after a parse-stage r(198), bare `wooldid' -> the designed message 'Error: the last wooldid call failed with r(198); the stored results predate that failed call. Refit wooldid before replaying.' -- reproduces. SEC4c: after the same post-regression r(322), `est restore good' then bare `wooldid' -> 'the last wooldid call failed with r(322); ... Refit wooldid before replaying.' SEC4d: the test they did not run -- I dropped the marker, ran `reg y x1' (e(cmd)=regress, a VIRGIN state in which no wooldid had ever succeeded) and typed bare `wooldid': it gives THE SAME r(198) 'too few variables specified'. SEC4e: with e(cmd)=regress and WOOLDID_LASTRC set, I recorded the state their proposed remedy would act on. I also read the guard at ado:26-46 and the shell's marker writes at ado:79-81, 174, 180, 271, 293, 301, 398, 401, 454, 482, 503, 513.

title: customweightmultiplier() silently reweights the treatment cells, so att_it / att_i / att_itime stop being the estimands their help entries define
surface: customweightmultiplier() x att_it / att_i / att_itime
claim: With customweightmultiplier(v), att_it is not "the simple, unweighted mean of all of the cohort-period-specific estimates" (sthlp:220-221) but a mean of those estimates weighted by sum_cell(w*v)/sum_cell(w) -- i.e. by v itself when v is constant within the cell. The same holds for att_i (sthlp:227) and att_itime (sthlp:234). No message names the substitution, and no option combination recovers the documented estimand in the same run.
observed: 8 counties (4 staggered adopters, 4 never), 10 years, 5 establishments per county-year with establishment weights, pop = 1 for six counties and 50 for two treated ones (an ordinary 50:1 spread). No cwm: att 2.7147886, att_it 2.74890010, att_i 2.9520313, att_itime 2.9518714; e(gteffects) w_att_it is 1 in every cell; att_it equals the simple mean of the cells exactly. With customweightmultiplier(pop): att 3.7412488, att_it 3.74381423, att_i 3.8071510, att_itime 3.8078950; w_att_it runs 1..50; per-cohort w_att_i totals are 1,1,50,50 instead of 1,1,1,1. The reported att_it is exactly the pop-weighted mean of the (unchanged) cells, 3.74381423, and is 36.2% away from the documented estimand 2.74890010. att and att_it now differ by 0.07% (3.7412 vs 3.7438), so the package's own weighted-vs-equal-cell heterogeneity contrast reads "insensitive" when the true equal-cell number is 27% lower. Mechanism verified against a raw-data oracle: the w_att_it column equals sum_cell(w*v)/sum_cell(w) to <=2.9e-16 in five arms, including v varying WITHIN the cell (cell weight = the w-weighted mean of v, 0.655-1.616) and v as a 0/1 subpopulation indicator (cell weight = the within-cell share, 0.20-0.86). Code: customweighttext = '* v' (ado:1581) enters the NUMERATOR of all four estimand weights (ado:1630,1637,1644,1650) while W_it = total(esamp*w) by(i,t) (ado:1619) and W_i = total(w*esamp) by(posttreatment,i) (ado:1620) are built from the sample weight alone. Secondary, measured (repro ARM D, v = pop*1.15^year): because W_i is by(posttreatment,i), the pretreatment att_i row and the main att_i row weight the cohorts differently -- per-cohort shares .008400/.009057/.479530/.503014 (main) vs .007422/.008119/.463144/.521315 (pretreatment), an 11.6% relative change for cohort 1 -- so the placebo row printed above the estimate is not the same weighted functional. The only user-facing signal is 'Note: all Estimates Shown Apply pop Weights Post-Estimation' (ado:11369/11529), which reads as confirmation of what was requested. e(gteffects)'s weight columns are honest (the sthlp:1136 identity reproduces every aggregate at <=4.8e-16), so a user who requests gteffects and reads the weight column can see this; a user who does not, cannot.
expected: The att_it / att_i / att_itime entries should cross-reference customweightmultiplier() and say it reweights the cells (respectively the cohorts), and the runtime note should name the estimands whose definition it changed. The expectation holds because sthlp:220-221/226-227/232-234 state the estimand as a simple unweighted mean with no caveat, while sthlp:218 tells only the att reader that the multiplier applies and sthlp:1107 says the estimand weights are 'multiplied by this variable' -- three entries that cannot all be true at once, and the one a user reads to CHOOSE an estimand is the one that is false. NOT proposed as the fix: renormalizing (w*v/sum_cell(w*v)). That would make v an exact no-op on att_it in a binary design and would destroy a real, otherwise unreachable estimand -- cells weighted by v with sample weights acting only within the cell, which is exactly what separates arm B's att_it (3.7438) from arm B's att (3.7412). The defect is the silence, not the arithmetic.
refuter_note: The ARITHMETIC is confirmed exactly: the cell weight is sum_cell(w*v)/sum_cell(w) (oracle match 3.7e-16 with a cell-constant v, 2.1e-16 with a within-cell-varying v); att_it moves 2.1660737 -> 3.0353185 under cwm(pop) on my panel. But three load-bearing parts of the claim are false. (1) 'No option combination recovers the documented estimand in the same run': in the cwm arm the simple unweighted mean of e(gteffects)'s estimate column over relyr>=0 is +1.1541e74632e42X+001 = 2.1660737126, BIT-IDENTICAL to the no-cwm run's reported att_it. gteffects -- an option the prober himself ran -- returns the documented estimand exactly, in the same run. (2) 'No message names the substitution': the runtime note 'Note: all Estimates Shown Apply pop Weights Post-Estimation' fires and says ALL estimates shown, accurately; and sthlp:1107 -- 'the weights normally used to produce the requested type of treatment effect (ATT, ATT_i, etc.) will be multiplied by this variable' -- names ATT_i explicitly and describes ado:1644 verbatim (the normal att_it weight is w/W_it; with the multiplier the code writes w*v/W_it). The code calls the mechanism documented at its second implementation site: wooldid_ptp (ado ~10404) rebuilds the same weight and comments 'cell totals use the raw weight, without any custom weight multiplier - the documented asymmetry'. (3) 'att and att_it now differ by 0.07%, so the heterogeneity contrast reads insensitive': an artifact of the prober's panel. On mine the gap WIDENS under cwm, 4.6% (2.2656 vs 2.1661) without to 5.7% (3.2087 vs 3.0353) with. The SECONDARY claim (att_i's pretreatment row weights cohorts differently from its main row under a time-varying multiplier) is refuted as cwm-specific: the DEFAULT att estimand already does this with no multiplier anywhere and a constant sample weight, at per-cohort POST/PRE share reldif .1506/.0324/.1185 -- LARGER than the 11.6% the prober attributes to cwm -- and at .1854/.0118/.1568 with a time-varying sample weight, while w_att_i's reldif is exactly 0 in both those arms and in the constant-cwm arm. The pre and post blocks span different periods, so any weight not constant within a cohort-block gives them different cross-cohort shares; a time-varying cwm merely moves att_i into the class att was always in. WHAT SURVIVES: sthlp:218 (att) carries the multiplier caveat while sthlp:220-221/226-227/232-234 (att_it/att_i/att_itime) state their estimand with no caveat and no cross-reference. That asymmetry inside the help is real and is worth one clause in each of the three entries -- a MISSING CROSS-REFERENCE, not a silent substitution. Severity medium -> low. Free confirmation while I was in there: a constant multiplier is an exact hex no-op on all four estimands and every SE, as it must be.
refuter_did: Built my own panel (14 counties, 10 years, 4 establishments/county-year, staggered onsets, 6 never-treated, pop 1..40) and ran four arms: A no cwm, B customweightmultiplier(pop), S a CONSTANT multiplier, D a time-varying multiplier. Compared e(gteffects)'s w_att_it column against a raw-data oracle sum_cell(sw*v)/sum_cell(sw), and compared the reported att_it against both the v-weighted and the simple unweighted mean of the cells. Separately ran an event-study set (r2_pre_and_missing.do, arms E1-E4) to test the secondary pre-row claim, with no-cwm controls carrying a time-constant and then a time-varying SAMPLE weight. Also read sthlp:218/220-234/1107 and ado:1581/1619/1620/1630/1644/1650/10404/11369.

title: At cluster() == i the MDT appears to deliver its 80% power only because the joint pre-trend test rejects 28% of the time under the null
surface: pretrendpower() -- mdt_wald/bias_wald and the Roth slope CI under cluster() at or above i
claim: On the at-i geometry (i = unit, cluster(unit)), the reported mdt_wald(80) achieves 0.80 rejection against the nominal cutoff and would pass a naive check, but the test's size there is 0.28; against a size-corrected 5% cutoff the same trend has power 0.46-0.51. The honest summary of that column is the (size, power) pair, not the power alone.
observed: 80-unit staggered panel, i = unit, cluster(unit), AR(1) errors, df_r = 79, 250 null replications: joint pre-trend F(3,79) rejects at 5% in 70/250 = 0.2800 CP95 [.2253,.3401]; the empirical 95th percentile of the null statistic is 2.158x the nominal critical value; Roth slope 95% CI coverage 213/250 = 0.8520; mean reported pre-period variances are 0.43-0.68 of their MC counterparts; m'S^-1 m is 367.8 reported vs 220.3 MC, so the reported MDT is 0.774x the covariance-implied one. 220 replications at the reported mdt_wald(80) = 0.16971: nominal-cutoff power 175/220 = 0.7955 CP95 [.7360,.8467]; size-corrected power 101/220 = 0.4591 CP95 [.3919,.5274]. The self-contained repro (150+150 reps, independent seeds) gives size 0.2800, nominal power 0.8333, size-corrected 0.5133.
expected: The MDT is documented as the trend detectable with the requested power by a 5%-level test. The run does print the at-i caution here, so the user is warned about the joint test's p-value -- but the caution says nothing about the detectable-trend columns, and those columns carry the same defect silently. The measured pair (0.28, 0.46) is what the column means on this design; an author checking only 'achieved 0.7955 against a claimed 0.80' would conclude the column is fine.
refuter_note: Two reasons to downgrade. (1) The magnitude does not replicate: on an independent at-i panel I get size 0.1000, not 0.28, so 0.28 is a property of their particular panel rather than of the at-i geometry. (2) What remains is a ruled item. known_bydesign.md section 1: 'Joint pre-trend / adversarial tests are oversized at or above i — 11-36% rejection at nominal 5% (G=40) ... Computed anyway with a named caution, in BOTH jointtests and pretrendpower() (PS-64/BS-9 as amended, 2026-09-07).' My 0.1000 at G=60 sits at the bottom of that ruled band, and the prober concedes the caution fires on this design — so this is rediscovery. Of my measured 0.100, SKP-NEW-1's estimated-covariance effect already accounts for 0.0562, so the at-i degeneracy contributes less than half. The one piece that is neither ruled nor rediscovery is a wording gap: the caution names the joint test's p-value only, while mdt_wald, bias_wald and roth_slope_ll/ul are built on the same covariance and printed without qualification — low, and covered more generally by SKP-NEW-1. CAVEAT: I did not diagnose WHY their panel gives 0.28; I measured a different at-i panel and did not vary theirs.
refuter_did: PART2 of s5_ex7_ati.do: 150 null replications on my own at-i panel (60 units, i = unit, cluster(i), AR(1) rho=0.5, T=12, staggered onsets 6/8/10 plus never-treated, esfixedbaseperiod esprelength(3) espostlength(2)), computing the joint pre-trend statistic from e(b_es_att)/e(V_es_att) and referring it to F(3, e(df_r)) exactly as wooldid does. Result: df_r=59, size 0.1000, GLS slope 95% CI coverage 0.8933, reported se / MC sd 0.8121. The ideal-model prediction of SKP-NEW-1 at k=3, df_r=59 is 0.0562, printed by the same do-file.

title: The requested event-study PRE window shifts the headline ATT by 5-11% through the reference-normalization pool
surface: esprelength(), espostlength()
claim: Changing esprelength() alone — with the data, estimand, VCE and e(N) unchanged — moves the reported att by up to 11%, because the reference-normalization pool is defined as the rows with relyr < -esprelength. espostlength() alone moves nothing. Two options that read as horizon display requests silently reprice the headline number.
observed: ds_canon, cluster(region), e(N)=480 and e(escomp_trtN)=192 throughout: no window -> att 1.0952323 (refN .); esprelength(1) espostlength(1) -> 1.1650189 (refN 96); esprelength(2) espostlength(3) -> 1.1045313 (refN 72); esprelength(3) espostlength(3) -> 1.0732189 (refN 48); espostlength(3) alone -> 1.0952323, bit-identical to the windowless run (refN 120). ds_unbal: .8591239 -> .9153002 -> 1.0297713 -> 1.0480560 as esprelength goes 0/1/2/3 (refN 81/62/44/30), and espostlength(3) alone leaves it at .8591239. Detected automatically by probe_ident.do's eswindow arm (worst relative move .1145 on unbal, .0519 on canon).
expected: This is sthlp:1370's rule doing exactly what it says and the numbers are correct for the sample each window implies — my zero-noise oracle reproduces the design truth to 1e-15 under both windows once the truth is recomputed on e(sample). So it is not a computation defect. It is filed because nothing at the point of use says it: esprelength() and espostlength() are described as horizon counts, the only reading note on the subject (sthlp:724) is about a different nuance (the pretreatment row), and a user comparing specifications will read a 11% swing in the headline ATT as a substantive finding. An author ruling is needed on whether a one-line caution belongs on esprelength().
refuter_note: The falsifiable half is true - esprelength() alone does move the reported att - but the causal framing 'silently reprices the headline number' is wrong. Whenever the specification is right the att is invariant to esprelength to 1-3 ulp and equals the design truth exactly; the only zero-noise design that moves is coarse-i aggregation on an unbalanced panel with unit heterogeneity, where the movement is pre-existing bias being reduced, not repricing being introduced. On noisy data the moves are inside a third of one SE, and the SE rises with the window exactly as the efficiency cost of spending pre-rows on lead dummies predicts. The rule is already stated at sthlp:1370. This is a request for a one-line caution on esprelength(), so severity medium -> low.
refuter_did: Ran the discriminating test the prober did not: four ZERO-NOISE designs in which the estimand is exactly identified and every pre-treatment effect is identically zero, sweeping esprelength(0/1/2/3). (A) balanced, homogeneous, i=unit: att = 2.0000000000 at every window, truth 2, hex differing in the last 1-2 ulp. (B) unbalanced with 25% interior gaps, dynamic ramp, i=unit: 3.2312252964 at every window, truth 3.2312252964. (D) same unbalanced dynamic design at i=cohort with NO unit heterogeneity: 3.2312252964 at every window. (C) the only mover - unbalanced, dynamic, i=cohort WITH unit fixed effects: 3.1568625983 -> 3.2103142551 -> 3.2289702229 -> 3.2381576431 against truth 3.2312252964, i.e. the narrow window is the BIASED one and the estimate walks monotonically TOWARD the truth as the window widens. (E) noisy (sd 1.0, 150 units, cluster(i)): 3.2328 -> 3.2399 -> 3.2791 -> 3.2114 with se 0.0942 -> 0.1049 -> 0.1345 -> 0.1504, largest move 0.35 SE and relative moves 0.2%-1.4%, with the SE rising monotonically as the reference pool shrinks.

title: Reversing the sort order of the data moves analytic SEs in the 8th significant digit
surface: HDFE projection path / analytic SEs
claim: An otherwise identical call after `gsort -i -t` (or after relabelling the unit ids, or after rescaling y) returns identical point estimates but SEs, t, p and interval endpoints that differ by up to 2.6e-8 relative; regtol(12) and regtol(13) do not shrink it.
observed: Metamorphic arm, 125 pairs: point estimates invariant to 1e-16 everywhere; three pairs moved derived columns — P0076 (sortrev, att robust controls(x1) esprelength(3) level(90) [aw=fwt]): se .0496413102955201 -> .0496413089998644, t -2.361831204036994 -> -2.361831265681627 (2.61e-8 relative); P0052 (idperm, customvce(cluster region) + subgroups(sgtiny) + jointtests): 1.5e-8; P0016 (yscale): 2.53e-9. probe_regtol.log: at regtol 9, 12 and 13 the rescaled-y point estimate matches to 1.11e-16 while the t column still differs by 1.32e-9, so the tolerance knob does not move it.
expected: Bit-identical results, since none of these transforms changes the estimation problem.
